lessons.title: Why this program exists — and why you cannot fix yourself
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
From the very beginning, God has been reaching toward His people. Every covenant He has made — with Adam, with Noah, with Abraham, with Israel, with David — tells the same story. God initiates. He draws near. He provides the way. And again and again, the people He loves discover that they cannot sustain their own obedience without Him. This program exists inside that same story. You are not the first person to have arrived at the end of their own resources. You are not the first person to have discovered that the life they built without God has a ceiling — and that the ceiling is lower than they thought. The entire Scripture is full of people who arrived exactly where you are and found that the God who made them was still there, still reaching, still able to do what they could not do for themselves. "We love him, because he first loved us." — 1 John 4:19 KJV That is the foundation of everything in this curriculum. Not your effort to reach God. His love reaching you. Not your decision to get better. His decision to provide the way. The twelve steps that follow are the road of response — the obedience of a person who has received love they did not earn and is now walking toward the God who offered it.

The God who has always initiated toward His people is not a force or a concept — He is one God, one Spirit, one LORD, making Himself known by name across all of Scripture.

HOW MAN DIAGNOSES — AND WHERE THE DIAGNOSIS FALLS SHORT

Man has always tried to explain the condition. The explanations change with the century. In one generation it is a moral failure — the person is weak, lacks character, has made poor choices. In another generation it is a disease — the person has a condition, a brain chemistry, a genetic predisposition. In another it is a trauma response — the person is wounded, reacting, surviving.

Every one of these frameworks contains something true. And every one of them stops short of the root.

The moral failure framework is right that choices matter and wrong that better choices are within easy reach of a person who has been bound. The disease framework is right that the condition has physical dimensions and wrong that medication and management are the deepest available answer. The trauma framework is right that wounds drive behavior and wrong that healing the wound is sufficient to change what the wound produced.

None of these frameworks have a category for what the Scripture names as the actual problem: the flesh. Not weakness. Not illness. Not damage. The flesh — the nature that governs the person who is living outside of God's governance — and the bondage that the flesh, operating without the Spirit, inevitably produces.

The flesh produces what it produces. It has always done so. And no framework that begins below the level of the spirit can address what begins there.

Scripture does not use the word disease to describe what sin produces. It uses the word flesh — a nature that governs the person who is living outside of God's governance. Flesh is not a medical condition to be managed with the right program. It is a spiritual condition that can only be addressed by a spiritual answer: a new birth, from above, of water and of the Spirit. Every other framework stops at the symptom. The Scripture goes to the root.

HOW GOD DIAGNOSES — AND WHAT THE ANSWER REQUIRES

Before the sound of John 3:8 can be fully understood, one question must be addressed — because it will arise and it deserves an honest answer.

Some people will say: I was born this way. The appetites, the patterns, the drives that led to the bondage — they say these were present from birth, written into who I am. Not a choice but a condition.

Let this be granted for a moment.

If it is true — if the flesh and its patterns are present from natural birth — then what Jesus said to Nicodemus applies with more force, not less.

"Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." — John 3:3 KJV

If you were born one way — and that way produces what it has produced — then the answer is not management of what you were born with. The answer is a new birth. A different kind. Born again — from above — of water and of the Spirit.

What the first birth produced, the second birth addresses at the root. The argument that you were born with these patterns is not an argument against this program. It is the clearest argument for it. What natural birth produced requires supernatural birth to address.

"Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again." — John 3:7 KJV

Jesus did not say you might benefit from being born again. He said you must. Not suggested. Required. And every person who comes honestly through this curriculum will arrive at that requirement — not as a demand imposed from outside, but as the conclusion the honest road produces.

"The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." — John 3:8 KJV

God asks the question twice in the same chapter. He does not ask it to be harsh. He asks it because the question contains the answer. If the first birth produced the condition, the new birth addresses it. That is the diagnosis. And this program is the road of honest preparation for it.

From the very beginning of the covenant story, God does not merely describe Himself. He names Himself. And what God does with His name across all of Scripture is worth paying attention to — because the pattern does not end with the Old Testament.

"And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." — Numbers 6:27 KJV

God did not say: they shall put a title upon them. He said: my name. The blessing follows the name. Not the effort. Not the attendance. Not the performance. The name placed upon the person.

This is a thread worth following all the way through.

WHO THIS PROGRAM IS FOR

This program is written for anyone whose life has become unmanageable because of a substance or a behavior they cannot control. Alcohol. Opioids. Cocaine or crack. Methamphetamine. Heroin. Marijuana. Prescription drugs — painkillers, benzodiazepines, stimulants. Combinations of these. Behavioral addictions that operate through the same mechanism.

The substance or behavior is not the root. The Scripture addresses the root — which is the same across every substance, every behavior, every person: the flesh governing what God was designed to govern. The specific substance is the branch. This program addresses the tree.

If your substance is here — and it is — you are in the right place.

"Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God." — Galatians 5:19-21 KJV This curriculum is not just a drug and alcohol program. It is a program for the works of the flesh. That list is long and it is varied. Drunkenness is on it. So is wrath. So is strife, envy, self-deception, and the pride that occupies the throne that belongs to God. The person who has never touched a substance but has spent a lifetime in anger, bitterness, or hidden sin is in the same program as the person whose substance use brought them to a visible crisis. The flesh is the problem in every case. The works differ. The root is the same. This program is not only for those in visible collapse. It is equally for those who are functional, stable, and outwardly composed — whose sin is private, whose bondage is internal, whose performance of faithfulness has never been interrupted by a consequence others could see.

This program does not begin at a person's best. It begins at the honest bottom — and Scripture shows consistently that the bottom is precisely where God has always chosen to appear.

"Woe to them that are at ease in Zion." — Amos 6:1 KJV The warning is not to the person in obvious wreckage. It is to the person who is comfortable — settled in the appearance of faithfulness, undisturbed by the slow accumulation of compromise no one else can see. The person at ease in Zion is in greater danger than the person in crisis, because the crisis at least creates conditions for honesty. "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves." — 2 Corinthians 13:5 KJV Every participant — regardless of background, history, or what brought them here — undergoes the same honest self-examination. There is no hierarchy of sin in this program. Pride and self-righteousness are not lesser offenses than public addiction. Hidden compromise is not more acceptable than visible failure. The examination is the same. The love that meets us in the examination is the same. And the God who does the work is the same. This is not behavior management. It is not image correction. It is the pursuit of genuine inward transformation — beginning with honesty about what is actually there.

If you are reading this while something in you is pulling toward what you know has destroyed you — this program was written for exactly that person.

Not the person who has it together. Not the person who has already decided they are done. The person sitting with the pull right now, today, who picked this up because they are out of other options.

That is the right place to begin.

The pull you feel is real. It is not a character defect, a weakness of will, or evidence that you are beyond help. It is evidence of exactly what Step 1 names: you are powerless over this thing. The pull is proof of the problem — which means it is proof that the program is addressing the right problem.

Read on. The road is longer than today's feeling. And the God this program is about has been waiting at the end of the road since before you started walking.

UNDERSTANDING HOW SCRIPTURE SPEAKS — THE LANGUAGE OF METAPHOR

Before entering the lessons that follow, there is something essential about how the Scripture communicates. The Bible is not a collection of flat, literal statements. It speaks in metaphor — in images drawn from the physical world that carry truths about the spiritual world that plain language cannot reach. Understanding this is not an academic exercise. It is a survival skill for the person working this curriculum. The Scripture uses physical images to carry spiritual weight because the deepest truths are too large for simple declarative sentences. When the Bible says trees, it often means people. When it says water, it often means life or the Word or the Spirit. When it says darkness, it often means the condition of a life without God's light. This was not accidental — it was deliberate. Jesus spoke almost exclusively in parables. The prophets spoke in images. The wisdom literature is saturated with them. Here are ten metaphors the Scripture uses that the recovery road will illuminate again and again:

TREES AS PEOPLE

"Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly... he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season." — Psalm 1:1-3 KJV Trees in Scripture often represent people — their character, their rootedness, their fruit. When Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree, he was above the crowd — elevated in position, disconnected from the level ground of honest encounter with Jesus. When Adam hid among the trees of the garden, the image holds a deeper layer: hiding among people who gave him cover for what he had done — pointing to others, saying "they do this or that, so what I did is reasonable." The trees become the justifications. The hiding is not physical — it is relational and psychological. "Everyone does this." "I am not as bad as them." The trees of other people's behavior become the cover for our own.

WATER AS LIFE, WORD, AND SPIRIT

"Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst." — John 4:13-14 KJV

Water in Scripture carries multiple layers simultaneously: physical life, the Word of God, and the Spirit. The woman at the well understood the conversation to be about the water she carried. Jesus was describing what He alone could give. The person who returns to the same sources — the substance, the relationship, the behavior — returns thirsty again. The water that does not run dry is not drawn from the same well as what they have been drinking.

FIRE AS GOD'S PRESENCE AND PURIFICATION

"For our God is a consuming fire." — Hebrews 12:29 KJV Fire in Scripture is the presence of God — burning without consuming what it does not condemn (the bush), or consuming entirely what is placed before it (the sacrifice). Refinement requires fire. The dross rises to the surface under heat. The things that cannot survive the fire are not the real thing — and the fire reveals this. The person in recovery is in the fire. What is rising to the surface is the material that needed to come up.

SALT AS COVENANT AND PRESERVATION

"Ye are the salt of the earth." — Matthew 5:13 KJV Salt in the ancient world preserved what would otherwise decay. A covenant "salted" was a covenant that would not corrupt over time. When Jesus called His disciples the salt of the earth, He was describing their preserving function in a world subject to decay. The person in recovery who finds genuine covenant relationship with God becomes a preserving presence — not immune to the decay around them, but a force that slows it rather than accelerates it.

THE VINE AND BRANCHES AS ABIDING AND DEPENDENCY

"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." — John 15:5 KJV The branch does not generate its own sap. It receives what the vine provides and produces fruit as a result of the receiving. The branch that is cut off does not produce less fruit — it produces none. And it begins to die. The person who has been living cut off from the source has been producing the fruit of a branch without a vine: nothing sustainable, nothing genuine, nothing that lasts past the next season. The reconnection to the vine is not improvement — it is restoration of the relationship that made fruitfulness possible.

LEAVEN AS HIDDEN INFLUENCE

"The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened." — Matthew 13:33 KJV Leaven works invisibly. You cannot see it working. But it changes everything it touches, thoroughly and irreversibly. In Galatians, Paul uses leaven as the image of small compromise that infiltrates the whole: "a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump." The one reservation in the Step 3 surrender. The one resentment left unaddressed in Step 4. The one omission in Step 5. What seems small is not small — it is leaven, working through everything it has access to.

THE LAMP AND LIGHT AS UNDERSTANDING AND CONSCIENCE

"The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly." — Proverbs 20:27 KJV

The lamp or candle in Scripture is often the capacity for honest self-examination — the spirit of man that God uses to illuminate what is hidden in the inner life. The inventory of Step 4 is a lit lamp taken into rooms that have been kept dark. What has lived in the dark has not ceased to exist because it was dark. The light reveals it. And what is revealed can be addressed.

THE FOUNDATION AS WHAT THE LIFE IS BUILT ON

"And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock." — Matthew 7:25 KJV The storm does not reveal the quality of the house — it reveals the quality of the foundation. Two houses can look identical through years of good weather. The storm is what shows which one was built on sand. The life in active addiction has often produced a presentable surface over a sand foundation. The steps are not the house — they are the process of discovering what the foundation actually is, removing the sand, and allowing God to lay what will hold through the storms that come.

THE YOKE AS GOVERNING AUTHORITY

"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me." — Matthew 11:28-29 KJV A yoke is a governing instrument. It determines the direction, pace, and purpose of what wears it. The person in active addiction wears a yoke — it is just not the yoke Jesus is describing. The addiction is the yoke. The shame is the yoke. The fear is the yoke. The labour and heaviness Jesus speaks to is the labour of carrying a governing authority that was never designed for the person wearing it. The exchange He offers is not freedom from governance — it is freedom from the wrong governor.

THE WEDDING GARMENT AS PREPARED READINESS

"And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless." — Matthew 22:11-12 KJV The man was at the wedding — in the right place, present at the right event. But he was not wearing what the event required. Presence at the right location is not the same as being prepared for what happens there. Many people in recovery are in the right place. They are attending. They are present. The question the curriculum raises is whether they are wearing what the event requires — the garment of genuine inward transformation rather than the clothing of appearance. The man was speechless because he had no answer. He knew.

THE FOOL'S CONFESSION

"The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." — Psalm 14:1 KJV The fool is not necessarily an atheist. He is a person who lives as though God is not the governing reality of their life — who has built a life that, in practice, requires no God to function. Every decision made without reference to God. Every strategy for managing the problem developed independently. Every plan for recovery built on what the self can produce. Most people who arrive here have lived as the practical fool without intending to. Not because they rejected God consciously but because the pull of the flesh is strong enough that it gradually became the operating system — the thing that actually made decisions — even while the belief remained verbal. The honest work begins here: not with God somewhere far off requiring you to earn your way back, but with the recognition that He has been present the whole time — and that the life built without Him has produced exactly what a life built without Him produces.

NO MAN CAN TAME THE TONGUE

"For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." — James 3:7-8 KJV If the tongue — the smallest member — cannot be tamed by human effort, what makes anyone believe the deeper appetites can be? The habits of decades. The patterns inherited from childhood. The ruts worn so deep that the wheel goes there automatically without a decision being made. James is not writing to unusual people. He is writing to people who have already received the message of the gospel and are walking in the life it produces. And even for them, the tongue is the remaining evidence that human effort has a ceiling. This is not said to discourage. It is said to diagnose accurately. The ceiling on human effort is not the end of the story. It is the beginning of the real one — the one where what is impossible for man becomes possible for God.

THE LEOPARD AND THE SPOTS

"Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil." — Jeremiah 13:23 KJV The question is rhetorical. No. The person accustomed to evil cannot simply decide to do good. The pattern runs too deep. It is not a matter of information or intention — the person who knows what is right and wants to do what is right still finds themselves doing what they have always done. But the question Jeremiah asks is not the last word. The God who cannot change the leopard's spots is not the question. The question is what the God who made the leopard can do. And that question has an answer that runs from Genesis to Revelation: He makes all things new. He gives a new heart. He puts a new spirit within. He does what the leopard cannot do for itself.

This is the pattern Scripture shows from beginning to end: God initiates, love reaches first, and the human response is always a return to what was already being offered.

WHERE THIS PROGRAM LEADS

This is not a self-improvement program. It is not behavior management. It is not image correction. It is the pursuit of a genuinely transformed life — the kind that begins with honesty about what is actually there, proceeds through the obedience that God has always required, and ends at a destination the person at Step 1 cannot yet see. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — 2 Corinthians 5:17 KJV New. Not improved. Not managed. New. That is what is available to the person who walks this road honestly. The twelve steps are not the source of that newness — they are the road that leads toward the God who is.

This program does not end with better behavior. It ends with a new identity — the identity of a person who has been genuinely transformed at the source, not merely managed at the surface. That is what is available. That is what the road leads toward.

The road that follows is not self-improvement. It is the road toward the God who makes all things new — and the steps are the honest preparation for what He alone can do.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ 1 John 4:19 KJV — "We love him, because he first loved us."

■ Psalm 14:1 KJV — "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God."

■ Jeremiah 13:23 KJV — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil."

quiz.question: According to 1 John 4:19 KJV what is the foundation of our love for God — and what does this say about how the program begins?
choices: Our decision to pursue recovery — the program begins with our choice to get better
We love Him because He first loved us — the program begins with love already given, not with our effort to earn it
Our recognition of the problem — the program begins when we understand the damage
Our willingness to change — the program begins with sufficient motivation
quiz.explanation: 1 John 4:19 — we love Him because He first loved us. The program does not begin with human effort reaching toward God. It begins with God's love already having reached toward us. The response — the twelve steps of obedience — is the road of response to love already given.

quiz.question: According to Psalm 14:1 KJV what does the fool say in his heart — and what does this reveal about how the addiction operated?
choices: The fool denies God exists — only atheists qualify as fools in this passage
The fool hath said in his heart there is no God — meaning he lived as though God were not the governing reality, even while believing verbally
The fool acts without thinking — describing impulsive behavior rather than heart condition

The fool trusts in himself — describing self-reliance as a primarily financial error Psalm 14:1 — the fool says it in his heart, not necessarily his mouth. The practical fool has built a life that operates without God as the governing reality — even if God is acknowledged verbally. Most people in active addiction did not reject God consciously. The flesh simply became the operating system while the belief remained verbal.

quiz.question: According to Jeremiah 13:23 KJV what does the leopard illustration say about the possibility of self-generated change?
choices: Change is possible with sufficient effort and the right environment
Some people cannot change but others with less severe patterns can
The person accustomed to evil cannot simply decide to do good — the pattern runs deeper than decision

Change requires time — the leopard analogy describes how slow the process is Jeremiah 13:23 — can the leopard change his spots? The question is rhetorical. No. Self-generated change at the level of deep-rooted patterns is beyond human capacity. This is not pessimism — it is accurate diagnosis. The ceiling on human effort is not the end of the story. It is the beginning of the question: what can the God who made the leopard do?

quiz.question: According to 2 Corinthians 5:17 KJV what does God produce in the person who is in Christ — and why does this matter for recovery?
choices: Improved behavior — a better version of the existing person
Managed sin — old patterns reduced to acceptable levels
A new creature — old things passed away, all things become new. Not improved. New.

Restored relationships — the primary evidence of the new creature is repaired connections 2 Corinthians 5:17 — written by Paul to born-again believers, describing what the new birth produces. Not improvement. New creation. The twelve steps are not the source of this newness — they are the road that leads toward the God who is its author. The destination is transformation that originates outside the person.

The honest starting place
1. Read 1 John 4:19 every morning this week before you do anything else. Write one sentence each day about what it means that love came first.
2. Write honestly — for your eyes and God's only: what pattern in your life has proven to be beyond your own ability to change? Not a general answer. The specific thing.

lessons.readingPlan:
Week 1 Day 1 — 2 Corinthians 5:14-21 What does it mean to be a new creature? What old thing do you most want to see passed away?
Week 1 Day 2 — Psalm 127:1-5 Where have you been building without God? What did that cost you?
Week 1 Day 3 — Romans 7:14-25 Paul describes the war inside himself. Does this sound familiar? Write honestly.
Week 1 Day 4 — Romans 8:1-11 What is the difference between walking after the flesh and walking after the Spirit?
Week 1 Day 5 — Galatians 5:16-25 List the works of the flesh. Circle the ones that have been part of your story.
Week 1 Day 6 — John 8:31-36 "The truth shall make you free." What truth have you been avoiding?
Week 1 Day 7 — Lamentations 3:19-33 What gives Jeremiah hope in verse 21-23? What does that mean for you?

lessons.title: The nature of sin — what the Word actually says
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Before the law was given, before the prophets spoke, before the covenant was written on stone — God already knew what was in the heart of man. When He looked at the earth in Noah's day, He saw that "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). This is not a new diagnosis. It is the oldest diagnosis. And every covenant God has made since then has been, in part, an answer to this condition. The program you are entering is not offering something apart from the covenant relationship with God. It is pointing toward the same God who has been addressing the same problem since the beginning — the problem of a human heart that, without Him, moves consistently away from what it was made for. Understanding what the Word actually says about sin is not meant to condemn. It is meant to diagnose accurately. An accurate diagnosis is an act of love. A physician who softens the diagnosis to protect your feelings is not helping you. The God who tells the truth about what is in the human heart does so because He has already provided the remedy — and the remedy only works if the diagnosis is accepted.

THE WORLD'S DIAGNOSIS

The world has given many names to what brought you here. Disease. Disorder. Trauma response. Chemical dependency. Genetic predisposition. None of these are entirely wrong about what they describe. The brain does change under sustained substance use. Trauma does shape patterns. History matters. But these explanations have a ceiling. They can describe the condition. They cannot cure it. They can name what is happening in the brain. They cannot reach what is happening in the heart. And this program — along with every covenant God has ever made — begins at the heart.

This program does not begin at a person's best. It begins at the honest bottom — and Scripture shows consistently that the bottom is precisely where God has always chosen to appear.

THE SCRIPTURE'S DIAGNOSIS

"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" — Jeremiah 17:9 KJV The prophet Jeremiah, writing in the Old Testament under the old covenant, identified the root that the new covenant was being designed to address. Not behavior. Not circumstance. The heart — the inner person, the source of every decision, the seat of every desire — is the starting place of the problem.

The world has built an entire culture on the opposite instruction.

"Follow your heart." It is in the movies, the graduation speeches, the love songs, the self-help books. It is the organizing principle of the age. The culture does not say: examine your heart, submit your heart, or ask whether your heart is right. It says follow it. Trust it. Obey it.

Consider the songs that have carried this message into every generation:

Frank Sinatra sang "My Way" — and an entire century decided that doing it your own way was the highest aspiration a person could have. Every decision made on the basis of "I want" rather than "God wills" is that song lived out.

"Follow Your Heart" — the title alone is a doctrinal statement. The Isley Brothers sang it. Whitney Houston sang it. Motown made it a movement. Pop culture handed it to every teenager who ever wanted permission to ignore what they knew was right.
"Listen to Your Heart" — Roxette. "I Gotta Be Me" — Sammy Davis Jr. "Express Yourself" — Madonna. "Born This Way" — Lady Gaga. "Do What You Feel" — the working title of a hundred albums across a hundred years of music that told people the self is the authority, the heart is the compass, and anyone who tells you otherwise is oppressive.
"Can't Help Falling in Love" — the heart takes over and the person simply cannot help what it does. Accountability is surrendered to feeling.

The world has been singing the same song since the garden — and the song is always some version of: trust yourself, follow yourself, be yourself, express yourself, do it your way.

Scripture answers with a different song entirely.

"The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation." — Exodus 15:2 KJV

Moses sang this after the crossing of the Red Sea — after the impossible had happened, after the pursuing army was gone, after the people stood on the other side of what they could not have crossed on their own. The song was not about what they had done. It was about what God had done. He is become my salvation. Not I found my way. Not I trusted my heart. God became the salvation. And God is the song.

"The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped." — Psalm 28:7 KJV

Not: my heart led me. My heart trusted in Him. There is a surrender in that sentence that the culture's version of the heart has never accepted. The heart is not the leader. The heart is the trusting organ. And what it trusts determines everything that follows.

Jeremiah 17:9 does not call the heart evil and leave the person without a solution. It calls the heart deceitful — and then two verses later, in verse 14, writes: "Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise."

The heart that cannot lead itself can be healed. That is what this program is building toward.

The addiction did not begin with the first use. It began in the heart — in the place where something other than God was given the worship that belongs only to God. The substance or behavior became the answer to a question the heart was asking. And the question the heart was asking was the same one it has always asked: where is my peace? Where is my relief? Where is my satisfaction? What will finally be enough? Those questions are not wrong questions. They are the right questions aimed at the wrong source.

WHAT DRIVES THE FLESH

"Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like." — Galatians 5:19-21 KJV Paul wrote this to people in the churches of Galatia who were born-again believers under the New Covenant — describing the patterns of the flesh they were still capable of if they walked away from the Spirit. The list is long and varied. Drunkenness is in it. So is wrath, envy, strife, and idolatry. Not ranked by severity. Not graduated by how visible the damage is. All of them are works of the same flesh. All of them originate in the same place. The person who has never struggled with substances but has lived for years in wrath and bitterness is on the same list. The person who has never raised a hand in violence but has maintained envy and strife is on the same list. There is no hierarchy here. There is only the flesh — and what it produces when it governs — and the Spirit, and what He produces when He governs.

DRUNKENNESS, PHARMAKEIA, AND THE CALL TO SOBRIETY

The Greek word translated witchcraft in Galatians 5:20 is pharmakeia — the use of substances, historically tied to practices that invited spiritual influence outside of God, but more broadly pointing to anything that alters the mind and opens a person to what God does not control. Alongside it sits drunkenness. Both deal with altered states — conditions where the person's discernment is weakened, where the governing capacity of the spirit is diminished, and where the door is left open to what was

never meant to enter. "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour." — 1 Peter 5:8 KJV Peter wrote this to born-again believers — people who had received the Spirit and were now being instructed in how to maintain the protection it provides. Sobriety is not a religious rule. It is the defensive posture of a person who understands what they are in the middle of. The adversary is not indiscriminate. He is strategic. He looks for the exposed position — the clouded mind, the lowered guard, the person who has yielded control of their awareness to something other than God. "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." — Ephesians 5:18 KJV The contrast could not be more direct. Paul wrote this to people in Ephesus who had received the Spirit — showing them the two directions available to the yielded life. You are under one influence or the other. The same capacity for yielding that once made you vulnerable to what the flesh craved is the same capacity that — redirected toward God — makes possible the filling the steps are building toward.

THE BODY IN EARLY RECOVERY

The body of the person in early sobriety is undergoing a real physiological transition. The nervous system that was regulated by a chemical is now being asked to regulate itself without it. Sleep is disrupted. Emotions are amplified. Appetite changes. The physical craving arrives with the urgency of hunger because, to the body that was trained on the substance, it is hunger of a kind.

This is not weakness. It is the physical reality of a vessel that was given over to chemical governance and is now being reclaimed.

"What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." — 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 KJV

The body matters. Its recovery matters. The physical struggle of early sobriety is not beneath the notice of the God who made the body — it is seen, it is understood, and it is part of what the program is addressing at every level.

If the physical withdrawal is severe, medical support is appropriate and is not a failure of faith. God can work through a physician as readily as through a pastor. The program begins with honesty — including honesty about physical need. Seek medical care if it is needed. Then come back to the program.

The physical transition does not last forever. The body normalizes. The sleep returns. The emotions stabilize. What feels unbearable in the first weeks becomes manageable in the first months — not because the person tried harder, but because the body was given time and the Spirit was given access.

GOD IS A SPIRIT

"God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." — John 4:24 KJV Jesus said this to a Samaritan woman — at a well, in the middle of her ordinary day, in the middle of a conversation about her specific and complicated personal history. He did not require her to clean up first. He did not require her to resolve the things she had lived through. He offered her living water before she had asked for it. God is not a concept. He is not a philosophical principle. He is not a higher power defined by whatever the person seeking him needs him to be. He is a Spirit — living, present, responding. And He fills what is genuinely surrendered to Him. What once occupied the mind and body — the substance, the behavior, the pattern — must be replaced by the Spirit who was always intended to fill it.

SIN AS IDOLATRY — THE WORSHIP PROBLEM

The addiction was never primarily a substance problem. It was a worship problem. Something took the throne. That something promised what only God can deliver — relief from pain, escape from pressure, a moment of peace, a feeling of adequacy, the sensation of being enough. And it delivered a version of those things — a version that degraded over time, that required more to produce less, that eventually consumed what it had been feeding on.

SIN AS BONDAGE — NOT MERELY BEHAVIOR

"Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." — John 8:34 KJV Jesus said this in the temple — to people who considered themselves Abraham's seed, already free. He was not describing people who had given up on religion. He was describing people who were actively religious and genuinely sincere — who had not yet understood that the sin they were managing was managing them. The servant of sin does not choose servitude consciously. The service begins with the first yielding — the first time the appetite was given what it demanded — and deepens with each subsequent yielding until the choice that once felt free no longer feels like a choice. What began as a decision becomes a disposition. What began as a

behavior becomes a bondage. "For sin shall not have dominion over you." — Romans 6:14 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Rome — announcing what the new life makes possible: sin does not have to govern. The dominion of sin over the life is not permanent. It is the condition of the person who has not yet received what God promises to those who walk in His covenant. The deliverance from the dominion is as specific as the bondage was — not a general improvement but a genuine transfer of governance from the sin that was managing the life to the God who created it. Addiction is not merely habit. It is not merely pattern. It is bondage — the specific spiritual condition of a person whose will has been yielded, over time and repeatedly, to something other than God, until the yielding became automatic. The twelve steps do not address this condition at the behavioral level. They address it at the level of the yielded will — redirecting what was yielded to the sin toward the God who can govern what the sin was governing.

THE DEATH THAT PRECEDES THE NEW LIFE

"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." — John 12:24 KJV The old life — the life governed by the flesh, the life organized around what the sin required — must die before the new life can grow. Not be improved. Not be managed more carefully. Die. The kernel that does not die abides alone. It produces nothing. The kernel that falls into the ground and dies produces fruit that the living kernel never could. Every person who arrives at this program has experienced some version of that death — the collapse of the life that was built around the addiction, the failure of the strategies that maintained it, the moment when what was being held together could no longer be held. That death is not the end. It is the ground. And what grows from the ground of that honest death is the fruit that John 12:24 promises — the much fruit that the living kernel, protecting itself above ground, never produced. "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." — 1 John 5:21 KJV John wrote this as the closing line of his first letter to born-again believers. The idol does not have to be a carved image. It is anything that receives the worship — the reliance, the trust, the daily seeking — that belongs to God alone. Recovery is not just the removal of the idol. It is the restoration of rightful worship. The throne that the addiction occupied was never meant to be empty. It was made for God. And the program works toward the day when what once sat on that throne has been cleared — and what was always meant to sit there has been received.

GOD EXAMINES THE HEART — NOT THE OUTWARD APPEARANCE

"But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." — 1 Samuel 16:7 KJV The performance of recovery — the attendance, the vocabulary, the improved behavior visible to others — is what people around you will assess. God is not assessing the performance. He is looking at the heart underneath

it. The motivation. The hidden reservation. The area of the life still being protected from full surrender. This is not a threat. It is a gift. The God who looks at the heart sees past every presentation to what is actually there — and loves what He sees enough to address it directly. The honest person has nothing to fear from the examination. The person performing recovery is the one who should be concerned.

SIN SEPARATES FROM GOD — THE DISTANCE THE ADDICTION CREATED

"But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear." — Isaiah 59:2 KJV The spiritual dryness most people in active addiction have experienced — the prayer that seemed to go nowhere, the attempt to connect with God that encountered what felt like a wall, the sense that God was far away or absent — is explained here. The iniquities created the separation. Not God's rejection but the barrier of unresolved sin standing between the person and the face of God. The barrier is real. And it can be removed. The steps that follow are the systematic dismantling of that barrier — the clearing of what stood between the person and the God who has been present the entire time, waiting for the return that Isaiah 59:20 describes: "the Redeemer shall come to Zion, and unto them that turn from transgression." The return is always met.

THE YEARS THE LOCUST ATE — AND WHAT GOD SAYS ABOUT THEM

There is a grief specific to addiction that is different from other kinds of grief.

It is the grief of having been the author of the loss. Not something that happened to you — something you did. The years spent in the far country were your years. The relationships damaged were your relationships. The children who grew up while you were somewhere else, the marriage that did not survive, the career that was not built, the version of yourself that did not exist — these losses are real, and they belong to the category of grief that has no external person to blame.

This grief is not the same as guilt. Guilt is about what was done. This grief is about what was not done — the life that was not lived because the addiction was living it instead.

The Scripture does not ask you to perform resilience about this. Naomi did not. She returned from Moab having lost everything and said: do not call me Naomi, call me Mara, for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. She named the bitterness. God did not rebuke her for it.

And then — in the same book, in the chapters that follow — God restored.

"And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you." — Joel 2:25 KJV

The locust years are named by God. He does not pretend they did not happen. He acknowledges that something consumed what should have grown — and He promises the restoration of what was consumed.

This is not a promise that the past will be undone. It is a promise that what remains will produce more than what was lost — that the future will outgrow the grief of the past. That is the covenant of the God who restores.

The grief belongs in the room. It is not weakness to mourn what the addiction took from you. It is honesty. And when the mourning is honest — when it is named and brought before the God who already knows — the restoration has a place to land.

NO LOCATION OUTSIDE HIS REACH

"Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." — Psalm 139:7-8 KJV The far country of the addiction was not outside God's awareness. The worst night, the lowest moment, the place the person is most ashamed to name — He was there. Not approving. Not indifferent. Present. Knowing. And having known it completely, He has not turned away. The return is not the reestablishment of a connection that was severed. It is the turning of the face toward the One who never left.

This is the pattern Scripture shows from beginning to end: God initiates, love reaches first, and the human response is always a return to what was already being offered.

THE THREE CATEGORIES OF THE FLESH — SATAN'S UNCHANGING PLAYBOOK

"Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices." — 2 Corinthians 2:11 KJV

Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Corinth — establishing a principle that runs through every step of this program: the person who understands how the enemy works is not helpless against him. Ignorance is not humility. Naming the playbook is not paranoia. It is the honest assessment that Scripture itself demands — and the prerequisite for the armor that Ephesians 6 provides.

The devices are not new. They have not changed. And understanding them is the beginning of not being taken advantage of by them.

"For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world." — 1 John 2:16 KJV Every work of the flesh in Galatians 5:19-21 sorts into one of these three. They are not random categories — they are the precise three that Satan used in the garden of Eden and the same three he brought to Jesus in the wilderness. The playbook has never changed because it has never needed to. It worked in the garden. It has worked in every generation since. The lust of the flesh: the appetite-driven works — drunkenness, fornication, uncleanness. The body craving what was not designed to govern. The lust of the eyes: the desire-for-what-is-seen — covetousness, envy, the works that arise when someone else has what the self wants. The pride of life: the self-promotion works — strife, heresies, seditions — the patterns of a self that refuses to be governed by anything outside itself.

The inventory of Step 4 will show that the specific works of the flesh in your life trace to one or more of these three roots. Understanding which root is strongest in you is not academic — it is the identification of where the most persistent work of Steps 6 and 7 will need to happen.

This program does not end with better behavior. It ends with a new identity — the identity of a person who has been genuinely transformed at the source, not merely managed at the surface. That is what is available. That is what the road leads toward.

The road that follows is not self-improvement. It is the road toward the God who makes all things new — and the steps are the honest preparation for what He alone can do.

TEACHER NOTES

Foundation Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. The diagnosis must be honest and the love must be visible simultaneously. The goal is not to make students feel worse than they arrived — it is to give them an accurate picture of what is actually being addressed so that the remedy makes sense. An accurate diagnosis is an act of love. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER This lesson draws from the Old Testament prophets, the Gospels, and the Epistles — all in the same session. Help students understand that the co...

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ John 4:24 KJV - "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

■ Galatians 5:19 KJV - "Now the works of the flesh are manifest..." (memorize through verse 21)

■ Psalm 139:7 KJV — "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?"

■ 1 Peter 5:8 KJV — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour."

ASSIGNMENT

Diagnosis assignment Private assignment. 1. Write your honest diagnosis. What do YOU believe drove your addiction? Wound, want, or worship - or your own words. 2. What have you used to fill the void that God belongs in? 3. If God is a Spirit who can fill that void - what would have to change about how you approach Him? Due: Before lesson 4

quiz.question: According to Jeremiah 17:9 KJV where does the Scripture locate the root of the addiction — and why does this matter for recovery?
choices: In the brain — which is why medical intervention is the primary solution
In the behavior — which is why behavior modification is the core of recovery
In the heart — which is deceitful above all things and requires a transformation that originates outside the person

In the environment — which is why changing surroundings produces lasting change Jeremiah 17:9 — the heart is the root. Not behavior, not circumstance. The addiction did not begin with the first use — it began in a heart asking the right questions at the wrong source. Recovery that addresses only behavior without reaching the heart has a ceiling. The program is aimed at what is underneath.

quiz.question: According to John 4:24 KJV what is God?
choices: A being with a physical body
Three persons in one trinity
A Spirit

A general spiritual force without personal character John 4:24 - God is a Spirit. God is not three persons — He is one Spirit, one LORD, fully revealed in the person of Jesus Christ. The doctrine of a Trinity of three co-equal persons does not appear in the teaching of the apostles. Every baptism recorded in Acts is performed in the name of Jesus, not in the titles Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — because Jesus is the name in which those titles are fulfilled. Not a concept not a force not a committee of three. One Spirit. This is the foundation of everything that follows.

quiz.question: What does this curriculum identify as the root of addiction?
choices: A genetic predisposition
A neurological disease
A spiritual void - a wound a want or a misplaced worship
A lack of willpower Addiction is a response to pain emptiness and a God-shaped void filled with the wrong thing. The solution is not management but filling that void with the only thing that fits.

quiz.question: According to Psalm 139:7-10 KJV is there any location the person in addiction went that was outside God's reach?
choices: Yes — God withdraws from places of active sin
No — there is nowhere to go from His Spirit or flee from His presence
Only if the person was attending church during that time

God is present only where believers gather in His name Psalm 139:7-10 — whither shall I flee from thy presence? There is no coordinate on the map of human experience outside the reach of God's hand. The far country of the addiction was not outside His jurisdiction.

quiz.question: According to Ephesians 5:18 KJV what is the direct alternative to being drunk with wine?
choices: Sobriety — abstaining from all intoxicants as a matter of personal discipline
Be filled with the Spirit — the contrast is direct: you are either under the influence of the flesh or the Spirit
Prayer — replacing the desire for alcohol with the discipline of daily devotion

Community — surrounding yourself with people who do not drink Ephesians 5:18 — be not drunk with wine wherein is excess but be filled with the Spirit. The contrast is absolute. You are under one influence or the other. There is no neutral ground. The same capacity for yielding that makes a person vulnerable to drunkenness is the capacity that — when surrendered to God — makes the filling possible.

lessons.readingPlan:
Week 3 Day 1 — Galatians 5:16-26 List the works of the flesh vs the fruit of the Spirit. Where do you see the works of the flesh most in your story?
Week 3 Day 2 — Romans 8:1-17 What does it mean to be carnally minded vs spiritually minded? Which describes you today?
Week 3 Day 3 — John 4:1-26 The woman at the well had been trying to fill a spiritual need with people. What have you tried to fill yours with?
Week 3 Day 4 — Isaiah 55:1-7 Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? What have you spent yourself on that could not satisfy?
Week 3 Day 5 — Ephesians 2:1-10 Dead in trespasses and sins then made alive. What is the difference between managing sin and being made alive from it?
Week 3 Day 6 — 1 John 1:6-10 Walking in darkness vs walking in the light. Which describes your pattern with the truth?
Week 3 Day 7 — Psalm 51:1-17 David's prayer after his worst failure. What does he ask for? Notice he does not ask to manage better.

lessons.title: Pure and undefiled religion — knowing the real from the counterfeit
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Throughout the history of the covenant, God's people have struggled with a consistent danger — not the absence of religion but the presence of the wrong kind. The prophets did not write to people who had abandoned worship. They wrote to people who were worshipping incorrectly — who had the form of the covenant relationship without the substance of it. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, and Hosea all speak to a people going through the motions of religion while their hearts were far from the God they were ostensibly serving. This is not a problem unique to ancient Israel. It is the pattern of every generation. And it is likely a pattern many people in this room have personally experienced — not the absence of God, but an encounter with what claimed to be God and did not deliver what only God can give.

This lesson is not a criticism of any institution. It is an honest account of what the Scripture itself says — that defiled religion exists alongside pure religion, that the form can precede the power by many years, and that the person who encountered one should not conclude they encountered both.

WHAT THE WORD SAYS ABOUT RELIGION

"Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world." — James 1:27 KJV James wrote this to born-again believers — describing what genuine covenant relationship with God looks like in practice. Not ceremony. Not attendance. Not correct vocabulary. Active care for the most vulnerable, and a life that maintains its separation from the patterns of the world around it. Pure religion is active. It moves outward. It costs something. It is the overflow of a life genuinely changed at the source — not the performance of a life that has learned the appearance of change. The existence of pure religion implies the existence of its counterfeit. James would not have described pure religion if there were no impure version to distinguish it from. Both exist. The question is which one a person has encountered — and whether the encounter with the counterfeit has closed the door to the genuine article.

This program does not begin at a person's best. It begins at the honest bottom — and Scripture shows consistently that the bottom is precisely where God has always chosen to appear.

WHAT DEFILED RELIGION LOOKS LIKE

"Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away." — 2 Timothy 3:5 KJV Paul wrote this to Timothy — a young evangelist he was equipping to carry the gospel faithfully in a world where the form of godliness had become common. The form is real enough: the language, the building, the services, the expectation that consistent attendance and sincere effort will eventually produce what only God's power can produce. People come and people try. They are sincere. They want it to work. And then the real problem surfaces — something that cannot be managed by effort and vocabulary — and the form has no answer for it.
"For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears." — 2 Timothy 4:3 KJV
"Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth." — 2 Timothy 3:7 KJV

Not everyone who has encountered religion has encountered its power. Some have found a form that confirms what they wanted to believe. The curriculum is written for those who are willing to let the Word say what it says.

SINCERITY IS NOT ENOUGH — TRUTH IS ALSO REQUIRED

This is one of the most important distinctions in the entire curriculum. A person can be entirely sincere and entirely wrong at the same time. Sincerity is the condition of the heart — the genuine intention to reach God, the real desire for what He offers. Truth is the condition of the path — whether what is being followed matches what God has actually revealed. The person who sincerely followed a form without power was not insincere. They were sincere about the wrong thing. And sincerity about the wrong thing produces the same result as insincerity about the right thing: nothing. Paul wrote to the born-again believers at Corinth about keeping the feast — "not with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." — 1 Corinthians 5:8 KJV

Both are required. Sincerity without truth is the form without power — genuine feeling aimed at the wrong object. Truth without sincerity is the correct doctrine delivered by a corrupt heart — which is its own form of the same bondage — religion as flesh, not Spirit. This program requires both. Sincerity — the genuine, unhidden, unmanaged presentation of what is actually there. And truth — the Scripture as the standard, not the feeling, not the tradition, not what the person was told by people who had not received the real thing themselves.

"Thy word is truth." — John 17:17 KJV Jesus said this to the Father — identifying the Word as the standard by which sincerity is tested and truth is measured. Not the teacher's opinion. Not the program's tradition. The Word. And the Word, read honestly and completely, is what this curriculum is built on. The building is there. The music is there. The vocabulary is correct and the schedule is full. But when someone needs to be genuinely set free — when what is broken in the human heart reaches the surface — nothing is available to address it at the root. No what the covenant provides — the complete answer to what sin has cost. No Holy Ghost. No real transformation. Just attendance and advice. This is not said as an accusation toward any person or any church. It is the diagnosis Paul gave to a pastor he loved, concerning a condition that has existed as long as the gospel has been preached. Where the form is present without the power — wherever that is found — the people inside it are not being served by what they deserve. They deserve the real thing. "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." — 1 Corinthians 5:8 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Corinth — calling them to the feast of genuine covenant relationship conducted in sincerity and truth. Not the management of appearance. Not sincerity without truth. The feast of pure and undefiled religion — the real thing conducted with both sincerity and truth before God and before one another. That is what this program is committed to offering. Not the comfortable form that leaves the person unchanged. The sincere and truthful engagement with the God who actually has the power to do what no human effort can produce. The person who went through the experience of form without power and concluded that God cannot help them has drawn the wrong conclusion from accurate data. They are right that what they encountered did not help them. They are mistaken about what they encountered. What they experienced was a sincere effort conducted without the power that only obedience to the full covenant can provide. That is not God's limit. It is the limit of a form that stopped short of what God requires. The real thing is available. And it is still what it has always been — the same God, the same covenant requirements, the same promise to those who seek Him with all their heart.

WHY THE FORM ALONE CANNOT HOLD PEOPLE

The form without power cannot hold people because it cannot give them the one thing that sustains: the love of God experienced through genuine obedience. "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them." — Psalm 119:165 KJV The peace described here is not the absence of difficulty. It is the settled stability of the person whose love for God has expressed itself in obedience — the person who has not merely attended but genuinely loved and kept. Nothing shall offend them — not because life is easy but because the love relationship with God is genuine and the covenant is real. The person who only attended could be offended by any difficulty, any imperfection in the institution, any unanswered question. The person who loves the law of God and keeps it has a peace that does not depend on the institution's performance.

"If ye love me, keep my commandments." — John 14:15 KJV Jesus said this to His disciples in the upper room — the night before the cross, in the context of everything He was about to give them. The love He is describing is not an emotion first. It is an obedience first. The love that does not produce obedience has not yet become the love that Jesus is describing. And the religion that does not produce genuine obedience — that settles for the emotion of faith without its expression in the life — has given people something that will not sustain them when the difficulty comes. "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." — 1 John 5:3 KJV John wrote this to born-again believers at the close of his first letter — defining the love of God in terms of obedience. This is the love of God: keeping His commandments. Not grievous — not a burden imposed on an unwilling person but the natural expression of a heart that has been genuinely changed at the source. The counterfeit religion offers the emotion without the transformation. The genuine covenant produces the transformation that makes the obedience the natural overflow of a love that is real. This program is built on what 1 John 5:3 describes: the love of God expressed in the keeping of His commandments. Not attendance. Not vocabulary. Genuine love that overflows into genuine obedience — and produces the peace of Psalm 119:165 in the life that keeps it. "Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it." — Matthew 7:14 KJV More people would walk through these doors if this program offered what is easy to hear — a comfortable path, a message without cost, a recovery that requires nothing of the whole person. There are many such programs. They fill their seats. We will not offer that. The narrow way is not ours to widen. To offer false comfort to a person in genuine need is not compassion — it is a stumbling block dressed as mercy. We serve Him in sincerity and truth — and that means what this program offers is not the performance of change but the genuine article. God's requirements have not changed. They have never changed. And they are the only thing that actually works at the root. Therefore this program teaches what God actually requires — not because we are stricter than others but because a person in genuine need deserves what is genuinely true. We will not trade the truth of the covenant for the appearance of success.

WHY PEOPLE FALL AWAY FROM THE COUNTERFEIT

Most people who have encountered a form of religion and found it empty did not fall away from genuine covenant relationship with God. They fell away from a form that could not produce the transformation it promised. The people were sincere. The effort was real. But sincerity cannot manufacture what only God's power can produce. Mark describes it exactly: they received the word with gladness, but because they had no root, when affliction or persecution arose they immediately fell away. The form produced an emotional response. It could not produce a root. And without the root, the falling away was not evidence that God cannot help — it was the natural result of a form that had no power to plant anything that would hold.

"Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them." — Psalm 119:165 KJV "If ye love me, keep my commandments." — John 14:15 KJV "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." — 1 John 5:3 KJV This is what the counterfeit could not offer — not because it did not try, but because it lacked the power that makes genuine obedience possible. The Scripture's definition of love for God is keeping His commandments. Not the emotion of love. The obedience that love produces. And the God who is real — the God who possesses power, not merely form — is the One whose commandments, when kept, produce the great peace of Psalm 119:165. The person who has fallen away from a form without power has not yet met the God who can plant what will hold. This program is the road toward that meeting.

THIS IS NOT BITTERNESS

The person who understands that defiled religion exists is not a bitter person. They are an honest person. Bitterness would insist that all religion is defiled and no God is real. Honesty acknowledges that the counterfeit exists — and that the existence of the counterfeit is, paradoxically, evidence that the genuine article is worth counterfeiting. No one counterfeits something worthless. The fact that defiled religion puts up the appearance of the real thing testifies to the value of the real thing. The question is not whether to abandon the pursuit. The question is whether to pursue the genuine article with the same energy that the counterfeit absorbed. "And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart." — Jeremiah 29:13 KJV The promise is not to the casual seeker. It is to the person who searches with all their heart. The person who encountered what claimed to be religion and found a form without power has often tried it with something less than all their heart — reasonably so, because the previous experience had not earned the full investment. This program asks for the full investment not as a prerequisite to receiving but as the posture that positions a person to receive what God promises to the diligent seeker.

WHAT GOD STARTS HE FINISHES

"Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." — Philippians 1:6 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Philippi — expressing confidence in what God was doing in people who had genuinely been born again through obedience to the gospel. God does not begin projects He does not finish. Whatever the institution failed to provide — God has not failed. The moment of conviction that preceded this program, the something that would not let you stay comfortable in the old life, the drawing that brought you to this room — that was God's initiation, not yours. He began something. His commitment is to perform it until the day of Jesus Christ — the full length of a life, and beyond.

The program does not depend on the reliability of whatever institution may have disappointed you. It depends on the reliability of the God who started what He intends to finish.

This is the pattern Scripture shows from beginning to end: God initiates, love reaches first, and the human response is always a return to what was already being offered.

NOTHING TOO HARD FOR HIM

"Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." — Jeremiah 32:17 KJV "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?" — Jeremiah 32:27 KJV God asks the question twice in the same chapter. He is asking it of Jeremiah in the middle of a siege — in the worst possible external circumstances — and the answer reverberating through the situation is: no. Nothing too hard. Not statistically difficult. Not probably manageable with enough effort. Nothing too hard. The specific damage, the specific duration, the specific depth of the pattern, the specific wreckage of the years — none of it exceeds the capacity of the God who stretched out the heavens by His arm. The person who believes their case is the exception has never read Jeremiah 32. They are presenting a case they believe exceeds God's jurisdiction. It does not.

This program does not end with better behavior. It ends with a new identity — the identity of a person who has been genuinely transformed at the source, not merely managed at the surface. That is what is available. That is what the road leads toward.

The road that follows is not self-improvement. It is the road toward the God who makes all things new — and the steps are the honest preparation for what He alone can do.

TEACHER NOTES

Foundation Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. This is the most pastorally sensitive lesson of the preface. The majority of people in recovery carry genuine wounds from religious experiences — experiences that were sincere on their part and that produced nothing lasting. This lesson validates that experience completely and without hedging, while directing the student toward the distinction between the counterfeit and the real. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER The prophetic tradition of the Old Testament i...

■ 2 Timothy 3:5 KJV - "Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away."

■ James 1:27 KJV - "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

quiz.question: According to James 1:27 KJV what is pure religion and undefiled?
choices: Attending church every Sunday
A personal relationship with Jesus
Visiting the fatherless and widows and keeping unspotted from the world
Following all religious rules perfectly James 1:27 defines pure religion by its fruit - caring for the vulnerable and maintaining holiness. The Word calls it pure meaning a defiled version exists.

quiz.question: According to 2 Timothy 3:5 KJV what should we do with those who have a form of godliness but deny the power?
choices: Pray for them and stay
Correct them and wait
Turn away from them

Report them to leadership 2 Timothy 3:5 - from such turn away. This is a command not a suggestion. Form of godliness without power is dangerous because it gives the appearance of transformation without the substance.

quiz.question: What does the lesson identify as the primary reason many people tried church and still ended up in addiction?
choices: They did not try hard enough
God was not willing to help them
They encountered a defiled form of religion that lacked transforming power

They chose addiction over God deliberately Defiled religion - religion that has form but no power - cannot produce transformation. People who encountered it and failed did not fail God. They were given something counterfeit.

quiz.question: According to Jeremiah 32:17 and 27 KJV what is the answer to the question "Is there any thing too hard for me?"
choices: Yes — some situations exceed even God's capacity
No — nothing is too hard for the LORD, the God of all flesh
It depends on the person's level of faith

Only things that are humanly possible are possible with God Jeremiah 32:17,27 — God asks this question twice in the same chapter. The answer is no. Not statistically difficult, not probably manageable — nothing too hard.

quiz.question: According to Philippians 1:6 KJV what is God's commitment to the work He has begun in you?
choices: He will finish it if you remain faithful enough
He began it and will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ
He started it but your free will determines the outcome

The work is complete at conversion — maintenance is your responsibility Philippians 1:6 — He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it. Not might. Will. The finisher of the work is God, not the person doing the steps.
