lessons.readingPlan:
Week 4 Day 1 — James 1:19-27 James defines pure religion as active — visiting the fatherless and widows, keeping unspotted from the world. Write honestly: have you seen this kind of active, costly faith expressed? What did it look like?
Week 4 Day 2 — 2 Timothy 3:1-7 Paul describes people with a form of godliness but without the power. Read the list carefully. Have any of these patterns been present in your own life — not in others, in you?
Week 4 Day 3 — Matthew 23:23-28 Jesus describes the appearance of righteousness without its substance. What does the image of the whited sepulchre show about the difference between what is visible and what is real?
Week 4 Day 4 — Isaiah 29:13-14 God says this people draw near with their mouth but their heart is far from Him — and their fear toward Him is taught by the precept of men. What is the difference between a taught response to God and an encountered one?
Week 4 Day 5 — John 3:1-8 Nicodemus was a religious teacher who came to Jesus at night. Jesus told him something was still missing. What did Jesus say was required — and what does the wind analogy show about how it comes?
Week 4 Day 6 — Acts 2:1-21 Read the account of what happened when the new covenant became operative. What was heard? What was seen? What did Peter say this was the fulfillment of?
Week 4 Day 7 — Ezekiel 36:26-27 God promises a new heart and a new spirit put within His people — not behavior improvement but a new source. How is this different from what a program of attendance and effort can produce?

lessons.title: How to use this program — structure, journal, and daily reading
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Every covenant God has made has come with instructions — not to burden His people but to show them how to walk in what He has provided. The Law was not punishment. It was the gift of knowing how to live as the people of God. The commands of the New Testament are not demands imposed on reluctant servants — they are the instructions of a Father who knows the road and wants His children to walk it well. This program has structure. The structure is not the program — it is the container that holds the program while the real work happens. The daily reading, the journal, the scripture memory, the quizzes, the mentor relationship — none of these are the transformation. They are the conditions that make the transformation possible. God does the work. These disciplines create the daily availability for that work.

Give the structure the respect it deserves — not because it will save you, but because the God who is doing the saving has asked you to show up consistently and He meets consistency with what only He can give.

THE DAILY READING PLAN

Each lesson comes with seven daily readings — one for each day of the week. These are not optional supplements to the lesson. They are the lesson continuing into the daily life. The Sunday teaching reaches the mind. The seven daily readings reach the habit. Read the assigned passage. Write a response to the reflection prompt. Keep it honest. The journal is not an assignment to be graded — it is a conversation with God about what the passage is showing you today. The Word is in the morning before the phone. Not after the news. Not after email. Not when time permits. Before. The first act of the waking day is the declaration that what God says governs what the day will hold — before the day has made its demands, before the flesh has been given its instructions, before the world has filled the attention that belongs to God first. This is not a rule. It is the practical expression of what the preface has been establishing: He is first. Everything else comes after.

THE JOURNAL

Write honestly. Not what sounds appropriately spiritual. Not what a mentor should see. What is actually happening — what the passage showed you, what it unsettled, what it confirmed, what you want to avoid. God already knows what is in the heart. The journal is not for His benefit. It is for yours — the practice of naming what is actually true, which is the skill the entire program is asking you to develop. The person who journals honestly recovers at a different rate than the person who journals for appearance. The difference is not the writing. It is the honesty.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

The verses are not in the curriculum for decoration. They are there because the Word hidden in the heart is the Word that functions under pressure. When the temptation comes there will not be time to look it up. The person who has carried Psalm 139:23 in their chest reaches for it in the moment of need without thinking. The person who has it on their phone reaches for their phone — and the phone leads somewhere else. Memorize the verse this week. Write it until you can say it without looking. Then say it out loud. The words in the mouth have a different weight than the words in the eye.

QUIZZES AND STEP EXAMS

The quizzes test whether the lesson has been understood — not performed. A student who passes without understanding has only performed. A student who retakes and passes has done exactly what the program intends: the material was received, processed, and understood. The passing score for lesson quizzes is 70%. Step exams require 80%. Graduation requires 85%. These are not arbitrary — they correspond to the depth of understanding each phase of the program requires. You are not being tested. You are being formed.

THE MENTOR CONNECTION

The mentor is not the program. The mentor is the person further along the road who has agreed to walk beside you for the year. They are not there to approve or disapprove of your answers. They are there because the

confession of Step 5, the accountability of Step 10, and the posture of Step 11 all require another human being present. The person who tries to work the steps without a mentor is trying to do in private what the steps were designed to do in relationship. Some things do not happen in isolation. Name it when you feel resistance to the mentor relationship — because that resistance is usually protecting something that the program needs to reach.

The mentor relationship is most important at the worst moment — not the best one.

If you relapse during this program, the first call you make is to your mentor. Not when you have the right words. Not when you have been clean for a week and feel ready. The same day. The mentor is the person who answers that call and says: come back. Not: I am disappointed. Not: what happened? The first word is: come back.

The mentor has agreed to walk beside you for the duration — and the duration includes the falls. Any mentor who withdraws at the moment of relapse was not functioning as this program defines the role. The person further along the road who has agreed to walk beside you knows that the road has falls in it. They walked it.

A NOTE ON THE LANGUAGE OF THIS CURRICULUM

The Scripture this program uses is the King James Bible — and the King James Bible never uses the word "to morrow." It says "to morrow" or "on the morrow." This is not an accident. The fool of Proverbs 27:1 says "Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth." James 4:13-14 says: "Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city..." — and then identifies the person who speaks that way as the one who does not know what shall be on the morrow. This curriculum follows the same language of the Word: it does not speak of "to morrow" as a settled thing. The road is walked today. Today's obedience. Today's inventory. Today's surrender. The to morrow belongs to God.

ONE WEEK AT A TIME

The steps that feel impossible from the beginning of the program become possible one week at a time. Do not read Step 9 at Step 2 and decide it is more than you can do. You are not at Step 9. You are at Step 2. Step 9 will arrive when it is supposed to arrive — after Steps 3 through 8 have done what they do. Trust the process because the process is designed by the same God who is doing the work.

THE BURNING BUSH — GOD APPEARS IN THE BACK SIDE OF THE DESERT

"And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush: and he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." — Exodus 3:2 KJV Moses was in the back side of the desert. Not at the height of his influence. Not when his circumstances had improved. At eighty years old, tending sheep that were not his, in a wilderness he had been in for forty years — having fled from the life he was supposed to lead. That is where God appeared. Not in the temple. Not at the peak of the career. In the back side of the desert. In the ordinary work of the most unremarkable day. The person who believes God requires a better version of them before He shows up has the wrong picture. He appears in the back side of the desert. In the wilderness that resulted from the years of running. In the ordinary work of an ordinary day. The bush is burning right now. In this room. While you are tending these sheep.

HE ALREADY KNOWS — THE CONFESSION IS NOT NEWS TO GOD

"For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether." — Psalm 139:4 KJV Every word before it is spoken. Every thought before it forms. Every hiding place before you entered it. The confession of Step 5 is not informing God of something He has not seen. He was present for all of it — not approving, but present. Knowing. And having known it completely, He has not turned away. This is what makes honesty possible. You are not risking His discovery. He already knows. The confession is the person finally agreeing with what God has always seen — stepping out from behind the cover and standing in the

open before the One who already knew. That is not frightening. That is relief.

THE NAME HE PLACES UPON HIS PEOPLE

From the beginning of the covenant, God has placed His name on His people as the identifying mark of belonging. When He instructed the priests to bless Israel, He said: "And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." — Numbers 6:27 KJV The name was not ceremonial decoration. It was identity, authority, and belonging — placed on a person by the One who had the right to name them. Throughout the covenant history, being "called by His name" was the mark of the person who belonged to Him. The steps that follow trace how this naming principle develops across the whole covenant — from the old covenant where God named a place, to the new covenant where He names a people. Every lesson in this curriculum is the road toward the moment when that name is placed on a person in the way the new covenant provides. Carry this question through every step: what does it mean to bear the name of the One who made you?

TEACHING APPROACH AND FOUNDATION

"Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men: Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, even a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid." — Isaiah 29:13-14 KJV

This lesson is built upon the understanding that truth is not established by tradition, popularity, or the reasoning of man, but by the revelation and operation of God Himself through His Word.

This curriculum does not approach Scripture from a man-centered standpoint, nor does it seek to preserve religious tradition where it conflicts with the Word of God. The intent is not to present a version of the gospel that is softened, adjusted, or made agreeable to human understanding, but to present what God has spoken as it is written.

The warning given in Isaiah reveals that it is possible to speak of God, honour Him outwardly, and yet be governed inwardly by teachings formed by men. When doctrine is shaped by human reasoning rather than divine revelation, it produces a form without substance — words without the witness, and instruction without the operation of God.

In response to this condition, God declared that He would do a marvellous work and a wonder. This work is not the continuation of man's system, but the interruption of it. God makes the wisdom of man insufficient and brings forth truth in a way that cannot be produced, sustained, or explained by human understanding alone.

Therefore, this curriculum is structured with these principles:

Scripture will be presented as written, without alteration or reinterpretation to fit tradition.

Truth will be established by the consistency of the Word, not by external systems of theology.

The focus will remain on what God does, not on what man assumes or constructs.

Any teaching that originates from the precepts of men will be tested and measured against the Word of God.

The goal is not information alone, but alignment — bringing the heart, understanding, and doctrine into agreement with what God has revealed and what He continues to confirm.

For where truth is established by God, it carries with it not only clarity, but witness.

HOW TO READ THE BIBLE THIS PROGRAM USES

God does not change. "For I am the LORD, I change not." — Malachi 3:6 KJV But the way God has dealt with His people has progressively changed across time — the way a parent deals with a child differently as that child grows from infancy through adolescence into maturity. The character of the parent is the same. The terms of the relationship develop as the relationship deepens and the child becomes capable of more. This is called covenant. God has made and fulfilled a series of covenants across human history — each one building upon what preceded it, each one pointing further toward what was coming. Understanding this is not advanced theology. It is essential to reading the Bible correctly. And every lesson in this curriculum uses the Bible.

THE OLD TESTAMENT — PROMISE AND PROPHECY POINTING FORWARD

The Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets were given to a specific people at a specific time. They reveal the character of God, the nature of sin, the pattern of human failure, and the promise of what God intended to do about all of it. Every page of the Old Testament is pointing forward to something not yet arrived.

THE GOSPELS — THE ARRIVAL OF THE PROMISED ONE

Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John record the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. They are written in the New Testament — but the events they describe take place before the new covenant is in full effect. A testament does not become operative until after the death of the one who makes it. "For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth." — Hebrews 9:17 KJV Everything Jesus said and did in the Gospels was being spoken to people still operating under the old covenant, pointing toward the new one His death would establish. The Gospels are the bridge. The new covenant becomes operative after the cross.

THE BOOK OF ACTS — THE NEW COVENANT IN OPERATION

Acts is the only book in the Bible where you can watch the new covenant teaching of the Gospels become lived experience. It is the record of what actually happened when people responded to the message of what Christ had accomplished. What did genuine new birth look like? What did obedience produce? What did God do in response to the people who heard and obeyed? When Acts is read carefully, the pattern is consistent and testable. This is why the curriculum returns to Acts — particularly Acts 2, Acts 8, Acts 9, Acts 10, and Acts 19 — as the place where doctrine meets reality. Not what people believed in theory. What actually happened when they obeyed. And it happened the same way — across different people, different locations, different backgrounds — every time it is recorded.

Where the practice recorded in Acts differs from what a student has previously been taught, experienced in a church, or absorbed from tradition — the standard is Acts, not tradition. Not denominational practice. Not personal experience. Not what a sincere teacher told them years ago. The question is always: what actually happened? Acts is the record of what actually happened. This is the model.

THE EPISTLES — LETTERS WRITTEN TO BORN-AGAIN BELIEVERS

Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, and the rest of the letters were written by Paul, Peter, James, John, and Jude to people who had already entered through the obedience Acts records. When the epistles describe the Spirit bearing witness, the gifts operating, the daily walk of the filled life — they are describing the experience of people who had already responded to the message. The entry point is Acts. The ongoing life is what the epistles address. The epistles do not replace what Acts established — they build upon it.

This means when Paul describes being "in Christ," "buried with Him," "walking in the Spirit," or "born again," he is describing people who have already obeyed Acts 2:38 — not people who have only believed intellectually. His salvation language assumes the Acts 2:38 foundation. Reading Paul's epistles without this context is reading the second chapter without the first. The foundation is Acts. The epistles are the instruction for life built on that foundation.

REVELATION — FROM THE PERSPECTIVE OF WHAT IS COMING

The final book speaks from the vantage point of what God will ultimately accomplish — the completion of every covenant, the final restoration of all things, the permanent dwelling of God with His people. It is read in light of everything that preceded it.

SCRIPTURE INTERPRETS SCRIPTURE — THE AUTHORITY OF ACTS

There is a warning worth placing at the beginning of the hermeneutics section, before the rules are given.

"For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables." — 2 Timothy 4:3-4 KJV

Paul wrote this as a warning to Timothy about what would happen to those who approached the Word looking for confirmation of what they already wanted to hear. The person who comes to the Scripture looking for permission is not studying — they are shopping.

And earlier, in the same letter, Paul describes a class of people who are perpetually in contact with religious material but never arrive at the truth:

"Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth." — 2 Timothy 3:7 KJV

These are not people who rejected the Scripture. These are people who engaged it continuously — but without the Spirit of Christ, without honest submission, without the willingness to obey what they found. The engagement produced information. It did not produce transformation.

This is the failure mode the hermeneutics section exists to address. The rules for reading are not academic exercises. They are the guardrails that protect the student who is willing to let the Word say what it says — even when it says something different than expected.

The person who reads with honest submission will arrive at the truth. The person who reads with an agenda will always find what they were looking for.

"All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." — 2 Timothy 3:16 KJV This declaration leaves no room for selective application. All Scripture. Not the portions that are comfortable. Not the portions that confirm what was already believed before the text was opened. All of it — profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction. The word reproof here means to expose what is false, to bring what is hidden into the light of what is true. The Scripture is not only a source of comfort — it is the instrument by which false doctrine is identified and truth is established. Therefore this curriculum affirms without reservation that the book of Acts is not merely a historical record. It is an inspired and authoritative witness of how the message was first proclaimed and consistently received. The events it records are not isolated or random — they are repeated patterns across different people, different locations, and different circumstances, presented without correction, contradiction, or revision anywhere else in Scripture. The letters of the New Testament were written to audiences who had already responded to the message. These writings provide depth, instruction, and explanation for established believers — but they do not erase or redefine the foundational response already demonstrated in Acts. Silence in the letters does not negate what has been clearly and repeatedly established in the record. Sound reading of Scripture requires that Scripture interpret Scripture — that clear examples inform understanding, and that consistent patterns carry the weight they deserve. Where the Word of God reveals a

response that is repeated, preserved, and never corrected, it must be received as both descriptive and instructive. Any approach that accepts the outcomes of the early church while dismissing the pattern that produced them introduces an inconsistency that the text itself does not support. It does so not on the basis of what the Scripture says but on assumptions imposed upon it. This curriculum does not make that selection. Acts stands as a doctrinally relevant and authoritative record — providing not only the history of the early church but the God-ordained pattern of response to the message. Clearly revealed. Consistently demonstrated. Fully aligned with the whole of Scripture.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR EVERY LESSON IN THIS CURRICULUM

When a lesson uses an Old Testament passage it is pointing to a principle or pattern that runs through all of Scripture. When a Gospel passage is cited it is showing what Jesus established and promised. When Acts is referenced it is showing what obedience to that promise produced in real people. When an epistle is quoted it is describing the life of people who have already entered through obedience. This framework governs how every scripture is being used. Read it with this understanding and what might otherwise seem like disconnected verses from different parts of the Bible will be seen for what they actually are: one God, one story, one progressive covenant — pointing from the beginning toward the same destination. "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all." — Ephesians 4:4-6 KJV
lessons.readingPlan:
Week 2 Day 1 — Joshua 1:1-9 God told Joshua to be strong and courageous three times. What does God know about what Joshua was facing? What does He know about what you are facing?
Week 2 Day 2 — Psalm 119:9-16 How does a young man cleanse his way? What does taking heed according to the Word look like practically for you this week?
Week 2 Day 3 — Psalm 1:1-6 Describe the difference between the man in verse 1-3 and verse 4-5. Which describes your life right now?
Week 2 Day 4 — Proverbs 4:1-13 Get wisdom get understanding. What is the difference between information and wisdom? Where have you had information but lacked wisdom?
Week 2 Day 5 — Matthew 7:24-27 Two houses. Same storm. Different foundations. What is your foundation made of right now?
Week 2 Day 6 — Hebrews 4:12-16 The Word of God is a discerner of thoughts and intents. Has the Word ever exposed something in you that surprised you?
Week 2 Day 7 — Psalm 139:1-10 God knows every word before it is spoken and every thought before it forms. How does knowing He already sees everything change how you approach the honesty of Step 5?

WE ADMITTED WE WERE POWERLESS — WITHOUT HIM WE CAN DO NOTHING

lessons.title: We admitted we were powerless — and why that is not weakness but the beginning of wisdom
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
God has always moved toward people who are hiding.

In the first pages of Scripture, after the garden, a question is asked — not because the One asking had lost track of anyone, but because the person hiding needed to hear their own answer out loud: "Where art thou?" — Genesis 3:9 KJV

It is not an accusation. It is an invitation. The God who already knew where they were, what they had done, and what it had cost — asked anyway. Because the honest answer to that question was the beginning of every conversation with God that has ever mattered.

Step 1 is that answer. It is not the lowest point a person can reach. It is the first honest point. The person who arrives at Step 1 and says what is actually true about their condition is further along the road than the person who has been managing the appearance of everything being fine for decades. Every return to God recorded in Scripture starts at the same place: an honest accounting of what is actually true.

"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." — John 15:5 KJV Jesus said this to His disciples on the night before the cross — in the Gospels, the night before the new covenant was established in His blood. He told them plainly: without Me, nothing. Not less. Not less effectively. Nothing. The branch that is not connected to the vine does not produce less fruit. It produces none, and eventually it withers. This is not a criticism of the branch. It is simply what is true about branches.

Faith, in its biblical sense, is not agreement alone. It is belief that submits, trust that moves, and conviction that obeys. The Scripture does not present faith as the conclusion of an intellectual process — it presents faith as the beginning of a changed life. Every step that follows is an expression of obedient belief.

The God before whom this admission is made is not vague — He is one Spirit, one LORD, the same God who has met people at their lowest point across the whole of Scripture.

The admission of Step 1 is not merely a recovery statement. It is the beginning of what Scripture calls repentance — the honest acknowledgment that the life lived under self-governance has produced what it has produced, and cannot undo what it has done. Every step that follows is built on this admission.

Every person is living under a name — the name of something or someone that has governed their life. The addiction gave its own name to the person: failure, hopeless, beyond recovery, defined by what they have done. Step 1 begins the long work of finding out whose name actually belongs on a person — and whose name the life was built to carry.

THE FAR COUNTRY — WHERE GOD BEGINS THE WORK

The far country has a name in the story Jesus told. Not a city. A distance. A condition. The prodigal son — the name the story gives him simply means the younger son, the one who took his inheritance early and left — ended up in a far country, having wasted everything with riotous living.

Luke 15:13 KJV: "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

The far country is where everyone in this program has been — or is still coming from. It is not a geographic location. It is the condition of a person who has taken what was given, moved as far as possible from the father's house, and spent everything on what could not satisfy.

The far country has its own economics. Luke 15:14: "And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want." The spending is followed by the famine. This is always the sequence in the far country. What the flesh promises will satisfy eventually produces a famine — a want that the substance or behavior can no longer even temporarily address.

Luke 15:15-16: he hired himself out to feed swine — a Jewish young man feeding unclean animals, the lowest possible position — and he was hungry. No one gave him anything.

This is the condition that Step 1 addresses: having spent all, in want, in the lowest position, and no one giving. Not because the world has turned particularly cruel. Because the far country is simply the place where what was wasted cannot be restored by more of what wasted it.

Luke 15:17: "And when he came to himself..."

That is Step 1. Coming to himself. Seeing the actual situation without the management and the justification and the story that kept the reality at arm's length. The moment the son came to himself — not to a plan, not to a resolution, not to a decision to do better — but to himself — that is the moment the return became possible.

He was in the worst place he had ever been. And that was precisely where the turn happened. It has always been the far country, not the father's house, where people come to themselves. God does not wait for the condition to improve before He begins the work. He begins it in the far country.

THE CRAVING AS EVIDENCE OF POWERLESSNESS

Romans 7 contains the most precise description of addiction in the Scripture. Paul the apostle wrote it to born-again believers at Rome — describing a pattern that every person in this room will recognize:

"For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." — Romans 7:19 KJV

Read that again. The good that I would — the thing I genuinely want to do, the choice I have made at the level of intention — I do not do. And the evil which I would not — the thing I have decided I do not want — that I do.

This is not a description of a person who has not tried. Paul the apostle is describing a person who has tried — who has the intention, who has made the decision, who genuinely wants the different outcome — and still cannot produce it by effort alone. That is the experience of the addicted mind. The craving arrives and the intention is not sufficient to stop what happens next.

The craving, as painful and as shameful as it feels, is not evidence that you are uniquely broken. It is evidence of the mechanism Paul describes — the flesh operating against the will of the person who has not yet found the power sufficient to govern the flesh. And that mechanism has a solution. It is not try harder. It is not want it more. It is what the remaining eleven steps are built to lead toward.

"O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." — Romans 7:24-25 KJV

The deliverance is available. The road to it begins here — with the honest admission that the craving is real, the willpower is insufficient, and the help required is outside the self.

When the craving comes during this program: name it. Write it down. Tell your mentor. Do not manage it alone — the managing alone is what produced the history that brought you here. The craving is not the enemy of the program. The hiding of the craving is.

WHAT THE TEXT SHOWS

The branch does not apologize for needing the vine. It is a branch. The design requires the connection. A branch that understood its own nature would not strain to produce fruit through its own effort — it would abide. It would stay connected. It would receive rather than generate. Step 1 is the admission that the person has been operating as a severed branch — straining to produce through effort what only the connection can provide. That the life without God has produced exactly what a life without God produces. And that the person is done pretending otherwise.

TWO PARTS OF STEP 1

The prodigal son came to himself not at the height of his strength but in a far country, among swine, having spent everything. That is where the turn happened. That is where it has always happened.

Most people do the first part and never get to the second. The first part is the admission of powerlessness: I cannot control this. The second part is the admission about life: the life I built around the management of this has become unmanageable. The first admission is frightening. The second is devastating. And both are necessary, because the person who admits only the first has acknowledged a problem. The person who admits both has acknowledged that the entire operating system needs to change — not just the behavior that was most visible.

"And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father." — Luke 15:17-18 KJV The prodigal son came to himself. He did not come to a strategy, or to a resolution, or to a plan for doing better. He came to himself — meaning he stopped pretending. He saw his actual situation clearly, without the management and the justification, and what he saw was the truth. That moment of clear sight — that is Step 1. He did not wait until he had a plan. He did not wait until he was in better shape. He arose while he was still in the far country and started back.

THE FIRST STEP IS NOT THE WORST STEP

There is a fear that admitting powerlessness is the bottom — that saying I cannot control this means accepting defeat. It is the opposite. The admission of powerlessness is the removal of the last obstacle between the person and the help they actually need. The person who is still insisting they have this under control cannot receive help, because they have not acknowledged they need it. The prodigal son, in the moment he came to himself, was in a worse external situation than he had ever been. He was in a far country, hungry, among swine, having spent everything. And that moment — that worst external moment — was the turning point. He arose and came to his father. And when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck. The robe came upon arrival. The ring came upon arrival. The feast began upon arrival — not before, not in anticipation of a performance, but at the moment of the return itself. The welcome was not contingent on the quality of the speech the son had prepared. It was the response of a father who had been watching the road. Admitting powerlessness does not make the situation worse. It makes the return possible.

If you are in the first days or weeks of sobriety, your body is doing things you did not authorize. The physical experience of early recovery is real — disrupted sleep, amplified emotions, physical cravings that arrive with the insistence of hunger. This does not mean the program is failing. It means the body is recalibrating from what it was trained to depend on toward what it was designed for.

The program does not require the body to be comfortable to begin. It requires honesty. Begin where you are, in the body you have, with the struggle that is actually in front of you. That is the right starting place.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every covenant God has made: the admission of what is true is always the beginning of what becomes possible. God has never started with a person's strength. He has always started with their honesty.

Step 1 names the problem clearly: powerlessness, and an unmanageable life. Step 2 introduces the only sufficient answer to what Step 1 has exposed — the God who is able. The person who has honestly completed Step 1 is standing in exactly the right place to receive what Step 2 offers. THE WIND AND THE SOUND "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." — John 3:8 KJV Jesus said this to Nicodemus — a religious leader, a teacher of Israel, a man who came by night because he knew something was missing in what he had. Jesus told him what the new birth sounds like: the wind that cannot be seen or predicted, but whose sound is heard. Every genuine birth of the Spirit produces evidence that can be heard. This is not an advanced theological point. It is the first description Jesus gives of what the new birth is like. He does not describe it as a decision, a prayer, or a change of mind. He describes it as something that produces a sound — something whose presence can be heard by those who are present when it occurs. The person entering this program is beginning a journey that the steps are designed to clear the way for. What they are being cleared for will make a sound when it arrives. That is what the Scripture says. Keep that in mind as the journey proceeds.

The person who has honestly completed Step 1 is not defeated. They are positioned. For the first time, the door is open — because they have stopped pretending it is not there. What comes through that door is not their effort. It is God's response to their honesty.

Admitting powerlessness is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a question the next step is written to answer.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ John 15:5 KJV — "I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."

■ Luke 15:17-18 KJV — "And when he came to himself, he said... I will arise and go to my father."

ASSIGNMENT

The two admissions 1. Write your honest answer to Part 1: What specifically are you powerless over? Not a category — the specific thing or things that have demonstrated that you cannot control them through your own effort. 2. Write your honest answer to Part 2: In what ways has the life you built around managing this become unmanageable? Name at least three specific areas. 3. Read John 15:5 daily ...

choices: Less fruit than it could with the vine
Fruit only in favorable circumstances
Nothing — without Me ye can do nothing

Fruit through greater effort and discipline John 15:5 — without Me ye can do nothing. Not less. Nothing. The design of the branch requires the vine. This is not a moral judgment — it is the honest description of how the relationship between the created and the Creator was designed to work.

quiz.question: According to Luke 15:17 KJV what did the prodigal son do that made the return home possible?
choices: He developed a plan for doing better
He came to himself — he stopped pretending and saw his actual situation clearly
He waited until circumstances improved before deciding to return

He asked others for permission to go back Luke 15:17 — he came to himself. Not to a strategy. To himself — meaning he saw his actual situation without the management and the justification. That moment of honest sight, in the worst external circumstances of his life, was the turning point that made the return possible.

quiz.question: What are the two parts of Step 1 — and why are both necessary?
choices: Admitting the problem and committing to a solution
Powerlessness over the addiction and the unmanageable life — both are necessary because the first admits the behavior and the second admits the operating system
Identifying triggers and building coping strategies

Acknowledging the past and committing to a different future Two parts: powerlessness over the specific thing, and the admission that the life built around managing it has become unmanageable. The first acknowledges the problem. The second acknowledges that the entire way the person has been operating needs to change — not just the visible behavior.

Week 5 Day 1 — Romans 7:14-25 Paul describes wanting to do right and doing wrong anyway. Write a specific example from your own life where this exact pattern played out.
Week 5 Day 2 — Proverbs 16:16-20 Where has pride cost you the most? Be specific not general.
Week 5 Day 3 — James 4:1-10 Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord. What does that look like practically for you today?
Week 5 Day 4 — Psalm 139:1-24 God already knows everything about you. What does it mean that He knows and still wants to lead you?
Week 5 Day 5 — Luke 15:11-24 The prodigal came to himself. What was the moment you came to yourself? If you haven't yet - what would it take?

lessons.title: Without Him we can do nothing — understanding the flesh and why willpower has a ceiling
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
From the beginning of the covenant story, God's people have encountered the same problem: the gap between what they intend and what they do. The law given at Sinai was not given because Israel was capable of keeping it. It was given to reveal what they were not capable of — and to point them toward the One who would do in them what they could not do for themselves. Every prophet who followed Sinai told the same story: the people sincerely intended to obey, and the flesh consistently overrode the intention.

This is not a failure of determination. It is the honest description of what the flesh is and how it operates. Understanding it clearly is not an excuse — it is the accurate diagnosis that makes the right remedy possible.

The admission of Step 1 is not merely a recovery statement. It is the beginning of what Scripture calls repentance — the honest acknowledgment that the life lived under self-governance has produced what it has produced, and cannot undo what it has done. Every step that follows is built on this admission.

THE NATURE OF THE FLESH

"For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." — Galatians 5:17 KJV Paul wrote this to people in the churches of Galatia who had already received the Spirit — describing the ongoing internal conflict even in the life that has been genuinely changed. The flesh and the Spirit are contrary to each other. They pull in opposite directions. And the person who has only the flesh — without the Spirit — is not fighting a battle they can win through greater effort. They are fighting with one hand tied behind their back against an opponent that has had decades to learn every weakness. What the text shows: the conflict is real and ongoing. It does not resolve through willpower. It resolves through the Spirit's governance of the life. The person who understands this stops expecting determination to produce what only the Spirit can produce — and starts positioning for the Spirit instead.

The prodigal son came to himself not at the height of his strength but in a far country, among swine, having spent everything. That is where the turn happened. That is where it has always happened.

WHY WILLPOWER HAS A CEILING

"For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not." — Romans 7:18 KJV Paul is describing his own experience — not before the gospel, but in the ongoing reality of the surrendered life — showing that even the person who wills the right thing does not automatically find the ability to perform it. The will is present. The performance is absent. This is not moral failure. This is the honest description of the flesh. The will can intend. The flesh cannot sustain. The person who has tried to stop through determination alone knows exactly what Romans 7:18 is describing — the intention was genuine, the performance did not follow, and the gap between them produced shame that often drove the next use. The ceiling on willpower is not a character flaw. It is the design of the flesh. The answer is not more willpower. The answer is the Spirit who governs from within what the will cannot produce from without.

THE FLESH AND ITS PATTERNS

The addiction did not arrive fully formed. It was built — pattern by pattern, choice by choice — until the groove was worn so deep that the wheel went there automatically. The flesh learned. It established the pathway. And the pathway, once established, does not simply dissolve because the person decides it should. "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil." — Jeremiah 13:23 KJV The prophet Jeremiah, writing under the old covenant, identified the same ceiling Paul would describe centuries later under the new. The person accustomed to evil cannot simply decide to do good at the level that actually changes the deep pattern. The depth of the groove exceeds the reach of the decision. This is not hopelessness. It is accurate diagnosis. And the accurate diagnosis points directly to the answer: the God who changes what human effort cannot change.

WHAT TRAINED THE FLESH — THE TRIGGER PATTERN

The flesh was not only broken from birth — it was trained. The addiction built grooves in the body and mind through repetition: this situation produces this feeling, and this feeling was relieved by this substance. The groove is real. It does not disappear when the substance stops.

This is what the recovery community calls a trigger. The Scripture calls the underlying principle the flesh being provoked by what it was trained to respond to — the association between a state, a place, a person, or an emotion and the behavior that followed.

"Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." — Lamentations 3:40 KJV

To search the ways is to look honestly at the patterns — not only the behavior, but the pattern that preceded the behavior. What situations have reliably produced the pull? What emotional states have consistently preceded the worst choices? What environments, relationships, and circumstances have the longest history of leading to the place Step 1 is naming?

These are not questions to produce shame. They are questions to produce strategy.

The person who knows their patterns is not helpless before them. The person who does not know their patterns will be surprised by them — repeatedly. Step 1 begins the honest assessment: not only what I did, but what preceded what I did. That pattern is the road map for what Steps 3 through 10 will need to address.

THE LONELINESS OF EARLY RECOVERY

The old social world was organized around using. When the substance stops, the community built around it often goes with it — the bar friends, the using partners, the group where not-using made you the outsider. This is a specific and acute loss that adds to the weight of early recovery.

It is also one of the most reliable precursors to relapse.

The isolation that follows early sobriety is not a character defect. It is the natural result of having left a world before finding another one. And the flesh — which was trained in that world, which knows the relief that world offered — will use the loneliness to make the return look reasonable.

"Turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me; for I am desolate and afflicted." — Psalm 25:16 KJV

Desolate. That word belongs in the honest prayer of the person in early recovery who has left the only community they knew. God is not embarrassed by that prayer. He is the answer to it.

The community this program provides is not a replacement for the old world — it is a different kind of world. A room of people who know what the loneliness feels like because they have sat with it themselves. The mentor relationship of Preface L4 is not optional — it is the specific provision for this specific loneliness.

Name the loneliness. Do not use it as a reason to return. Bring it here instead.

WHAT ACTUALLY PRODUCES CHANGE

"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." — Ezekiel 36:26 KJV God spoke this promise through the prophet Ezekiel — in the Old Testament, pointing forward to what the new covenant would accomplish. Not: I will help you manage your stony heart better. Not: I will give you better strategies for working around it. I will take it away and give you a new one. The transformation the steps are building toward is not behavior modification. It is a new heart — which produces different desires, different responses, different patterns at the source. The steps create the conditions for that transformation. The transformation itself is God's work in the surrendered life.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every covenant God has made: the admission of what is true is always the beginning of what becomes possible. God has never started with a person's strength. He has always started with their honesty.

Step 1 L2 has named why the ceiling on human effort is real and why it is not a character flaw. Step 1 L3 addresses the specific mechanism the flesh uses to protect itself from the honest examination that Step 1 requires — denial. The student who understands the flesh clearly is ready to recognize how it operates in their own thinking.

SIN BINDS — THE TRUTH ABOUT SPIRITUAL SLAVERY

"Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." — John 8:34 KJV Jesus said this plainly, to people who considered themselves free — who had never been in bondage to any man. He did not argue their external claim. He addressed the inner one: whoever commits sin is its servant. The bond is not chosen once. It is renewed every time the pattern is repeated — the service deepens with each act of commission. This is not a statement about weakness. It is a statement about bondage. The person whose pattern of sin has become established — whose flesh has grooved the same path a hundred times until it goes there without deciding — is in bondage. Not as a metaphor. As the literal condition of a will that has surrendered its governance to something other than God. "For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace." — Romans 6:14 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Rome — not as a description of their current condition but as the declaration of what becomes true in Christ. Sin shall not have dominion. Not: sin will be uncomfortable. Not: sin will feel bad. Sin shall not have dominion — the rulership, the lordship, the governing authority over the life — belongs to what God provides through grace, not to the pattern the flesh established through years of service. The addiction was never primarily a substance problem. It was a dominion problem. Something ruled where only God should rule. The recovery that addresses only the substance without addressing the dominion has treated the symptom and left the source. Step 1 names the dominion honestly — without Him I can do nothing. The dominion of the flesh has reached its ceiling. The dominion of God through grace has no ceiling. That is not the language of a self-help program. It is the language of a person who has come to the end of one rulership and is learning what it means to come under another. THE TONGUE AND THE HEART
"For of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh." — Luke 6:45 KJV Jesus said this in His sermon — showing the connection between the inner life and what comes out of the mouth. The tongue is not an independent problem. It is the evidence of the heart's condition. Whatever governs the heart eventually governs the tongue — because the tongue reports what the heart contains. This is the reason no man can tame the tongue through effort alone. The tongue does not take direction from the will. It takes direction from the heart. To change what comes out of the mouth requires a change at the level of what fills the heart. The steps are clearing the ground for exactly that — not a managed tongue, but a transformed heart whose overflow changes what the mouth speaks naturally, without effort. What fills the heart after the clearing is the question the program is moving toward.

THE INHERITANCE YOU DID NOT CHOOSE

Most people in recovery have done a family of origin assessment — not to assign blame but to trace the pattern. Where did this come from? Who had it before you? What arrived in the house before you made your first decision? Most people find, when they trace honestly, that much of what they thought they chose was already running through the family line. The anger that appeared in a grandfather and then in a father and then in the mirror. The way of managing pain that felt instinctive because it had been modeled from birth. The ceiling on what people like them could expect — the family's quiet agreement about what was available and what was not. These inheritances arrived without being asked for. They shaped the life without permission. And the will — however determined, however sincere — has a specific limit when it encounters what was inherited at the level of the flesh. You can change your address. You cannot change your blood. The Scripture has a name for this. It calls it being in Adam. Not in Adam personally — in the inheritance that one man's choice released into every generation that followed. "For as in Adam all die" — 1 Corinthians 15:22 KJV. The patterns of the flesh, the hiding, the management of what is seen, the wall that human effort has always found — these did not begin with you. They are the inheritance of natural birth. Every person who has ever lived received them. This is not pessimism. It is the accurate diagnosis that makes the remedy make sense. Because the Scripture does not stop at the diagnosis. It describes a last Adam — "the last Adam was made a quickening spirit" — 1 Corinthians 15:45 KJV. A second inheritance. One whose obedience released a different kind of life into every generation that receives it. The first Adam's inheritance arrived through natural birth. This one requires a different birth — the one Jesus described to Nicodemus when He said: you must be born again. The steps are the road of honest preparation for receiving what the first inheritance cannot provide.

The person who has honestly completed Step 1 is not defeated. They are positioned. For the first time, the door is open — because they have stopped pretending it is not there. What comes through that door is not their effort. It is God's response to their honesty.

Admitting powerlessness is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a question the next step is written to answer.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 1 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. The goal of this session is to remove the shame attached to the ceiling on willpower while maintaining the full weight of personal responsibility. Both matter. The flesh is real and its ceiling is real — and the person who tried and failed to control through willpower was not morally deficient. They were operating with the wrong tool. quiz.question: According to Romans 7:18 KJV what does Paul say about the relationship between willing the right thing and performing it?
choices: The will and the performance are aligned when the person is disciplined enough
To will is present — but how to perform that which is good he finds not
The performance follows naturally from genuine intention

Willpower produces performance when applied consistently Romans 7:18 — to will is present with me but how to perform that which is good I find not. The will is genuine. The performance does not automatically follow. This is the honest description of the flesh — not a moral failure but the accurate limit of what human will can produce.

quiz.question: According to Galatians 5:17 KJV what is the relationship between the flesh and the Spirit?
choices: The flesh and Spirit work together toward the same goal
The flesh diminishes as the Spirit grows stronger over time
The flesh lusteth against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh — they are contrary to each other

The flesh is eliminated when a person genuinely surrenders Galatians 5:17 — the flesh and the Spirit are contrary to each other. The conflict is real and ongoing. It does not resolve through determination — it resolves through the Spirit's governance of the life. Paul wrote this to born-again believers.

quiz.question: According to Ezekiel 36:26 KJV what does God promise to give — and why does this matter for recovery?
choices: A new set of rules to govern behavior more effectively
A new heart and a new spirit — replacing the stony heart with transformation at the source
A new environment that removes the triggers for old patterns

A new understanding of the consequences of the old behavior Ezekiel 36:26 — I will give you a new heart and a new spirit. Not better management of the old heart. A new one. The transformation the steps are pointing toward is not behavior modification — it is a change at the source that produces different desires and different patterns from within.

lessons.title: Denial — the armor the flesh builds and how the truth dismantles it
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Throughout the covenant story, God's consistent response to human hiding is not punishment — it is a question. Where are you? He asked Adam. What doest thou here, Elijah? He asked the man under the juniper tree. What is that in thine hand? He asked Moses. The question is not for God's information. It is for the person's — because the person who names where they actually are has taken the first step out of the hiding that the flesh builds around itself. Denial is not stupidity. It is survival. The mind protects what it is not yet strong enough to face. Understanding this is not an excuse for it — it is the honest account of how it works, which is the first step toward dismantling it.

The admission of Step 1 is not merely a recovery statement. It is the beginning of what Scripture calls repentance — the honest acknowledgment that the life lived under self-governance has produced what it has produced, and cannot undo what it has done. Every step that follows is built on this admission.

WHAT DENIAL ACTUALLY IS

"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?" — Jeremiah 17:9 KJV The deceitful heart does not only deceive others. Its first and most consistent victim is the person who owns it. Denial is the heart's capacity to look directly at the truth and construct a story that makes the truth bearable — or invisible. Not through conscious lying, though conscious lying can be part of it. Through the genuine conviction that what is being managed is not as serious as others claim. The person in denial is not always aware they are in it. That is what makes it effective. The armor of denial is built precisely so that the person wearing it cannot see what it is hiding.

The prodigal son came to himself not at the height of his strength but in a far country, among swine, having spent everything. That is where the turn happened. That is where it has always happened.

WHAT THE TEXT SHOWS

"And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden." — Genesis 3:8 KJV The hiding was immediate. The fig leaves came before the question. The construction of the cover story was faster than the consideration of coming clean. This is denial in its original form — the automatic response of the exposed self to cover what has been uncovered. God walked toward them anyway. The question — Where are you? — was not accusation. It was the invitation to stop hiding. The person who answers that question honestly, even in the worst moment, has begun to come out from behind the trees.

THE SHAPES DENIAL TAKES

Minimizing: it is not that bad. Comparing: other people have done worse. Justifying: given what I have been through, this makes sense. Rationalizing: I could stop if I really wanted to. Projecting: the real problem is the people around me. Spiritualizing: God understands why I need this. Every one of these is the flesh building walls around what Step 1 needs to reach. They feel like reasonable thoughts because the flesh is skilled at making them feel reasonable. The test is not whether they feel reasonable. The test is whether they are true.

THE PERSON WHO HAS BEEN HERE BEFORE

If this is not the first time — if you have worked this program or something like it before, if you have had sobriety and lost it, if you are returning after a relapse — this section is written directly to you.

"For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again." — Proverbs 24:16 KJV

The rising is the definition of the just man. Not the not-falling. The falling is acknowledged as a reality — seven times is not a number chosen to be comforting, it is a number chosen to be honest. And the righteous man is not the one who never fell. He is the one who rose again.

The person who returns to this program after a relapse is not starting over. They are continuing. Every honest return to the admission of Step 1 is the program working — not failing. The program is designed for the person who returns. The problem is not the fall. The problem is the disappearance — the person who falls and does not come back.

"Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise." — Micah 7:8 KJV

When I fall, I shall arise. The rising is already assumed in the statement. The person who says this is not celebrating the fall — they are declaring that the fall is not the last word.

What to do if you have relapsed:

Come back immediately — the longer the gap between the fall and the return, the more shame builds, and the more shame builds the harder the return becomes. Come back the same day if possible. Come back the same week at the latest.

Tell your mentor — not eventually, not when you have the right words, not when you feel ready. Now. The secrecy that follows a relapse is the most dangerous part of the relapse. The fall is recoverable. The hiding of the fall is what produces the next fall.

Do not rename yourself by the fall — the relapse does not define who you are. It defines a moment you went back to the far country. The far country is not your home. Come home.

Return to Step 1 — not as punishment, but as the honest place to begin. What is still unmanageable? What did the relapse show about the triggers that had not been addressed? The inventory of the relapse is the most productive inventory the program can produce.

THE LIGHT THAT DISMANTLES IT

"But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." — 1 John 1:7 KJV John wrote this to born-again believers — describing the ongoing posture of the person walking in genuine covenant relationship. Walking in the light is not arriving at perfection. It is the daily commitment to visibility — to not hiding what is actually there, to bringing what is true into the open where God and the community can address it. The remarkable promise attached to walking in the light is not that it feels comfortable. It is that the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth. The cleansing happens in the light. What stays in the dark, stays.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every covenant God has made: the admission of what is true is always the beginning of what becomes possible. God has never started with a person's strength. He has always started with their honesty.

Lesson 3 has named what denial is and how it operates. Lesson 4 completes Step 1 — the full honest admission of both powerlessness and the unmanageable life, and what that admission opens. The student who has identified the specific forms their denial has taken is ready for the completion lesson.

DARKNESS HATES THE LIGHT — JOHN 3:19-20

"And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved." — John 3:19-20 KJV Jesus said this. And He said it not as a condemnation of unusual people — but as a description of the ordinary human response to the exposure that light brings. Men loved darkness. The preference for the dark is not the result of insufficient information. It is love. The person who hides in the trees has developed an affection for the cover. The darkness is familiar. It does not expose. It allows the management of what is seen — and over time, the management becomes the identity. The light is not neutral toward the darkness. Darkness hates the light. Not tolerates it. Not coexists with it uncomfortably. Hates it. The reason is stated plainly: the light reproves. It shows what is there. And the thing that loves staying hidden hates what would expose it. This is why denial is not simply a failure of information. The person in denial is not unaware that the information is available. The person in denial has made the choice — consciously or not — to stay in what the light would remove. And the flesh that has built its survival on the management of what is seen will resist the light with every tool available to it. "But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God." — John 3:21 KJV The person who does truth — who is moving toward what is actually true rather than what is comfortable to present — comes to the light. Not because it is painless but because the truth that is being done in them is the truth that can bear examination. What is wrought in God has nothing to hide from the light of God. The question of Step 1 L3 is not only: what have you been hiding? It is: what has developed a love for the hiding? Name it honestly. The naming is the beginning of coming to the light.

THE NAMES YOU HAVE BEEN LIVING UNDER

Long before the addiction had a clinical name, someone gave you a different kind of name. Not a legal name. The name that followed you into every room — the one attached to you in your family, in your neighborhood, in your own head at night. The name that told you what you were worth, what you could expect, who would ever want you around. Some of those names were spoken out loud. Some were communicated without words — through what was withheld, through what was said about you when you were not supposed to be listening, through the way certain people looked at you or stopped looking at you. But you received them. And names received early go deep. The Scripture shows that naming is not neutral. What something is named determines how it is treated, what is expected of it, what authority is exercised over it. In the very beginning, Adam named what he had authority over — and what he named, that was its name. The person who named you had authority over how you understood yourself. Some of that authority was legitimate. Some of it was not. All of it shaped you.

And the addiction confirmed names. That is one of its cruelest functions — it finds the name you were already living under and ratifies it. Failure. Worthless. Too far gone. Can't be trusted. Just like your father. The substance did not write those names. It simply provided daily evidence that the names were accurate. And the longer the addiction ran, the deeper those names were carved. "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — 2 Corinthians 5:17 KJV This program is not offering you a better performance of the name you already carry. It is offering the beginning of a different name altogether. One that was not given by the people who hurt you. One that was not ratified by the choices the flesh produced. One that belongs to the One who has the only authority to name what He made. The honest inventory of denial you are completing in this lesson is the first act of refusing to live under names that were never His to give.

The person who has honestly completed Step 1 is not defeated. They are positioned. For the first time, the door is open — because they have stopped pretending it is not there. What comes through that door is not their effort. It is God's response to their honesty.

Admitting powerlessness is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a question the next step is written to answer.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 1 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. Handle denial gently and precisely. The goal is not to accuse — it is to illuminate. The person who feels accused shuts down. The person who recognizes themselves in an accurate description is free to respond honestly. Use the shapes of denial as a mirror, not a hammer. ■ Jeremiah 17:9 KJV — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

ASSIGNMENT

Write a specific example of each one you recognize. 2. What is the one thing you have not told your mentor yet? Write it privately first. Then bring it to your mentor. 3. quiz.question: According to Jeremiah 17:9 KJV what does the Scripture say about the heart — and how does this explain denial?
choices: The heart is basically good and tends toward right choices when informed
The heart is deceitful above all things — its first victim is the person who owns it
The heart is neutral and responds to the environment it is placed in

The heart is controllable through discipline and proper thought patterns Jeremiah 17:9 — the heart is deceitful above all things. Denial is the heart's capacity to look at the truth and construct a story that makes it bearable or invisible. The person in denial is often not consciously lying — they genuinely believe the story the deceitful heart has constructed.

quiz.question: According to Genesis 3:8 KJV what was the immediate response to exposure — and what does God's response show?
choices: They confessed immediately and received forgiveness
They hid among the trees — and God's response was a question, not punishment, inviting them to name where they were
They defended their actions and offered justification

They waited for God to find them and pronounce judgment Genesis 3:8 — the hiding was immediate. The cover was constructed before God arrived. God's response was a question — Where are you? — the invitation to stop hiding and name the actual location. This is the model for how Step 1 addresses denial: not accusation but the invitation to honest naming.

choices: Walking in the light produces comfort and the absence of struggle
Walking in the light produces fellowship and cleansing — it requires the daily commitment to not hiding what is actually there
Walking in the light produces performance that others can observe and affirm

Walking in the light produces automatic freedom from the patterns that produced the hiding 1 John 1:7 — if we walk in the light we have fellowship and the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth from all sin. The cleansing happens in the light. Walking in the light is not arriving at perfection — it is the ongoing posture of bringing what is true into the open rather than maintaining the cover.

lessons.title: The full admission — completing Step 1 and crossing the threshold
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Every significant return in the covenant story follows the same pattern: the person comes to the end of their own resources, sees their situation clearly, turns toward the God who has been waiting, and receives what they could not produce for themselves. Hosea 14:1 — Return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity. Joel 2:12 — Turn ye even to me with all your heart. Jeremiah 3:22 — Return ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. The return is always received. This has been the pattern from the beginning. And the return always begins with the same thing: the honest admission of where the person actually is.

The admission of Step 1 is not merely a recovery statement. It is the beginning of what Scripture calls repentance — the honest acknowledgment that the life lived under self-governance has produced what it has produced, and cannot undo what it has done. Every step that follows is built on this admission.

THE FULL ADMISSION

Step 1 in its complete form has two parts. Most people do the first and call it finished. Part One: We admitted we were powerless over our addiction. This is the admission about the specific thing — the substance, the behavior, the pattern. I cannot control this. It controls me. When I try to manage it, it eventually overruns the management. The evidence of powerlessness is not the desire to stop — it is the repeated experience of being unable to stay stopped despite genuine intention. Part Two: Our lives had become unmanageable. This is the admission about everything built around the management of the first admission. The relationships shaped by keeping the secret. The financial decisions made to sustain the pattern. The emotional energy spent on maintaining the story. The spiritual distance that the whole enterprise created. The life itself — not just the specific behavior — has become something other than what it was meant to be. Both admissions are required. The person who admits only the first has named a problem. The person who admits both has cleared the ground for the entire program.

The prodigal son came to himself not at the height of his strength but in a far country, among swine, having spent everything. That is where the turn happened. That is where it has always happened.

THE FATHER RUNNING WHILE YET A GREAT WAY OFF

"But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." — Luke 15:20 KJV The father was watching before the son turned. The return had not yet been completed — the son was a great way off, still walking, still on the road — and the father was already running. When the son arrived, the robe came. The ring came. The feast began. Not in anticipation of the return — at the moment of it. The welcome did not require the speech the son had prepared. It required only that he come. This is the picture of what God meets the honest admission with. Not judgment for the distance traveled in the wrong direction. Not a probationary period before the restoration begins. Compassion that ran toward the person before they arrived.

The person who writes out the honest admission of both parts of Step 1 — who stops managing the story and says what is actually true — is the son still a great way off. And the Father is already running.

WHAT THE ADMISSION OPENS

The admission of Step 1 does not improve the circumstances. The morning after Step 1 is completed, the relational damage is still there. The financial consequences are still there. The patterns are still there. What changes is not the circumstances — it is the ground the person is standing on. The person still managing the story is standing on a foundation that requires continuous maintenance. Every new piece of information that might expose the story has to be managed. Every relationship has to be kept at a safe distance. The entire life is organized around protecting the cover. The person who has completed Step 1 honestly is standing on a different foundation. Not a repaired version of the old one. A cleared ground. The story no longer requires maintenance because it has been replaced by the truth. And the truth, however difficult, is a stable foundation in a way that management never is.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every covenant God has made: the admission of what is true is always the beginning of what becomes possible. God has never started with a person's strength. He has always started with their honesty.

Step 1 has been completed. The admission has been made — both parts, honestly. Step 2 introduces the God who meets that admission — not with judgment but with the question He has always asked: what doest thou here? And with the answer He has always offered: I am able. The person who has cleared the ground in Step 1 is ready to encounter the God of Step 2.

NAOMI — DO NOT RENAME YOURSELF BY YOUR PAIN

When Naomi returned to Bethlehem after years of loss — her husband dead, both sons dead, left with only her Moabite daughter-in-law — the women of the city said: Is this Naomi? And she answered them: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." — Ruth 1:20-21 KJV Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter. She had named herself after what had happened to her. The losses were real. The grief was real. The assessment of what she had lost was accurate. And she had allowed what had happened to become who she was — trading her given name for the name her suffering had written. But the Scripture does not call her Mara. Through the entire book that bears her name and the name of her daughter-in-law, the Scripture calls her Naomi. God did not accept the renaming. And by the last chapter, through Ruth's faithfulness and Boaz's provision and a grandson placed in Naomi's arms, the community said: there is a son born to Naomi. The name she had tried to surrender was restored by what God did in the season that followed her return. The person who has arrived at the full admission of Step 1 is often at Naomi's returning moment — empty, having gone out full, looking at the distance between what was and what is. The temptation is to adopt the Mara name permanently. The grief has earned it. But God does not rename His people by their worst season. He is still calling Naomi by her name. He is still calling you by yours.

The person who has honestly completed Step 1 is not defeated. They are positioned. For the first time, the door is open — because they have stopped pretending it is not there. What comes through that door is not their effort. It is God's response to their honesty.

Admitting powerlessness is not the end of the journey. It is the beginning of a question the next step is written to answer.

The grief of the wasted years is real — and it belongs in Step 1.

The person who arrives at Step 1 is not only surrendering a behavior. They are beginning to grieve what the behavior cost them. The years. The relationships. The version of themselves that did not exist because the addiction was existing in their place. This grief is not the enemy of the program. It is part of the honest accounting the program requires.

Do not rush past the grief. Do not perform resilience before the mourning is real. Naomi named her bitterness before Ruth returned anything to her. The naming came before the restoration.

What the addiction took from you is worth grieving. The person who grieves it honestly is the person who will not return to the thing that took it.

"Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." — Psalm 30:5 KJV

The morning comes. But the night of honest mourning must be allowed to be what it is before the morning can mean what it means.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 1 Lesson 4 — Step 1 Exam MEMBER LESSON. This is the completion lesson. The exam tests whether the student has understood the step. More importantly, this session is where the honest admission is actually made — in writing, with the mentor. Do not rush past the assignment to get to the exam. The exam is the easier part. The written admission is the actual work of the session. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER The return passages of the Old Testament — Hosea 14, Joel 2, Jeremiah 3 — show th...

■ Luke 15:20 KJV — "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."

■ Hosea 14:1 KJV — "Return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity."
