Here is the specific evidence of my powerlessness: [at least three specific examples of how the substance/behavior overrode your genuine intention to stop]. Part 2: My life has become unmanageable in these specific ways: [name at least four areas — relationa...

quiz.question: What are the two complete parts of Step 1 — and why does the second part matter as much as the first?
choices: Admitting the problem and committing to a solution — the commitment is what Step 1 is building toward

Powerlessness over the specific addiction and the unmanageable life — both are required because the first names the symptom and the second names the entire operating system that built itself around it
Acknowledging past behavior and identifying future triggers — both parts prepare for what comes next

The admission to God and the admission to another person — both are required for full accountability Two parts: powerlessness over the specific thing, and the unmanageable life. The first names the behavior. The second names the whole life that was organized around managing the behavior. Both are required for the full truth of Step 1 to be spoken and the full ground to be cleared.

quiz.question: According to Luke 15:20 KJV at what point did the father begin to run toward the prodigal son?
choices: After the son had given his full speech of repentance
After the son had demonstrated a period of sustained change
While he was yet a great way off — before the return was complete

After the son had repaid what he had wasted Luke 15:20 — while he was yet a great way off. The father was watching before the return was complete. He ran before the speech was given. The robe and ring were being prepared before the son arrived. This is the picture of what God meets the honest admission with — not waiting for sufficient performance, but running toward the person who has turned.

quiz.question: What does completing Step 1 honestly change — even though the circumstances remain the same?
choices: It changes the feelings about the circumstances by producing hope for improvement
It changes the foundation the person is standing on — from the maintained story to the stable ground of truth
It changes the relationships by removing the need for accountability

It changes the severity of the consequences that are still being experienced The circumstances do not change the morning after Step 1. The relational damage is still there. The financial consequences are still there. What changes is the foundation. The story no longer requires maintenance because it has been replaced by truth. And truth is a stable foundation in a way that management never is.

lessons.title: Came to believe — why the God you believe in must be real, specific, and able
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Step 1 cleared the ground. It removed the management, the story, and the illusion of control. What remains when the ground is cleared is the question that every covenant God has ever addressed: now what? The person who has honestly admitted powerlessness is standing in exactly the place where God has always met His people — at the end of what they could produce for themselves, ready to encounter what only He can provide. The covenant story, from its beginning, is the story of a God who introduces Himself specifically. Not as a philosophical concept. Not as a force available for interpretation. He said to Moses: I AM THAT I AM. He said to Abraham: I am the Almighty God. He said to Israel: I am the LORD thy God which brought thee out of the land of Egypt. God consistently identifies Himself in specific terms, with specific history, with specific demonstrated ability. Step 2 is the step where the person who cleared the ground in Step 1 encounters this specific God — not a vague higher power of personal construction, but the God who has been consistent across every era of the covenant and who is able to do what Step 1 revealed cannot be done without Him.

In Step 1 we named something most people spend their lives avoiding — the honest admission that self-governance had failed completely. Step 2 is where that admission finds its answer.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not a nameless force. He is a God who reveals Himself — specifically, by name. Isaiah records something worth noting: "I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me." — Isaiah 45:4 KJV. God surnames. A surname is a family name placed upon someone by another. It carries identity, ownership, belonging. The God we are being asked to believe in is the God who places His name on His people. That is the kind of God worth believing in.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not a concept but a person who responds to the person who turns toward Him. The Scripture that records this turning uses a word worth knowing: repentance — the change of mind and direction that opens the door to what God has always been ready to give.

CAME TO BELIEVE

The word came matters. Not: believed. Not: decided to believe. Came to believe — the language of a journey. The faith that Step 2 describes is not a switch that flips. It is a road that is walked. And the road begins exactly where the person is — not where they think they should be. "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" — Genesis 18:14 KJV God asked this question to Abraham, in the Old Testament, in the covenant account of the promised son. The question is rhetorical. The answer is no. And the question has never been withdrawn. It is asked to every person who arrives at Step 2 carrying the weight of what they believe about their own situation: too damaged, too far gone, too long in the pattern, too specific a case for the general remedy to apply. Is anything too hard for the LORD? The question demands an honest answer. And the honest answer — based not on how things feel but on who God has consistently shown Himself to be across the entire covenant story — is no.

God does not wait for a person to clean up before He reveals Himself. He appeared to Moses in the back side of the desert — at eighty years old, tending sheep that were not his own. The bush was burning in the wilderness, not the temple.

WHY A VAGUE GOD CANNOT HELP

The higher power of personal construction — vague enough to be comfortable, broad enough to include whatever the person prefers — cannot help. Not because the intention behind it is wrong. Because the power required for

the transformation Step 1 has exposed as necessary is specific, real, and not available in a concept. "For I am the LORD, I change not." — Malachi 3:6 KJV Malachi wrote this at the close of the Old Testament — the last prophetic word before four hundred years of silence, and the declaration that everything that had been consistent about God throughout the covenant story would remain consistent. He does not change. The God who parted the sea is the same God who met the prodigal while yet a great way off is the same God who is being introduced in Step 2. The consistency across the covenant arc is the ground of the belief. A vague higher power cannot offer this consistency because it has no history. The God of Scripture has one — and that history is the evidence that Step 2 is asking the student to examine.

TWO REQUIREMENTS FOR COMING TO GOD

"But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him." — Hebrews 11:6 KJV Two things are required for the person who comes to God. First: believing that He is — that He exists, that He is real, that He is specific. Not a concept. Not a projection. An actual being who is present and active. Second: believing that He rewards those who diligently seek Him — that seeking Him produces something, that the approach is met with a response, that the God who initiates the covenant also responds to the person who walks toward Him. The person at Step 2 does not need to have both of these at full strength. Hebrews 11:6 describes the direction of travel, not the required starting point. Mark 9:24 records an honest prayer that has been prayed by every person who has arrived at this step: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. That prayer is the beginning of the journey that Hebrews 11:6 describes.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not indifferent to the physical state of the person coming to Him.

Jesus did not confine His ministry to the spirit. He healed the body. He met physical suffering with physical action. The woman with the issue of blood was healed physically — her body stopped doing what it had been doing for twelve years. Blind eyes were opened. Deaf ears were unstopped. The God who made the body meets the body where it is.

"And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless." — 1 Thessalonians 5:23 KJV

Wholly. Spirit, soul, and body — all three. The God of peace is working on all three simultaneously. The physical struggle of early recovery is not outside His jurisdiction. He is present in the physical as surely as in the spiritual. Believe that He is — and that He rewards those who diligently seek Him, in whatever condition the seeking begins.

THE WOMAN AT THE WELL — THE GOD WHO ALREADY KNEW

Sychar is a Samaritan city — and Samaritans were people the Jewish world had decided were unworthy of serious religious engagement. The woman who came to the well at the sixth hour — midday, the heat of the day, not the morning when the other women gathered — came at that hour because she was not welcome at the earlier hour. She had five husbands and was living with a sixth man. Her history preceded her at every well in the city.

She came alone. And Jesus was there.

"Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink." — John 4:7 KJV

He asked her for something. Not the other way around. He initiated. He spoke to a Samaritan woman — which His disciples marveled at when they returned. And in the conversation that followed, He told her everything she had ever done.

"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did." — John 4:29 KJV

This is the God this step asks us to believe in.

Not a God who requires a sanitized version of a person before He will engage with them. Not a God who needs the history to be different before He will initiate the conversation. A God who went through Samaria specifically — John 4:4 says He must needs go through Samaria, and the Jews did not go through Samaria — and sat at a well at midday and asked a woman with a complicated history for a drink of water.

She was not at the height of her spiritual journey. She was not in a position of respectability. She was at a well, alone, in the heat of the day, with a history she was not proud of. And Jesus called her into the most significant theological conversation recorded in the Gospels.

The God this step asks us to believe in is the God who goes through Samaria to find the person who has been avoiding the morning gathering for years. Who already knows everything. Who initiates anyway.

"The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men, Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" — John 4:28-29 KJV

She left her waterpot. She came for water and left without it — because she had encountered something that made the water secondary. That is what the genuine encounter with this God produces. Step 2 is the step that introduces you to the God who already knows. The question is whether you are willing to stay at the well long enough for the conversation.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This is the consistent pattern of Scripture: God reveals Himself specifically, not generically. He told Moses His name. He told the Samaritan woman everything she had ever done. He is not a concept. He is a God who knows the specific person He is addressing — who reveals Himself by name, and whose name the Scripture gives us.

Step 2 L1 has introduced the question — is anything too hard? — and the two requirements for coming to God. Lesson 2 deepens the encounter with the specific God who meets that question: His consistency across the covenant, His demonstrated ability, and why the belief Step 2 describes is not a feeling but a decision grounded in evidence.

THE DEATH THAT PRODUCES LIFE

"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." — John 12:24 KJV Jesus said this about Himself — describing what His death would produce. But the principle He named is the same principle that Step 1 enacted and Step 2 now stands at the threshold of. The corn of wheat that does not fall into the ground and die remains alone. It does not multiply. It does not change. It stays exactly as it was — a single seed, intact, producing nothing. The old life — the management, the hiding, the self-governance, the flesh running itself — had to die for what Step 2 is pointing toward to become possible. Not weakened. Not reformed. Dead. The admission of Step 1 was that death — the acknowledgment that the self-governing life had reached its end and could not produce what only God provides.

What comes next is not improvement of the old life. It is the life that emerges from the death of the old one. "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." — Romans 6:4 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Rome — describing what the death of the old life and the emergence of the new one looks like. Buried. Raised. Walking in newness of life. Not the old life improved. Not the old life managed. A new life that emerged from the burial of what could not produce what God requires. Step 2 is the first step of that new life — the coming to believe in the God who raises what was dead. The person standing at Step 2 has left the old life in Step 1. The question now is whether they will believe in the God who has something entirely different to give them on the other side.

BETHEL — THE ENCOUNTER THAT CHANGES IDENTITY

Jacob left home with nothing but his own plans and his own history — a man who had deceived his way through every significant moment of his life, running from what his choices had produced. He slept in the open with a stone for a pillow. And there, in that specific place of his lowest point, God met him. "And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it. And, behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac." — Genesis 28:12-13 KJV God did not meet Jacob after he had cleaned up his history. He met him on the road out of his worst decision, at a random stopping point with a rock for a pillow. And the encounter changed the name of the place — Jacob called it Bethel, the house of God — and it marked the beginning of the change of the man. Recovery needs defining encounters — not only gradual effort. The person who is accumulating program time without a genuine encounter with the God the program points toward is in Bethel with their eyes closed. The stone is under their head. The ladder is there. The question is whether the encounter has happened. What has God interrupted to meet you? Name the stone you were sleeping on.

The person who leaves Step 2 having genuinely come to believe is not the same person who arrived. Something has shifted — not in the circumstances, but in what they are oriented toward. Belief, when it is real, reorders everything that follows.

Belief without a corresponding decision remains exactly where it started. What Step 3 requires is the moment belief becomes a choice.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Hebrews 11:6 KJV — "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

■ Genesis 18:14 KJV — "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?"

■ Malachi 3:6 KJV — "For I am the LORD, I change not."

What did God do? 2. Write your honest answer to Genesis 18:14: What specifically do you believe might be too hard for God in your situation? Name it specifically. 3. Nothing is too hard for the LORD — the question is rhetorical and the answer applies to every situation in Step 2
The answer depends on the faith level of the person asking

This was asked in a situation that every natural assessment would say was impossible. The question is not withdrawn. It is asked to every person who arrives at Step 2 with the specific weight of their specific case.

God's consistency means the results of seeking Him are predictable and controllable Malachi 3:6 — I am the LORD, I change not. The consistency of God across the covenant story — from Abraham to Moses to David to the disciples — is the evidence base for Step 2. The person examining the covenant history is not being asked to believe without evidence. They are being asked to examine the most consistent record in human history.

lessons.readingPlan:
Week 7 Day 1 — John 4:1-26 Jesus told the woman she was worshipping what she did not know. What have you been relying on without fully knowing what it was?
Week 7 Day 2 — Hebrews 11:1-16 Faith produces action in every person listed. What action has your faith produced? Or has it been belief without movement?
Week 7 Day 3 — James 2:14-26 Faith without works is dead. How does this apply to your recovery - not just believing that God can but acting as if He will?
Week 7 Day 4 — Genesis 18:9-15 Is anything too hard for the LORD? Name the thing that feels too far gone. Write it. Then write Genesis 18:14 underneath it.
Week 7 Day 5 — Romans 8:9-17 Jesus told Nicodemus that every person born of the Spirit is like the wind — you hear the sound of it. Romans 8 describes the Spirit bearing witness with our spirit. What does the passage say the Spirit produces? What observable evidence does Paul point to? And what questions does honest reading of this passage raise about your own experience?
Week 7 Day 6 — Mark 9:17-27 The father said Lord I believe help thou mine unbelief. Write your own version - naming exactly where your belief runs out.
Week 7 Day 7 — Psalm 46:1-11 God is our refuge and strength a very present help in trouble. Write about a time God was present in your trouble even if you did not recognize Him.

lessons.title: The God who was and is and is to come — His consistency across the covenant is the ground of belief
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
One of the consistent accusations the prophets addressed was the accusation made against God when circumstances went badly: He has forgotten. He is not watching. He does not see what has happened here. Psalm 77 opens with exactly this — the person in distress asking whether God has forgotten to be gracious, whether His promises have failed. And the answer the Psalm arrives at is the same answer the entire covenant story provides: remember what He has done. The history is the evidence. The God of Step 2 is not an idea to be evaluated for usefulness. He is the God of a specific, documented covenant history — a history in which He has demonstrated His character across thousands of years and hundreds of specific encounters with specific people in specific desperate circumstances. The belief Step 2 describes is not a leap in the dark. It is a decision based on the most thoroughly documented consistency in human history.

In Step 1 we named something most people spend their lives avoiding — the honest admission that self-governance had failed completely. Step 2 is where that admission finds its answer.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not a concept but a person who responds to the person who turns toward Him. The Scripture that records this turning uses a word worth knowing: repentance — the change of mind and direction that opens the door to what God has always been ready to give.

THE SAME YESTERDAY TODAY AND FOREVER

"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever." — Hebrews 13:8 KJV The writer of Hebrews addressed this to born-again believers — reminding them that the One they had received was not changing. What He had been in the Gospels He remained in their daily experience. What He had been in the Old Testament covenant He carried into the new. The covenant story does not describe a God who evolved or improved or changed His character based on the era. It describes one consistent character across every covenant era. What the text shows: the person who encountered God in the worst moment of their life — in the far country, in the wilderness, in the prison — encountered the same God who met Abraham, who strengthened Elijah under the juniper tree, who restored David after the disaster of his own choosing. The same. Not a similar being. The same One.

GOD IS A SPIRIT — JOHN 4:24

God does not wait for a person to clean up before He reveals Himself. He appeared to Moses in the back side of the desert — at eighty years old, tending sheep that were not his own. The bush was burning in the wilderness, not the temple.

"God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." — John 4:24 KJV Jesus said this in the Gospels — to a Samaritan woman at a well, in the middle of her ordinary day, in the middle of a conversation about her specific and complicated personal history. He did not begin with her failures. He offered her living water before she had asked for it. But then He named what was there — specifically, without accusation, without flinching — and in the naming the cycle was interrupted. Cycles break at Sychar not by trying harder but by encountering Someone who knows the full count and offers the water anyway, and then speaks the truth that neither confirms the identity the cycle built nor pretends it is not there. And when the conversation reached her actual situation — five husbands, and the current one not her husband — He did not withdraw the offer. He named what He knew and continued extending what He had already offered. God is a Spirit — not a concept, not a philosophical principle, not a vague benevolent force. A Spirit — present, knowing, able to fill what is genuinely surrendered to Him. The woman at the well left her water pot and went into the city. Something had happened that changed the direction of her day. The God who met her that afternoon is the God of Step 2.

THE GOD WHO SEES

"And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me: for she said, Have I also here looked after him that seeth me?" — Genesis 16:13 KJV Hagar was not one of the chosen people. She was not part of the covenant household by birth. She was an Egyptian servant who had been used and then driven away — sent out by the very people God had called, into the wilderness, with nothing but her son and the water she had carried from Abraham's house. She ran out of water. She set her son under a shrub. She moved away — a bowshot's distance — because she could not bear to watch him die. She sat down opposite him and lifted up her voice and wept. Let that image hold for a moment. She did not leave him. She moved far enough that she could not see, but not so far that she could not hear. And she wept. That is not abandonment. That is a mother who has reached the end of everything she could carry — and has not left, but cannot stay where she is. "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is." — Genesis

21:17 KJV Where he is. Not where she needed him to be. Not after the situation had improved. Not after she had found her way back to better circumstances. Where he is — in the wilderness, under the shrub, at the absolute end of the water. And then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. The well was there before she heard the voice. It was there before she reached the end of the water. It was there when she thought there was nothing. She could not see it because the grief had closed her eyes to what was present right beside her. To every woman in this room who has sat at a distance from something she loved — who has moved away because she could not bear to watch — who has run out of what she was carrying and found nothing left — To the mother whose children have been taken by this life, by the courts, by the chaos that addiction builds. To the mother who placed her child under the shrub of foster care or a relative's house or a situation she could not prevent — and moved a distance away because she could not watch. To the woman who has wept in the wilderness of consequences she did not fully choose and cannot fully undo. He has heard the voice of the child where he is. Not where you needed the child to be. Not after reconciliation has happened or the situation has resolved. Where he is. God's address is not your address for the situation. His reach is not limited to what you can see from the distance you have been keeping. The well was there the whole time. In the place that looked like the end of everything — the well was there. God opened her eyes and she saw it. This is the God of Step 2. Not a distant concept. Not a philosophical construct. Not a general spiritual force defined by whatever anyone needs him to be. The God who calls a specific woman by her name, in a specific wilderness, at the specific end of her water, and opens her eyes to what was there the whole time. Thou God seest me. She named Him. She gave Him that name out of that specific moment in that specific place — because the God who saw her when no one else did was a God worth naming. He sees you here.

GOD SURNAMES HIS PEOPLE

"I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me." — Isaiah 45:4 KJV God does more than call — He surnames. A surname is a family name placed on a person by another. It carries identity, belonging, authority. And God declares that He surnames His people — that He places His own name on them as the mark of who they are and whose they are. "And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." — Numbers 6:27 KJV In the old covenant, the name was placed through the priestly blessing — spoken over a people, covering them with the identity of the God who claimed them. The pattern continued through the covenant history: to be "called by His name" was to be marked as belonging to Him, bearing His authority in the world.

The curriculum will trace where this pattern arrives in the new covenant — what it looks like when God places His name not only on a house or a place but on a people who bear it in the world. For now: what does it mean that the God who saw Hagar in the wilderness she did not choose sees you in the wilderness you did not choose? He was present in hers. He is present in yours. And the well was there before she could see it. And the well is there. It was there before you knew to look for it. He is opening your eyes to it now. "For the LORD your God is a merciful God; he will not forsake thee, neither destroy thee." — Deuteronomy 4:31 KJV Not forsake. Not destroy. He is the God who sees — and what He sees, He does not abandon. Hagar named Him: Thou God seest me. That is the name still true today, in every wilderness, for every person who has run out of what they were carrying and cannot see the well that has been beside them the whole time. And God found her. Specifically. Personally. Knowing her name and her situation before she named it. He sent a messenger and the first words were not judgment — they were: where have you come from and where are you going? The question that God asked was not a demand for an accounting of her failure. It was the opening of a conversation. He already knew. He was giving her the space to say where she actually was. She called His name: Thou God seest me. The God who sees. In the wilderness. In the place she had not chosen to be. In the moment when she had no resources left and no road visible ahead. There are women in this program who know exactly what Hagar knew. The wilderness was not a metaphor. It was the house after everything fell apart. It was the day the children were taken, or the day she realized she was raising them alone, or the moment she sat in a place she had never imagined she would be and could not see any way forward. The shame of it. The invisibility of it. The feeling that God could not be looking at what she was looking at — because surely He would have done something by now. He sees. He has always seen. The wilderness has never been outside His reach and the people in it have never been outside His attention. What Hagar discovered in the desert is the same God who is present in every version of that wilderness: the single mother at the end of her resources, the woman whose children have been removed by the consequences of her own choices, the woman who walked through things no one around her knows about and has been carrying it alone because there was no one safe to tell. Thou God seest me. That is not a theological proposition for the wilderness. It is the discovery that changes everything — because the God who sees is also the God who provides. He told Hagar what to do next. He gave her a road when she could not see one. And He made a promise to her that He kept. The person at Step 2 who believes their situation is too specific, too damaged, or too far gone for God's attention has not yet met Hagar's God. Come and meet Him. The wilderness is where He finds people, not where He loses track of them. It is specifically the kind of place He tends to show up.

LORD I BELIEVE — HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF

"And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." — Mark 9:24 KJV This prayer is in the Gospels — spoken by a father in front of Jesus, asking for the healing of his son, honest enough to name the gap between what he wanted to believe and what he actually held. He did not wait until the

unbelief was resolved before he prayed. He prayed with the unbelief present and named it honestly. This is the prayer that Step 2 makes room for. Not: I have arrived at full faith and I am presenting it for approval. Lord, I believe — here is what I am holding. Help thou mine unbelief — here is where the gap still is. The prayer is received. The healing follows.

THE GOD WHO DOES NOT CHANGE — AND WHAT THAT MEANS FOR IDENTITY

The consistency of God across all of Scripture is not merely a theological observation — it is the ground on which this step asks us to stand. He was the same God in the garden, the same God at Sinai, the same God who spoke through the prophets, the same God who arrived in the flesh.

"I am the LORD, I change not." — Malachi 3:6 KJV

That unchanging nature has a face in the New Testament. When the disciples asked Jesus to show them the Father, He said something that the whole of the Old Testament had been pointing toward:

"Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." — John 14:9 KJV

The God this step asks us to believe in is not abstract. He has a face. He has a name. And the One who showed that face to the disciples — who healed the sick, raised the dead, and spoke with the authority that left men amazed — is the same God who initiates, who reaches, who has never changed.

What does it mean that the God you are being asked to believe in has a face? Hold that question as the steps proceed.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This is the consistent pattern of Scripture: God reveals Himself specifically, not generically. He told Moses His name. He told the Samaritan woman everything she had ever done. He is not a concept. He is a God who knows the specific person He is addressing — who reveals Himself by name, and whose name the Scripture gives us.

Lesson 2 has shown the consistency of the God of the covenant — the same across every era, present in every wilderness, seeing what the person in Step 2 believes might be too specific or too damaged for His attention. Lesson 3 addresses the counterfeit — why many people encountered a form without power before arriving here, and what the real thing actually looks like when the power is present. THE NAME HE PLACES UPON HIS

PEOPLE

"And they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." — Numbers 6:27 KJV This is the closing command of the Aaronic blessing — the instruction God gave to Moses about how the priests were to bless the people of Israel. At the end of the blessing, the Name is placed. Not suggested. Not offered as an option. Put upon them. The blessing and the Name are inseparable. God has always placed His name upon His people. Not as a label but as an identity — the name that carries covenant relationship, that marks the one upon whom it is placed as belonging to the God who placed it. A name in covenant is not merely what you are called. It is what you bear — the authority and identity of the one whose name rests upon you. As the steps proceed, the question of whose name you bear — and what it means to bear it — will become increasingly significant. For now, hold this: God has a name. He places it upon His people. And the blessing follows the placing.

The person who leaves Step 2 having genuinely come to believe is not the same person who arrived. Something has shifted — not in the circumstances, but in what they are oriented toward. Belief, when it is real, reorders everything that follows.

Belief without a corresponding decision remains exactly where it started. What Step 3 requires is the moment belief becomes a choice.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 2 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. The goal of this session is to build the evidence base for belief — not to produce emotional certainty but to ground the decision to believe in something more substantial than feeling. The covenant history is the evidence. Walk students through it as a body of testimony, not as doctrine to be accepted. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER Hebrews 13:8 is an epistle — written to believers already born again into the covenant life, reminding them of the unchanging natu...

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Hebrews 13:8 KJV — "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."

■ John 4:24 KJV — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

■ Mark 9:24 KJV — "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."

■ Genesis 16:13 KJV — "Thou God seest me."

ASSIGNMENT

The honest prayer 1. Write Mark 9:24 in your own words — filling in specifically what you believe and specifically where the unbelief is still operating. 2. Read Psalm 77 this week. Write out how the Psalmist moves from distress to trust. What was the turning point? 3. Name one person in the covenant story from Hebrews 11 whose situation looked impossible. Write what they believed and what God did...

quiz.question: According to Hebrews 13:8 KJV what is true about Jesus Christ across time — and why does this matter for Step 2?
choices: He changes according to the needs of each era
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday today and forever — the consistency of the covenant God is the evidence base for belief
His methods change but His character remains the same

He was more accessible in the biblical era than He is now Hebrews 13:8 — the same yesterday, today, and forever. The God who met Hagar in the wilderness, who ran toward the prodigal, who offered living water to the Samaritan woman, is the same One Step 2 introduces. The consistency across the entire covenant history is the most substantial evidence base available for belief.

quiz.question: According to Genesis 16:13 KJV what did Hagar name God after He met her in the wilderness — and what does this show about where God appears?
choices: She named Him the God of all comfort — showing He appears when worship is offered
She named Him Thou God seest me — showing the God of the covenant sees and meets in the wilderness specifically
She named Him the God of Abraham — showing His appearance was tied to covenant lineage

She named Him the God of the impossible — showing He appears when circumstances are beyond natural remedy Genesis 16:13 — Thou God seest me. Hagar was alone, fleeing, without resources. The God of the covenant met her specifically, personally, in the wilderness. The covenant history does not show a God who is available to the successful and absent to the desperate. It shows the opposite.

quiz.question: According to Mark 9:24 KJV what did the father pray — and what does this show about what kind of faith Step 2 requires?
choices: He declared complete faith before asking — showing Step 2 requires resolved certainty
He said Lord I believe and named the unbelief alongside it — showing Step 2 makes room for the honest prayer that holds both
He described his past faithful acts — showing Step 2 requires demonstrated history of belief

He asked others to believe on his behalf — showing Step 2 can be completed through proxy faith Mark 9:24 — Lord I believe; help thou mine unbelief. The prayer names both what is held and where the gap is. The healing follows. Step 2 does not require the unbelief to be resolved before the approach is made. It requires the honest prayer that names both.

lessons.title: The counterfeit and the real — why form without power fails and where the real thing is found
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The Scripture distinguishes between pure and undefiled religion on one hand, and defiled religion on the other. Both are real. The problem of defiled religion is not new. The prophets of Israel wrote consistently to people who were going through the motions of covenant relationship while the heart was not engaged. Isaiah 1:11-15 records God's rejection of the sacrifices and assemblies of a people who maintained the form while abandoning the substance. Amos 5:21-24 records the same: I hate, I despise your feast days — Let judgment run down as waters and righteousness as a mighty stream. The form was intact. The covenant was not. This pattern runs from the Old Testament through the New. And the person who arrived at Step 2 having sincerely tried a form without power — having gone to church, having said the prayers, having maintained the attendance — and found that nothing changed, has encountered the pattern the prophets addressed. They are not the first. And the failure of the counterfeit is not evidence that the real thing does not exist.

In Step 1 we named something most people spend their lives avoiding — the honest admission that self-governance had failed completely. Step 2 is where that admission finds its answer.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not a concept but a person who responds to the person who turns toward Him. The Scripture that records this turning uses a word worth knowing: repentance — the change of mind and direction that opens the door to what God has always been ready to give.

THE COUNTERFEIT

"Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away." — 2 Timothy 3:5 KJV Paul wrote this to Timothy — an evangelist he was equipping for the difficulty of serving genuine believers in a world full of imitations. The form of godliness: the language, the building, the services, the expectation that sincerity plus attendance will eventually produce the change that only God's power can produce. The form looks right. It uses the same words. It follows the correct schedule. But when the person who is genuinely broken needs something that cannot be manufactured by human effort or institutional structure, the form has nothing to offer. It can produce attendance records and advice. It cannot produce the new heart Ezekiel described or the filling Ephesians 5:18 points toward.

God does not wait for a person to clean up before He reveals Himself. He appeared to Moses in the back side of the desert — at eighty years old, tending sheep that were not his own. The bush was burning in the wilderness, not the temple.

WHY PEOPLE FALL AWAY FROM COUNTERFEIT RELIGION

"These are they likewise which are sown on stony ground; who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with gladness; And have no root in themselves, and so endure but for a time: afterward, when affliction or persecution ariseth for the word's sake, immediately they are offended." — Mark 4:16-17 KJV Jesus described this in the Gospels — in the parable of the sower, during His ministry. Immediate gladness. No root. Endure for a time. Gone when pressure comes. This is not describing weak or uncommitted people. It is describing people who received the message without what produces endurance. The gladness was real. The response was sincere. But a response without root cannot survive real life. The person who encountered what was presented as religion sincerely and fell away did not fail. They received the message without the root system. The seed was real. The soil was insufficient. And the insufficient soil is the consistent result of the form without the power.

THE REAL THING

The real thing changes what is underneath — not just what is visible. It does not modify behavior. It changes the nature that produces the behavior. And more than changing — it fills. The God of Scripture does not merely observe the surrendered life from a distance. He takes up residence in it. "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever." — John 14:16 KJV Jesus promised this in the Gospels, the night before the cross — pointing forward to what the new covenant would provide. Not a better set of rules. Not improved instruction. A Comforter who abides — who takes up permanent residence in the life that has been genuinely surrendered and genuinely received Him. The person who encountered the counterfeit encountered a form that pointed toward this but could not provide it. The real thing provides what the form only described.

THE FULNESS OF GOD — WHERE IT ACTUALLY DWELLS

The counterfeit religion that this lesson addresses — the form without power — has always involved a God who is distant, partial, or filtered through a system. The Scripture locates the fullness of God differently.

"For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily." — Colossians 2:9 KJV

Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Colossae — describing not a partial manifestation or a representative of God, but the complete dwelling of everything God is, bodily, in one person. All. The fulness. The Godhead — the complete nature of who God is — dwelling bodily in Christ.

This is not a secondary theological point. It is the answer to the question the counterfeit raises: if there is a form without power, where does the power actually reside? In the fulness. In the One in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwells.

The God this curriculum is about is not one of three. He is the One in whom all of the One dwells. That distinction matters — not as a doctrinal argument, but as the difference between the form and the substance.

What does it mean to seek the One in whom all the fulness dwells? That is the question this step is designed to answer experientially, not just intellectually.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This is the consistent pattern of Scripture: God reveals Himself specifically, not generically. He told Moses His name. He told the Samaritan woman everything she had ever done. He is not a concept. He is a God who knows the specific person He is addressing — who reveals Himself by name, and whose name the Scripture gives us.

Lesson 3 has shown why the counterfeit fails and what the real thing provides. Lesson 4 addresses what faith looks like in action — the decision to believe before the circumstances confirm it, and what that decision sets in motion.

WHAT POWER LOOKS LIKE WHEN IT ARRIVES

The counterfeit has form but no power. The genuine article has both. And the Scripture does not leave the question of what power looks like when it arrives to personal interpretation — it gives an observable account. In Acts 2, the people who received what was promised did not sit quietly and feel different internally. Something happened that onlookers could see and hear. Those who did not understand it accused them of being full of new wine. Those who did understand it — Peter, quoting the prophet Joel — said: this is that. This is what God promised. This is what genuine arrival of the Spirit looks like. The student who has only encountered the form has a frame of reference for what religion looks like when nothing arrives. This lesson — and the road of the curriculum — is building toward an honest encounter with what the Scripture describes when the real thing does arrive. Carry this question: if something observable was promised, what is the honest accounting of what I have and have not experienced?

MARAH — THE BITTER PLACE GOD HEALS IN PLACE

"And when they came to Marah, they could not drink of the waters of Marah, for they were bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree, which when he had cast into the water, the waters were made sweet." — Exodus 15:23-25 KJV Marah means bitter. The people had just crossed the Red Sea — three days out of Egypt, three days of miraculous deliverance behind them — and the first water they found was undrinkable. The bitterness arrived before the provision was visible. God did not move the people away from Marah. He healed the water at Marah. In place. He showed Moses a tree — and the casting of that tree into the bitter water made it sweet. The healing came to the bitter place, not after the bitter place was left behind. The person who expects recovery to mean the removal of the bitter circumstances before the healing begins will wait at Marah indefinitely. The circumstances in which the addiction operated — the relationships, the consequences, the losses, the ongoing difficulty — these are often the Marah where God intends to work. The tree goes into the bitter water. The sweetness comes where the bitterness was. Not somewhere else. Here.

The person who leaves Step 2 having genuinely come to believe is not the same person who arrived. Something has shifted — not in the circumstances, but in what they are oriented toward. Belief, when it is real, reorders everything that follows.

Belief without a corresponding decision remains exactly where it started. What Step 3 requires is the moment belief becomes a choice.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 2 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. Many students carry the specific wound of sincere religious effort that produced nothing lasting. This lesson must validate that experience completely without feeding the bitterness it can produce. The frame: what they encountered was the form without the power. The form is real. The power is also real. The failure of the counterfeit is not evidence against the genuine. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER 2 Timothy 3:5 is an epistle — Paul writing to Timothy about w...

The form without power can instruct, organize, and encourage. The real thing fills — takes up residence in the life that has genuinely received it. That is the difference the lesson is pointing toward.

lessons.title: Faith in action — choosing to believe before the circumstances confirm it
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The faith that the covenant story describes is consistently active before the evidence is visible. Abraham left Ur for a destination he had not yet seen. Noah built an ark in the absence of rain. The children of Israel stepped into the Red Sea while the water was still a wall on both sides. The pattern of covenant faith across the Old Testament is not the faith that waits for the circumstances to confirm the belief and then believes. It is the faith that acts on what God has said, in the direction of what has not yet arrived. This is what Hebrews 11:1 describes: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." Faith carries weight — substance — before the thing it is aimed at is visible. This is not irrational. It is the consistent response of every person in the covenant story who encountered the God who was able and chose to act on that encounter before the outcome was confirmed.

In Step 1 we named something most people spend their lives avoiding — the honest admission that self-governance had failed completely. Step 2 is where that admission finds its answer.

The God this step asks us to believe in is not a concept but a person who responds to the person who turns toward Him. The Scripture that records this turning uses a word worth knowing: repentance — the change of mind and direction that opens the door to what God has always been ready to give.

THE SUBSTANCE OF THINGS HOPED FOR

"Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." — Hebrews 11:1 KJV Substance and evidence. Not feelings and impressions. Something real — weighty, present, active — aimed at something not yet visible. The faith of Step 2 is not the feeling of certainty. It is the decision to act in the direction

God does not wait for a person to clean up before He reveals Himself. He appeared to Moses in the back side of the desert — at eighty years old, tending sheep that were not his own. The bush was burning in the wilderness, not the temple.

of what God has shown Himself to be, before the circumstances confirm it. The person who waits until the circumstances improve before believing has reversed the order. The step is Came to believe — not: circumstances improved and then I believed. The belief comes before the confirmation. And the acting on the belief is what opens the road that leads to the confirmation.

Faith, in its biblical sense, is not agreement alone — it is belief that submits, trust that moves, and conviction that obeys.

Hebrews 11:1 KJV defines faith as substance and evidence — not theory, but something that produces action. If faith has substance, it must take form. That form is obedience.

This is why James is direct: "Faith without works is dead." — James 2:26 KJV. Not weak — dead. Belief that does not obey is not functioning as faith at all. It may be intellectual agreement, but it lacks life.

Consider Abraham. He did not prove faith when he heard the promise — he proved faith when he moved in response. When he left his country, when he offered Isaac, his belief became visible through obedience. His actions did not replace faith; they revealed it.

Noah built when there was no rain. That is obedient belief — acting on what God said before circumstances confirm it.

Romans 1:5 and 16:26 KJV use a precise phrase: "the obedience of faith." Obedience is not separate from faith — it is the expression of it. If obedience is absent, faith has not reached its full form.

The line this draws is hard but necessary: Belief that does not obey is incomplete. Faith that does not act is unproven. Confession without submission is empty.

True faith produces response. It hears and it moves.

This is why the call of God is never simply believe — it is believe unto something: repentance, transformation, submission, and a changed life. Faith always has direction, and that direction is obedience.

The steps that follow are the road of obedient belief. Not because obedience earns anything — but because real faith cannot remain still.

FAITH WORKING BY LOVE

"For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love." — Galatians 5:6 KJV Paul wrote this to the Galatians — born-again believers — describing the nature of the faith that actually produces. Not the faith that arrives at correct theological positions. The faith that works by love. That is active. That moves in the direction of what it believes because it has been genuinely moved by what it has encountered. The belief of Step 2 is not a theological position to be adopted. It is the decision — made by a person who has seen the history of the covenant God and encountered the love behind it — to move in the direction of that God before the destination is fully visible.

THE DECISION, NOT THE CERTAINTY

Step 2 does not require certainty. It requires the decision. The decision to believe is made at the point where the evidence is sufficient even though it is not complete — where the history of the consistent God is enough to act on, even while the question is still being explored. "And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him." — 1 Kings 18:21 KJV Elijah's question on Mount Carmel — in the Old Testament, in the confrontation between the God of the covenant and the god the people had been dividing their allegiance between — is the question Step 2 is asking. How long halt ye between two opinions? The halting — the indecision, the management of two possible sources of help — is what Step 2 is ending. The decision is the step.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This is the consistent pattern of Scripture: God reveals Himself specifically, not generically. He told Moses His name. He told the Samaritan woman everything she had ever done. He is not a concept. He is a God who knows the specific person He is addressing — who reveals Himself by name, and whose name the Scripture gives us.

Step 2 is complete when the person has made the decision — to believe that the God of the covenant is real, is specific, is able, and is the answer to what Step 1 exposed. Step 3 follows immediately: now that the decision has been made, what does it mean to turn the whole life over to this God? The belief of Step 2 is the foundation. The surrender of Step 3 is what is built on it. HOW TO PRAY — FOR GOD'S WILL, NOT YOUR OWN WISHES "Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts." — James 4:3 KJV James wrote this to born-again believers — identifying the specific reason that sincere prayer sometimes produces nothing: the asking is aimed at what the self wants rather than at what God is doing. The prayer that asks God to endorse the self's plan is the prayer that James describes. It is sincere. It is earnest. And it receives nothing — because it is aimed in the wrong direction. "Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." — Matthew 6:10 KJV Jesus gave this model of prayer before any petition for personal need. The kingdom first. The will of God — in earth as it is in heaven — before any request for daily bread, forgiveness, or deliverance. The prayer that aligns

with God's will is the prayer that receives — not because God is rewarding the correct formula but because the prayer aimed at God's will is the prayer that is already moving in the direction He is moving. This is how to pray: Begin with who God is — not with what you need. Let the acknowledgment of His character set the direction of the prayer before the petitions begin. Ask what God is doing — not what you want Him to do. The prayer that asks to join what God is already doing is the prayer that finds the answer already in motion. Surrender the outcome — specifically and honestly. Name what you want. Then release the timing and the method to God. The prayer that holds the outcome is the prayer that is still governed by the self. The prayer that releases the outcome is the prayer that has genuinely placed the matter in the hands of the One who can actually move it. Ask for what the Word promises — not what the flesh desires. The promises of God are the legitimate objects of believing prayer. Ask specifically for what the Scripture shows God has already committed Himself to give. That prayer will not return void. The confidence John describes in 1 John 5:14 — that God hears what is asked according to His will — becomes available The confidence is not in the volume of the asking. It is in the direction. According to His will — the prayer that moves in the direction God is moving — is the prayer that is heard. And the prayer that is heard is the prayer that receives.

The person who leaves Step 2 having genuinely come to believe is not the same person who arrived. Something has shifted — not in the circumstances, but in what they are oriented toward. Belief, when it is real, reorders everything that follows.

Belief without a corresponding decision remains exactly where it started. What Step 3 requires is the moment belief becomes a choice.

The more important work of this session is the written decision — the student's own articulation of what they believe about the God Step 2 has introduced and why. This is not a theological statement. It is the honest record of where the student is standing at the end of Step 2. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER Hebrews 11:1 is an epistle — describing the nature of the faith that operates...

lessons.title: Not my will but Thine — what it means to actually make the decision
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The covenant story has always required a decision. God presented the terms and waited for the response. Abraham had to leave Ur before the destination was revealed. Israel had to step into the Jordan before the water parted. The obedience preceded the confirmation in every case. And the specific word God required was always some version of the same thing: not what you planned, not what you arranged, not what your strength can produce — Mine. Step 3 is the moment the person who has admitted powerlessness in Step 1 and encountered the able God in Step 2 makes the actual decision. Not the intention to decide eventually. Not the agreement that surrender is a good idea in principle. The decision. Today. With this specific will. This specific life. "Not my will, but thine, be done." — Luke 22:42 KJV Jesus prayed this in the Gospels, in the garden of Gethsemane, the night before the cross — the moment the full weight of what the new covenant would require landed on the One who was making it. The prayer was not the prayer of someone for whom surrender was easy. It was the prayer of someone who felt the full weight of what was being asked and surrendered anyway. That is the prayer of Step 3.

In Step 2 we came to believe that restoration was possible — but belief alone, as we saw, is not enough to produce it. Step 3 is where belief becomes a decision.

The surrender of Step 3 is a transfer of authority. It is the decision to live under God's governance rather than the self's. There is a word for this in the Scripture — calling on the name of the Lord. Not the recitation of a formula, but the genuine turning of the person toward the God who has made Himself known by name and promised to answer those who call on Him genuinely.

The surrender of Step 3 is the outward form of what the Scripture calls repentance at the level of will — not remorse, but the actual turning of the governance of the life toward God. Remorse stays in the far country. Repentance arises, and comes home.

WHAT THE DECISION ACTUALLY IS

The decision of Step 3 is not the decision to feel differently about God. It is not the decision to attend more consistently or try harder or adopt better practices. It is the transfer of authority — the actual, specific surrender of the will that has been running the operation, and the placement of that will under the governance of the God who is able. "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." — Romans 12:1 KJV Paul wrote this to believers in Rome who had already entered the covenant life — describing the ongoing act of surrender that the life in God requires. A living sacrifice. The sacrifice is not made once and complete. It is the daily, ongoing presentation of what is genuinely available to the One who has been given the governance. Step 3 is the first and foundational presentation. What follows builds on it daily.

The decision of Step 3 is made by a person who has not yet been changed — who is still in the condition that made Step 1 necessary. That is exactly the right person to make it.

WHAT IS BEING SURRENDERED

The will. Specifically, the will — the part of the person that has been making decisions about what to do, what to pursue, what to protect, what to avoid. The will is not bad. It is a good thing given for the right purpose. The problem is not that the person has a will. The problem is whose governance the will has been under.

The surrender of Step 3 is not the destruction of the will. It is the reorientation of it — from self-governance to the governance of the God who is able to direct it where it was designed to go.

The decision of Step 3 has a specific application in the moment the craving arrives.

When the pull comes — and it will come — the surrender of Step 3 is not a past event to remember. It is a present action to take. Not my will but Thine is not only a prayer spoken in a quiet morning. It is the sentence said out loud in the car, in the store, in the moment before the decision is made.

"1 Corinthians 10:13 KJV — There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."

The way of escape is real. But it requires the person to be looking for the door. The surrender of Step 3 trains the person to look for the door rather than to stand and negotiate with the pull.

In the moment of craving — a specific protocol: Stop. Name what is happening out loud or on paper. Say the Step 3 prayer: not my will but Thine. Move — physically leave the situation if possible. Contact someone — the mentor, another person in the program, anyone who is not in the craving with you.

The craving is time-limited. It peaks and it passes. What it needs is a bridge to the other side — and the surrender of Step 3 is that bridge.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern across the covenant is clear: God does not take what has not been given. Surrender is the door. It has always been the door. Every transformation recorded in Scripture begins with a person giving something over that they had been holding.

The decision has been named and its content identified. Lesson 2 addresses what it looks like to walk in that decision daily — how the Word lights the road and what obedience looks like as a daily practice rather than a single event. SURRENDERED TO THE NAME THAT GOVERNS "I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me." — Isaiah 45:4 KJV God spoke this to Cyrus — a Persian king who did not know the God of Israel — and named him before his work had begun. God does more than call by name. He surnames. A surname is the family name — the identity that is carried from one generation to the next, the mark of whose household you belong to. The decision of Step 3 — not my will but Thine — is the beginning of a different governance. Not only the surrender of daily choices but the deeper surrender of the name under which the life is conducted. The self's name, the self's identity, the self's plan for what the life is for — all of it placed under the governance of the One who has always had a name, who has always placed that name upon His people, and who has always blessed what was surrendered to bear it. As the steps proceed, the significance of whose name you bear will become increasingly clear. For now: the surrender of Step 3 is the beginning of a life conducted under a different authority than the self's authority. And that authority has a name.

THE POOL OF SILOAM — OBEDIENCE BEFORE THE RESULT APPEARS

Jesus put clay on the blind man's eyes and said: go, wash in the pool of Siloam. The man did not ask how the clay would help. He did not negotiate the method. He did not wait until he understood the mechanism. He went. "He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." — John 9:7 KJV The healing was not in the understanding. It was in the going. The man could not see where he was going — he was blind. He walked by faith in the instruction he had received, toward the pool he was told to go to, and he came back seeing. Step 3 — the decision to turn the will and the life over to the care of God — is the pool of Siloam moment of the program. The person at Step 3 does not yet have the sight that Steps 4 through 12 will develop. They are making a decision whose full meaning will only become clear after the decision has been kept. The instruction is: go. Surrender. Walk toward the pool you cannot yet see clearly. The sight comes after the washing, not before. The decision of Step 3 does not require you to understand how it will produce what it promises. It requires you to go.

The decision of Step 3, when it is real, changes what the person is from that moment forward. Not because they feel different — because they have placed something they were governing under a different governance. That transfer is the beginning of a life that works differently than the one that brought them here.

The person who has genuinely surrendered does not fear what the inventory will find. What belongs to God can be looked at honestly.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Luke 22:42 KJV — "Not my will, but thine, be done."

■ Romans 12:1 KJV — "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."

ASSIGNMENT

The decision made 1. Write your Step 3 prayer in your own words — modeled on Luke 22:42. Name the specific cup you are surrendering and make the specific decision. 2. Name one area of your life where self-governance has been making decisions. Write specifically what surrendering that area to God looks like this week — one concrete decision that reflects the transfer of governance. 3. Read Romans 1...

He prayed not my will but Thine — showing Step 3 is the actual transfer of governance from self to God, made with full awareness of the cost

He prayed for understanding — showing Step 3 requires theological clarity before the decision is made Luke 22:42 — not my will but Thine be done. The prayer was not easy. The full weight was felt before the surrender was made. Step 3 is not the pretense that surrender is costless. It is the decision that comes after the weight has been honestly felt — and the choosing of the God who is worth the cost.

Holding correct theological beliefs — the sacrifice is the intellectual surrender of wrong thinking Romans 12:1 — present your bodies a living sacrifice. The living sacrifice can walk away from the altar — which is what makes it costly and what makes it meaningful. Step 3 is the first presentation. The daily decision to stay on the altar is the ongoing content of what Step 3 begins.

The emotions are surrendered — feelings are placed under God's control rather than allowed to govern behavior

The future is surrendered — all plans and expectations are abandoned in favor of whatever comes Step 3 surrenders the will — the part of the person that has been making decisions about what to do, pursue, protect, and avoid. The will is not destroyed. It is reoriented from self-governance to the governance of the God who is able to direct it where it was designed to go.

lessons.title: The will of God — how the Word lights the road and what obedience looks like daily
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The writer of Hebrews addresses born-again believers — reminding them of the great cloud of witnesses, the record of obedience across the covenant story, and the specific invitation: lay aside every weight and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us. The race is set — it is already there, already designed, already funded. What remains is the running of it. Step 3 set the direction. But direction requires a road. The will that has been surrendered needs to know where it is going — not in a general way but in the daily, specific way that actual obedience requires. The God who receives the surrender also lights the road. "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." — Psalm 119:105 KJV

In Step 2 we came to believe that restoration was possible — but belief alone, as we saw, is not enough to produce it. Step 3 is where belief becomes a decision.

The God to whom the governance of the life is being transferred is not a committee — He is one Spirit, one LORD, fully present and fully able.

The surrender of Step 3 is the outward form of what the Scripture calls repentance at the level of will — not remorse, but the actual turning of the governance of the life toward God. Remorse stays in the far country. Repentance arises, and comes home.

The Psalmist wrote this under the old covenant — describing the function of the Word as the practical light that shows the next step. Not a floodlight illuminating the entire distance. A lamp for the feet and the path — showing what is immediately ahead, what the next step requires, what to do today with the surrender that was made.

WHAT THE WORD DOES

"This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success." — Joshua 1:8 KJV God spoke this to Joshua at the beginning of the transition from Moses to the conquest of the promised land — in the Old Testament, at a moment of new leadership and new obedience required. The instruction was specific: the Word does not depart from the mouth, it is meditated on day and night, and the purpose is observing to do. Not observing to know. Observing to do. The Word is the light that shows the road of obedience. But it shows the road for walking, not for studying while standing still. The person who reads the Word and does not walk in what it shows has received the light without following it. The light is given for the path. The path requires walking.

The decision of Step 3 is made by a person who has not yet been changed — who is still in the condition that made Step 1 necessary. That is exactly the right person to make it.

THE DAILY PRACTICE OF SURRENDER

"Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths." — Proverbs 3:5-6 KJV This Old Testament wisdom addresses the practical content of what the Step 3 decision looks like on an ordinary Tuesday morning. Trust with all thine heart. Lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways — not the significant spiritual ones, all of them — acknowledge Him. And He shall direct thy paths. The direction of the paths is the promise attached to the daily acknowledgment. The person who makes the Step 3 decision once and does not continue in the daily acknowledgment finds that the direction begins to wander. The daily acknowledgment — the morning given to God before the phone, the prayer before the decision, the Word before the schedule — is the ongoing maintenance of what Step 3 began.

THE PHYSICAL DISCIPLINES AS PART OF THE DAILY SURRENDER

After Elijah called down fire from heaven and outran the horses of Ahab to Jezreel, he sat under a juniper tree and asked God to take his life. He was not in spiritual failure. He was exhausted — physically, emotionally, spiritually depleted after the greatest victory of his ministry.

And the angel of the LORD touched him and said: Arise and eat.

"And the angel of the LORD came again the second time, and touched him, and said, Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee." — 1 Kings 19:7 KJV

Before the still small voice. Before the commission to anoint the next king. Before the instruction for the next assignment. God met the physical need. Arise and eat. The cake baked on coals. The cruse of water. Twice. Because the journey was too great.

The daily surrender of Step 3 includes the physical disciplines that make the journey possible:

Sleep — the unguarded mind is the vulnerable mind. The person who is not sleeping is not able to examine themselves, pray effectively, or maintain the relational work that recovery requires. Sleep is a spiritual discipline.

Food and water — the body that is neglected is the body that drops the guard earliest. Eat. Drink water. The physical body is the vessel in which the recovery is happening.

Movement — the body that was given over to chemical management benefits from physical engagement. Walk. Move. Do not sit still with the craving.

Structure — the surrendered day has a shape. Wake at the same time. Pray at the same time. The structure of the day is the practical expression of the daily surrender of Step 3.

The angel said arise and eat before God spoke the next instruction. The physical provision preceded the spiritual direction. Honor that sequence.

HOW TO PRAY FOR GOD'S WILL — NOT YOUR OWN

Prayer in Step 3 is not the same prayer it was before Step 3. The surrender of Step 3 is not a one-time event — it is the posture the daily life now occupies. And that posture changes everything about how a person approaches God.

"Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts." — James 4:3 KJV

James wrote this to born-again believers — describing the condition of prayer that does not receive. The asking is real. The person is genuinely praying. But the asking is aimed at what the self wants rather than what God purposes. Most people in early recovery have a long history of exactly this kind of prayer — asking for relief without repentance, for consequences to stop while behavior continued, for God to fix the situation while they remained unchanged at the center of it. The prayers were sincere. They produced silence. And the silence was interpreted as absence — when what it actually was, was a God who will not fund what He did not design.

"If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you." — John 15:7 KJV

The promise is real: ask what ye will and it shall be done. But the promise is tied to the condition that governs the asking — if my words abide in you. The person whose asking is shaped by the Word that abides in them is asking in alignment with God's will. That is the prayer that receives.

"And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us." — 1 John 5:14 KJV

The condition is not correct vocabulary or sufficient sincerity. It is alignment with His will.

PRACTICAL PRAYER FOR THE PERSON WORKING STEP 3

Morning — before the day begins: Lord, what is Your will for this day? Show me where You are working and let me walk toward it rather than away from it.

In difficulty — before the decision is made: Not my will but Thine. Repeat Step 3's language in the moment before the choice is made. The daily renewal of the surrender in the moment of decision is the practical expression of what this step established.

In petition — for specific things: Lord, if this is Your will I am asking for it. If it is not, I am asking for what is. Hold what you ask for loosely. Jesus prayed this in Gethsemane about the most significant moment in the covenant: He stated what He asked. He placed the outcome in the Father's hands.

Ask specifically. Hold it loosely. Trust the One who hears.

"But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly." — Matthew 6:6 KJV

The prayer that is aligned with God's will — the prayer that abides in the Word and asks from that abiding — is heard. The answer may not look like what was requested. It may redirect. It may delay. But the hearing is real, and the person who has genuinely surrendered their preference to God's governance is the person whose prayer 1 John 5:14 describes.

THE WORD THAT BECAME FLESH — WHAT SURRENDER IS SURRENDERING TO

The surrender of Step 3 has a specific object. It is not surrender to a concept, a force, or a system. It is surrender to the God who entered His own creation.

"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." — John 1:1 KJV
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." — John 1:14 KJV

The Word was God. Not part of God, not a representative of God — the Word was God. And that same Word became flesh. The infinite entered the finite. The eternal put on time. The God of all creation chose to dwell among the creatures He had made.

This is who the surrender of Step 3 is directed toward. Not a historical figure who was inspired by God. Not a teacher who pointed toward God. The Word who was God, made flesh — fully present, fully available, fully capable of governing the life that the self has proven incapable of governing.

The surrender is not difficult because God is far away. It is difficult because the self has been in charge for a long time. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us precisely so that the distance would have no excuse.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern across the covenant is clear: God does not take what has not been given. Surrender is the door. It has always been the door. Every transformation recorded in Scripture begins with a person giving something over that they had been holding.

The Word and the daily practice have been established. Lesson 3 addresses what happens when the daily surrender is not maintained — the nature of the ongoing decision that Step 3 requires to stay alive in the life.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 3 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson is practical. The decision of Step 3 L1 needs daily structure to become the lived reality rather than a one-time event. Help students identify the specific daily practices that constitute the ongoing maintenance of the Step 3 surrender. Joshua 1:8 is the transition into the promised land — the specific instruction at a moment of new beginni...

■ Proverbs 3:5-6 KJV — "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths."

■ Joshua 1:8 KJV — "Thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein."

ASSIGNMENT

Identify one specific area where you are leaning on your own understanding rather than acknowledging God. Write what acknowledging Him there would look like specifically this week. 3. quiz.question: According to Joshua 1:8 KJV what three things are required for the person who is walking in the surrender of Step 3?
choices: Reading, praying, and attending — the three practices of the surrendered life
The Word not departing, meditating day and night, and observing to do — moving from knowing to walking
Fasting, confession, and service — the three acts of surrender

Believing, trusting, and waiting — the three postures of the yielded will Joshua 1:8 — the book shall not depart, meditate therein day and night, observe to do. Three things in sequence: the ongoing presence of the Word, the continuous meditation, and the action that follows — observing to do, not observing to know. The obedience is the road.
