choices: The major life decisions — God directs the significant choices when consulted
The spiritual activities — God directs the life when the religious practices are maintained
In all thy ways — the acknowledgment is total, covering every area of the daily life

The areas of specific struggle — God directs most actively where the need is greatest Proverbs 3:5-6 — in all thy ways acknowledge Him. Not in some thy ways. All. The financial decision, the relationship choice, the daily schedule, the management of the body. The direction follows the acknowledgment. Partial acknowledgment produces partial direction.

quiz.question: According to Psalm 119:105 KJV what specific function does the Word serve — and what does this mean for the daily practice of Step 3?
choices: The Word is the final destination — it shows where the journey ends
The Word is a lamp for the feet and light for the path — showing the next step, not the full distance
The Word is the measure of success — it shows how far the person has come

The Word is the source of comfort — it sustains the person through the difficult parts of the journey Psalm 119:105 — a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my path. Not a floodlight. A lamp for the feet — what is immediately ahead. The daily reading is the daily lamp. It shows the next step. The step after that is shown when the current step is taken.

lessons.title: Daily surrender — the decision made in Step 3 is kept one day at a time
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The covenant people of Israel were given manna in the wilderness — bread from heaven, provided daily, with the specific instruction not to gather more than one day's portion. The attempt to gather for two days produced bread that bred worms and stank. The lesson was not about food. It was about the daily dependence that the wilderness was designed to teach: you receive today what you need for today, and to morrow you return for what to morrow requires. Step 3 follows the same design. The surrender is real. The decision was made. And the daily practice of living in that decision is exactly as its name suggests: daily. Not weekly. Not in response to crises. Daily. One day at a time is not a recovery slogan. It is the design of the manna. "Give us this day our daily bread." — Matthew 6:11 KJV Jesus taught this prayer in the Gospels — the prayer of the person who has surrendered the governance of their life to the Father. Not: give us this week's provision. This day. The daily asking is the daily acknowledgment of the daily dependence. The person who has genuinely made the Step 3 decision asks daily because the daily asking is the daily maintenance of what the decision established.

In Step 2 we came to believe that restoration was possible — but belief alone, as we saw, is not enough to produce it. Step 3 is where belief becomes a decision.

The surrender of Step 3 is not a feeling — it is an act. The person who surrenders does not wait to feel surrendered before they surrender. They do the thing that surrender requires — and the feeling, when it comes, follows the obedience. This is the obedience of faith at work. Faith does not wait for the circumstances to confirm the decision. It makes the decision and the circumstances are addressed by the God who receives the surrender.

The surrender of Step 3 is the outward form of what the Scripture calls repentance at the level of will — not remorse, but the actual turning of the governance of the life toward God. Remorse stays in the far country. Repentance arises, and comes home.

THE LIVING SACRIFICE AND THE ALTAR

"I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice." — Romans 12:1 KJV The living sacrifice, once noted in Lesson 1, requires additional attention here. The sacrifice of the old covenant was placed on the altar and stayed there. The living sacrifice is different — it has legs. It can walk away. And the flesh, given the opportunity, will walk away from the altar and back toward what it has always known. The daily surrender is the daily decision to return to the altar. Not because the previous surrender was insufficient — because the living sacrifice requires the daily choice to remain in the position of surrender rather than walking back toward self-governance. This is not failure of the original decision. It is the honest description of what living sacrifice actually means.

The decision of Step 3 is made by a person who has not yet been changed — who is still in the condition that made Step 1 necessary. That is exactly the right person to make it.

The living sacrifice of Romans 12:1 includes the body in withdrawal, the body in exhaustion, the body that is cooperating imperfectly with a decision the spirit has made.

The person whose body is still recalibrating from the substance is not less surrendered because the body has not yet caught up with the decision. The surrender was made by the will. The body follows the will — not immediately, not without cost, but it follows.

"I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice." — Romans 12:1 KJV

Present what you have. The body that is struggling is still a body that can be presented. Offer it — imperfect, recalibrating, fighting the training it received — as the living sacrifice. God receives what is offered honestly. He does not require the offering to arrive in better shape.

DOUBLE-MINDEDNESS AND THE SURRENDERED LIFE

"A double minded man is unstable in all his ways." — James 1:8 KJV James wrote this to born-again believers — naming the specific enemy of the surrendered posture. Double-mindedness is the maintenance of two directions simultaneously: the surrender of Step 3 in one area and

the retained self-governance of another. The will that has been presented in the significant areas and protected in the private ones. The instability that double-mindedness produces is not a mystery. A person pulling in two directions at once is not moving anywhere. The daily surrender is the daily examination of what is still being protected — and the daily choice to present that area alongside what was already on the altar.

The surrendered life includes a practical decision about people, places, and things that reliably undermine the surrender. Some environments are not safe yet. That is not a spiritual failure — it is an honest assessment.

"Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men. Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away." — Proverbs 4:14-15 KJV

The avoidance Proverbs describes is not fear — it is wisdom applied to the knowledge of the self. The person who has been honest in Step 4's inventory (or who is working toward it) knows which situations have the longest history of producing the worst outcomes. The surrendered life does not require walking back into those situations to prove the surrender is real.

"Make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof." — Romans 13:14 KJV

Provision is what you supply in advance. The person who passes the bar, calls the using friend, or returns to the neighborhood without a plan has made provision — has supplied in advance the conditions the flesh has historically exploited. The daily practice of surrender includes the practical decision: I am not going there today. Not because I am afraid. Because I know what happens when I do, and the surrender of Step 3 is worth protecting.

Three questions for the weekly review with your mentor: What environments did I enter this week that put me in a high-risk state? What people from the old life did I contact — and what did that contact produce? What situations am I planning for next week that I need to plan around rather than into?

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern across the covenant is clear: God does not take what has not been given. Surrender is the door. It has always been the door. Every transformation recorded in Scripture begins with a person giving something over that they had been holding.

The daily practice of surrender has been shown in its true character — not a one-time event but the daily orientation of the living sacrifice. Lesson 4 is the Step 3 completion — the honest accounting of what has actually been surrendered and the beginning of Step 4.

THE SPIRIT GIVEN TO THE OBEDIENT

"And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him." — Acts 5:32 KJV Peter said this to the council — in the middle of the covenant account of the early church — stating plainly who receives what God gives. Not those who have accumulated sufficient sincerity. Not those who have attended long enough. Those who obey Him. The daily surrender of Step 3 is not only a recovery discipline. It is the posture of obedience that Acts 5:32 describes — the ongoing yielding of the will that positions a person to receive what God gives to the obedient. Carry this: what does it mean that the Spirit is given to those who obey? What does that obedience include?

The decision of Step 3, when it is real, changes what the person is from that moment forward. Not because they feel different — because they have placed something they were governing under a different governance. That transfer is the beginning of a life that works differently than the one that brought them here.

The person who has genuinely surrendered does not fear what the inventory will find. What belongs to God can be looked at honestly.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 3 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson addresses the most common failure point in Step 3: the belief that the decision was made once and is therefore complete. lessons.title: What has actually been surrendered — completing Step 3 and living in it
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The covenant God made at Sinai included this requirement: obedience, not intention. The people said at the foot of the mountain, all that the LORD hath spoken we will do. They meant it. And they failed. The pattern across the covenant history is not a shortage of sincere intention — it is the gap between the decision made and the life that actually follows. Step 3 is a decision. A real one. This lesson asks a harder question: what has the decision actually cost? Not in theory. Not in the moment the decision was made. In the daily life that followed. What was surrendered? What is still being held?

In Step 2 we came to believe that restoration was possible — but belief alone, as we saw, is not enough to produce it. Step 3 is where belief becomes a decision.

The surrender of Step 3 is the outward form of what the Scripture calls repentance at the level of will — not remorse, but the actual turning of the governance of the life toward God. Remorse stays in the far country. Repentance arises, and comes home.

THE PRODIGAL'S ARITHMETIC

"And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger! I will arise and go to my father." — Luke 15:17-18 KJV The prodigal made a decision in a far country. But the decision required the journey — the actual arising and going. The decision and the obedience that follows the decision are not the same thing. A person can make the decision sincerely and still be sitting in the far country. Step 3 completion asks: have you arisen? Not just decided to arise. Actually begun the walking.

The decision of Step 3 is made by a person who has not yet been changed — who is still in the condition that made Step 1 necessary. That is exactly the right person to make it.

WHAT HAS ACTUALLY BEEN SURRENDERED

The will is the seat of the self. Turning it over means that the daily decisions — where to go, what to pursue, what to hold, what to protect — are no longer governed by the self's preference but by what God has shown through His Word. Name the areas honestly: - Time. Who actually governs how it is used? - Relationships. Are any being maintained against what God is clearly showing? - Money. Is it moving toward what God directs or toward what the self wants? - The future. Is the plan still the self's plan with God as a support, or God's plan with the self in submission? "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps." — Proverbs 16:9 KJV

The heart devises. The LORD directs. These are not always the same direction. The person who has genuinely surrendered in Step 3 has handed the directing to God — not eliminated their own thinking but placed it under His governance.

THE RESERVED AREA

Every person who works Step 3 has something they turned over and something they did not. Not because they were dishonest in the decision — but because the self protects what it is not ready to release, sometimes without announcing what it is doing. "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." — Hebrews 4:12 KJV The Word reaches what the self cannot reach in itself — the thought behind the thought, the intention underneath the stated intention. Bring the reserved area to the Word. Not as a condemnation. As the surgical instrument that is precise enough to separate what has been surrendered from what has not.

DAILY SURRENDER — THE MAINTENANCE OF STEP 3

"I die daily." — 1 Corinthians 15:31 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Corinth — describing not a single death but a daily practice. The decision of Step 3 is not a one-time event after which surrender is accomplished and complete. It is the beginning of a daily practice — the ongoing choice to place the will back under God's governance each morning before the day's competing demands have made that difficult. The person who made the decision in Step 3 and has not renewed it daily is living on a transaction that has not been maintained. Daily surrender is the maintenance of what Step 3 started.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern across the covenant is clear: God does not take what has not been given. Surrender is the door. It has always been the door. Every transformation recorded in Scripture begins with a person giving something over that they had been holding.

Step 3 clears the ownership question. Step 4 begins the inventory — the honest examination of what has been living in the life that God now governs. The person who has genuinely surrendered in Step 3 is the person prepared to look honestly at Step 4 — because the life no longer belongs to the self whose reputation the inventory might damage.

BETHESDA — THE MAN WHO WAITED THIRTY-EIGHT YEARS

The pool of Bethesda means house of mercy. And there was a man at that house of mercy who had been waiting for thirty-eight years. "When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole? The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me in the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me." — John 5:6-7 KJV Jesus asked him a direct question: do you want to be made whole? And the man answered with an explanation of why it had not happened yet. The conditions were never right. Someone else always got there first. He had no one to help him in the right way at the right moment. Thirty-eight years of explanation. Jesus did not debate the conditions. He did not address the explanation. He said: rise, take up thy bed, and walk. And the man who had waited thirty-eight years for the conditions to improve rose and walked immediately.

The honest accounting of what has been surrendered in Step 3 includes this question: is there an area of the life where you have been explaining why the full surrender has not happened yet? The conditions never quite right. The circumstances not yet favorable. Someone or something always stepping in before you can reach the water. Jesus' question to the man at Bethesda is the same question Step 3 L4 asks: wilt thou be made whole? The answer is either yes — with the action that follows — or it is an explanation.

The decision of Step 3, when it is real, changes what the person is from that moment forward. Not because they feel different — because they have placed something they were governing under a different governance. That transfer is the beginning of a life that works differently than the one that brought them here.

The person who has genuinely surrendered does not fear what the inventory will find. What belongs to God can be looked at honestly.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 3 Lesson 4 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson does the completion work of Step 3. Its function is accountability — not condemnation, not celebration, but honest examination of whether the decision made in Step 3 L1 has produced actual surrender or only the intention of surrender. The heart is corrupt and should not be consulted at all Proverbs 16:9 — the heart devises but the LORD directs. Genuine surrender in Step 3 is not the elimination of thought but the placement of direction under God rather than the self.

lessons.title: Search me O God — the searching and fearless moral inventory and why God asks for it
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When God spoke to Samuel concerning a new king for Israel, He said: "the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." The inventory of Step 4 begins at the same place God begins — not the outward appearance but what is actually there. David, who would be chosen that day, later wrote: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." The inventory is not self-punishment. It is the invitation for God to do what He was always going to do — reach past the surface to what is real.

Step 3 was a decision. What follows now is the evidence of whether that decision was real — or only the intention of one.

The God before whom this inventory is being made already knows every line of it. He is one Spirit, one LORD — Psalm 139:1-4 KJV — and He asks for the inventory not because He needs the information, but because the student does.

The inventory of Step 4 works in both directions. It reveals what has been living in the life — but it also reveals what name the life has been lived under. Every pattern in the inventory is the fruit of a governing authority. The honest inventory does not merely list sins. It reveals the name under which those sins were produced.

The inventory is honest accounting before God. It is not coincidental that this follows surrender — it is the natural next movement of genuine repentance. The person who has truly turned does not fear looking at what the turning is leaving behind.

WHAT THE INVENTORY IS

"Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting." — Psalm 139:23-24 KJV The inventory is a written, honest accounting of what has been living in the life — the resentments, the fears, the harmful patterns, the areas where the self has operated outside of what God requires. It is not a confession to be performed. It is an examination to be completed. "The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly." — Proverbs 20:27 KJV God uses the human spirit as the instrument of the search. The inventory is not a search conducted alone — it is a search conducted by a person whose spirit has been made available to the God who uses it as His candle. Bring the candle into the rooms that have been kept dark.

David wrote Psalm 139 — Search me, O God — after the worst failure of his life. The inventory does not require a clean record. It requires an honest one.

WHY THE INVENTORY IS NECESSARY

Most people who arrive at Step 4 carry years of accumulated material they have never examined honestly. Not because they are dishonest people — but because the examination is uncomfortable and the self protects what it has not processed. As Step 1 L3 established from John 3:20 — the things closest to the darkness are the last ones the person sees. The darkness that hates the light of examination is not only in the obvious things. It is in the small sustained resentments that have been justified for years. It is in the fear that has been driving decisions no one else has seen. It is in the pattern of self-protection that has damaged relationships the person values. Bringing it into the light is not the punishment — it is the beginning of the relief.

THE FOUR COLUMNS

The inventory is not a journal of feelings. It is a structured accounting with four parts for every entry:

1. Who or what — the person, institution, or situation 2. What happened — what they did or what occurred 3. How it affected me — my self-esteem, security, relationships, finances, or physical safety 4. My part — what I contributed, what I did with what happened The fourth column is where most people resist. It is not an erasure of what was done to them — genuine harm is real and the inventory does not minimize it. It is the honest accounting of what the person did with the harm they received. That accounting is what Step 4 actually requires.

WHAT TO INCLUDE

Every resentment. Every fear. Every harm caused. Every pattern of behavior that has damaged others or damaged the self. The inventory is thorough because the transformation needs accurate information. A partial inventory produces a partial result. "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." — Proverbs 28:13 KJV The covering does not protect — it prevents the mercy that is waiting on the other side of the honest accounting.

DAVID — THE INVENTORY GOD ASKED FOR

David — the name means beloved. And he was. Scripture says he was a man after God's own heart before the events of 2 Samuel 11 — before Bathsheba, before Uriah, before the sequence of decisions that produced the worst chapter of his life.

After it, God sent Nathan the prophet. Not to condemn David in public. To bring him to an honest accounting in private.

Nathan told a story — a rich man, a poor man, one lamb — and David erupted in judgment against the rich man. "The man who did this shall surely die." And Nathan said: "Thou art the man."

David did not have the luxury of the inventory Step 4 provides. He had a prophet who brought it to him. But the inventory Nathan conducted and the inventory Step 4 asks for are the same thing: an honest accounting, in specific terms, of what the heart has done and what it has cost others.

Psalm 51 is David's response to that inventory. It is the record of what a person writes when they have looked honestly at what they have done. "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness... I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me." — Psalm 51:1,3 KJV

He did not say: I made some mistakes. He said: I acknowledge my transgressions. The inventory that produced Psalm 51 is a Step 4 inventory.

David was in the lowest moral position of his life when God sent Nathan. The beloved man. The man after God's own heart. At the bottom of what his choices had produced — and that is precisely where God began the work of restoration.

The inventory is not the end of what you have done. It is the beginning of what God will do with your honesty about it.

THE ROAD FORWARD

Scripture shows consistently that honest examination before God precedes restoration. David examined. Job examined. Paul examined. The inventory is not novel — it is the ancient practice of the person who takes God's governance seriously.

The inventory is written in Step 4 and shared in Step 5. Do not skip ahead to Step 5 before the writing is done. The sharing of what has not been fully written is not Step 5 — it is the appearance of Step 5. Complete the inventory. Write every column. Then go to Step 5.

The person who emerges from an honest Step 4 knows themselves differently. Not more harshly — more accurately. And the person who knows themselves accurately before God is the person God can actually work with. The inventory is not the end. It is the clearing that makes the next step possible.

What is written on these pages does not yet have its full power. There is something the next step requires that this one alone cannot accomplish.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Psalm 139:23-24 KJV — "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting."

ASSIGNMENT

Begin the inventory 1. Get a notebook dedicated to Step 4. Write the four column headers on the first page. 2. Write the names of the ten people or situations that produce the strongest reaction when you think of them. These are your starting point. 3. Fill in columns one through three for each. The fourth column comes in Lesson 2. 4. Pray Psalm 139:23-24 before each writing session. Due: Before L...

choices: To punish him for sin — Step 4 is the acknowledgment of punishment deserved
To search his heart know his thoughts and see any wicked way — Step 4 is the same invitation for God to examine honestly what is actually there
To restore his feelings — Step 4 is primarily an emotional healing exercise

To reveal prophecy — Step 4 opens spiritual gifts Psalm 139:23-24 — search me, know my heart, try me, know my thoughts, see if there be any wicked way. The inventory is the posture of making the inner life available for the examination God was always going to conduct.

choices: Covering produces peace; confession produces discomfort

Covering produces no prosperity; confession and forsaking produce mercy

Covering is acceptable until Step 5; confession belongs in Step 5 only Proverbs 28:13 — he that covereth his sins shall not prosper. The covering does not protect the person — it prevents the mercy that is available on the other side of the honest accounting.

lessons.title: Know my heart — resentment, fear, and the most dangerous areas of the inventory
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Of all the things Paul warned the church at Ephesus to guard against, he named this one with particular urgency: "Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled." The root. Not the visible offense but the root under the ground — the thing that produces fruit long after the original wound.

Step 3 was a decision. What follows now is the evidence of whether that decision was real — or only the intention of one.

Taking the inventory is an act of faith — specifically the faith that says: what God shows me in this process, however uncomfortable, is better than what I have been protecting by not looking. The person who writes the inventory honestly is acting on what they believe about God's capacity to handle what the inventory reveals. That act — the writing, the looking, the naming — is faith made visible.

The God before whom this inventory is being made already knows every line of it. He is one Spirit, one LORD — Psalm 139:1-4 KJV — and He asks for the inventory not because He needs the information, but because the student does.

The inventory is honest accounting before God. It is not coincidental that this follows surrender — it is the natural next movement of genuine repentance. The person who has truly turned does not fear looking at what the turning is leaving behind.

Resentment and fear are the two most common roots in the inventory. They are also the two most commonly protected. This lesson gives them the same scrutiny Hebrews 12:15 requires.

RESENTMENT — THE ROOT THAT CONSUMES THE CONTAINER

"Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled." — Hebrews 12:15 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers — showing them what unaddressed bitterness does to a community and to the person carrying it. The root of bitterness troubles the person. It defiles others. It reaches beyond the original wound and poisons what the wound had nothing to do with. The word resentment means literally to re-feel. Every time the resentment surfaces — in the moment before sleep, at the mention of the name, in the situation that resembles the original — the person re-experiences the original wound. The re-feeling is not healing. It is consumption. The resentment is consuming the container it is stored in. Write every resentment in the inventory. Not the ones that seem significant enough to mention. Every one. The small sustained ones are often more damaging than the large obvious ones — because the large ones the person named and addressed. The small ones have been running unexamined for years.

David wrote Psalm 139 — Search me, O God — after the worst failure of his life. The inventory does not require a clean record. It requires an honest one.

THE FOURTH COLUMN ON RESENTMENT

The fourth column does not ask whether the resentment was justified. It asks: what did I do with the wound? Did I use it as a reason to harm someone else? Did I use it as a license for behavior I knew was wrong? Did I hold it as a justification for not doing what God was clearly asking? The fourth column is the honest accounting of what the resentment was used for — after the original wound was received.

FEAR — THE DRIVER BEHIND THE DECISIONS

"For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." — 2 Timothy 1:7 KJV Paul wrote this to Timothy — a young evangelist who carried significant responsibility. The spirit of fear has a source, and it is not God. What God gives is the spirit of power, love, and sound mind. Fear is the counterfeit of each of these — it produces paralysis instead of power, self-protection instead of love, and anxious distorted thinking instead of the sound mind. Fear drives more decisions in the addicted life than most people realize. Fear of abandonment. Fear of inadequacy. Fear of what will happen without the substance. Fear of other people's opinions. Fear of success as much as fear of failure. List every fear in the inventory alongside the resentments.

THE FOURTH COLUMN ON FEAR

What has the fear been governing? What decisions were made from fear that should have been made from faith? What relationships were managed from the fear of abandonment rather than from genuine love? What opportunities were refused because of the fear of failure? The fourth column on fear is the honest accounting of how fear has been functioning as the operating system of the life.

THE TRIGGER COLUMN — INVENTORY APPLIED TO THE FUTURE

The resentment and fear columns look backward — at what has happened and what has driven the decisions. The trigger column looks both backward and forward: what specific situations, people, emotional states, and environments have the longest history of preceding the worst choices?

This is inventory applied to the future. The honest examination of Step 4 is not complete without asking: where am I most likely to be ambushed going forward, based on the pattern this inventory reveals?

The trigger column has four categories:

SITUATIONS — what types of events, gatherings, or circumstances have historically preceded using? (celebrations, conflicts, boredom, specific time periods — holidays, weekends, evenings alone)

PEOPLE — who, by name, has a history of producing the pull? This is not a list of people to condemn. It is a list of relationships that require a plan.

EMOTIONAL STATES — what internal conditions have most reliably opened the door? (loneliness, anger, success, rejection, fear of abandonment, financial stress)

ENVIRONMENTS — what physical locations carry the strongest associative pull?

Write all four categories. Give them to your mentor before Step 5. The trigger column is not completed once — it is revisited in the daily examination of Step 10 and updated as the pattern becomes clearer.

"A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished." — Proverbs 22:3 KJV

Foreseeing is not weakness. It is the practice of the prudent person who has taken the inventory honestly and is now applying what the inventory revealed.

THE SELF-ESTEEM, SECURITY, AMBITION, AND PERSONAL RELATIONS COLUMNS

For every resentment and fear, mark which of these four areas was affected: - Self-esteem: how I see myself Security: what I feel I need to be safe - Ambitions: what I am trying to accomplish or protect - Personal relations:

how specific relationships were affected Most entries will touch more than one. The pattern across multiple entries shows what the self has been organized around — what it has been protecting, pursuing, or trying to maintain at cost to everything else. "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" — Psalm 27:1 KJV The answer to the fear inventory is not the absence of the things feared. It is the presence of the One who is sufficient in the face of every one of them. The inventory names the fear. The road forward names the answer.

Scripture shows consistently that honest examination before God precedes restoration. David examined. Job examined. Paul examined. The inventory is not novel — it is the ancient practice of the person who takes God's governance seriously.

WHAT THE SPIRIT OF MAN HEARS

"The spirit of man is the candle of the LORD, searching all the inward parts of the belly." — Proverbs 20:27 KJV The spirit of man is the instrument God uses to illuminate what is in the inner life. The inventory is not only a mental exercise — it is the experience of the spirit, made available to God, beginning to function as the candle He intended it to be: illuminating what the outer person cannot see, reaching what the mind's examination cannot reach. Jesus told Nicodemus that the wind blows where it will and thou hearest the sound of it — so is every one born of the Spirit. The Spirit's presence produces evidence that can be heard. The spirit of man, when it is genuinely made available to God, begins to register what the candle reveals — and that registration has a quality that is different from the ordinary noise of the mind. There is a sound in the inner life when the genuine work is happening. The inventory, when it reaches the real material, produces that sound. What is the candle showing you in the examination that the outer examination could not reach?

The person who emerges from an honest Step 4 knows themselves differently. Not more harshly — more accurately. And the person who knows themselves accurately before God is the person God can actually work with. The inventory is not the end. It is the clearing that makes the next step possible.

lessons.title: And see if there be any wicked way in me — harms, defects, and the complete picture
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When Jesus described what to do if you are bringing your gift to the altar and remember that your brother has something against you — He was not describing a hypothetical. He was describing the ordinary reality of people who have harmed others and have not addressed it. The inventory of harms is the honest accounting of who has something against you. Not who harmed you. Who you harmed. This is the column most people resist most. It is also the column that produces the most freedom.

Step 3 was a decision. What follows now is the evidence of whether that decision was real — or only the intention of one.

The inventory is honest accounting before God. It is not coincidental that this follows surrender — it is the natural next movement of genuine repentance. The person who has truly turned does not fear looking at what the turning is leaving behind.

HARMS CAUSED — THE HONEST LIST

"Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother." — Matthew 5:23-24 KJV The harms column asks one question: who has something against me? Write every name. Do not qualify by whether the harm was intentional, whether the other person contributed, or whether the relationship has since improved. Write the name and what happened. The amends come in Step 9. This step is the list. Include harms to: - Family members — the most common category and the most commonly minimized - People in past relationships — the harm that was caused even where harm was also received - Employers and colleagues — the theft of time, trust, and resources - Institutions — the financial, legal, and ethical harms - The self — the body harmed, the potential surrendered, the years consumed

David wrote Psalm 139 — Search me, O God — after the worst failure of his life. The inventory does not require a clean record. It requires an honest one.

CHARACTER DEFECTS — SEEING THE PATTERN

Scripture shows consistently that honest examination before God precedes restoration. David examined. Job examined. Paul examined. The inventory is not novel — it is the ancient practice of the person who takes God's governance seriously.

"But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man. For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies." — Matthew 15:18-19 KJV The harms are the fruit. The character defects are what produced them. The inventory of defects looks at the pattern across the harms column — not each incident in isolation but the trait of character that kept producing the same kind of harm in different situations. Common defects the inventory reveals: - Dishonesty — the habit of managing what others see - Self-seeking — the pattern of using others to meet the self's needs - Inconsideration — the consistent failure to account for the effect of decisions on others - Pride — the refusal to admit error or receive correction - Fear-driven control — the management of relationships to prevent what is feared Name the defects. Not as condemnation — as the honest identification of what Step 6 will ask God to remove.

THE LUST OF THE FLESH THE LUST OF THE EYES AND THE PRIDE OF LIFE

"For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world." — 1 John 2:16 KJV

These three categories cover the full range of the defects the inventory reveals. The lust of the flesh: appetite driven. The lust of the eyes: desire for what is seen. The pride of life: the self-promotion and self-protection that governs when the self is on the throne. Most character defects sort into one of these three. Locate yours.

THE THREE TEMPTATIONS — SATAN'S UNCHANGING STRATEGY

"Lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices." — 2 Corinthians 2:11 KJV

Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Corinth — establishing a principle that runs through every step of this program: the person who understands how the enemy works is not helpless against him. Ignorance is not humility. Naming the playbook is not paranoia. It is the honest assessment that Scripture itself demands — and the prerequisite for the armor that Ephesians 6 provides.

The devices are not new. They have not changed. And understanding them is the beginning of not being taken advantage of by them.

"For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world." — 1 John 2:16 KJV These three are not random. They are the only three categories Satan has ever used. He has been working from the same playbook since the garden — and the inventory of your Step 4 will show that every harm you have caused and every harm that has been done to you traces back to one or more of them.

WHEN SATAN USED THEM ON ADAM AND EVE

"And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food" — the lust of the flesh: the appetite, the craving, the physical want that overrides the instruction. "and that it was pleasant to the eyes" — the lust of the eyes: the desire for what is seen, the covetousness of what belongs to someone else or what has been forbidden. "and a tree to be desired to make one wise" — the pride of life: the self-promotion, the desire to be more than what God made, to occupy the throne that belongs to God alone. Three categories. One temptation. And it worked — not because the temptation was unprecedented, but because the pattern was not recognized and the Word was not held.

WHEN SATAN USED THEM ON JESUS

Satan brought the same three categories to Jesus in the wilderness — Matthew 4:1-11 KJV. "Command that these stones be made bread" — the lust of the flesh: the legitimate need (hunger) weaponized as the justification for stepping outside of God's timing and provision. "Cast thyself down: for the angels shall bear thee up" — the pride of life: the temptation to prove, to perform, to demand that God demonstrate His care by protecting a presumptuous act. "All these kingdoms will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me" — the lust of the eyes: the offer of what can be seen, the shortcut that bypasses the cross, the prize without the obedience. Each time, Jesus answered the same way: "It is written." Not with an argument. Not with a feeling. Not with His own reasoning about what seemed reasonable. With the Word. The Scripture as the instrument of reproof — exposing the false, establishing the true, shutting the door the temptation had tried to open. "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." — 2 Timothy 3:16 KJV Reproof is the exposure of what is false in the light of what is true. Jesus demonstrated it in the wilderness. The inventory you are completing in Step 4 is the same instrument applied to your own life — the Word brought to bear on the patterns that have run under the radar of your conscious reasoning, exposing what the three temptations produced in you across years of unchallenged operation.

THE RECOVERY APPLICATION

Look at the harms column of your inventory through this lens. Every harm caused or received will sort into one of the three categories. The harm driven by appetite — substances, food, sex — the lust of the flesh. The harm driven by what was seen and wanted — money, status, another person's life or spouse or opportunity — the lust of the eyes. The harm driven by the need to be more, to be seen as more, to protect the self's position at any cost — the pride of life. The pattern is not unique to you. It is the oldest pattern in human history. Satan has never updated the playbook because he has never needed to. The same three categories that worked in the garden have worked in every generation since. But Jesus showed that the Word, applied specifically to the specific temptation in the specific moment, is sufficient to close the door. Not the memory of the Word. The Word itself — spoken, quoted, held to. "It is written." That is the recovery from the three temptations. Not willpower. Not insight. Not a better understanding of your triggers. The Word applied as reproof to the three categories that have been running your life.

THE MOMENT OF HONESTY

"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9 KJV The promise is not conditional on the severity of what is confessed. It is conditional on the honesty of the confession. Every harm included in the inventory is a candidate for the cleansing that 1 John 1:9 promises. Every harm omitted is a candidate for continuing to operate in the life.

THE GRIEF COLUMN — WHAT THE ADDICTION TOOK FROM YOU

The inventory of harms caused is not complete without the accounting of harms received — specifically, what the addiction took from your own life.

This is not self-pity. Self-pity uses the losses as a reason to continue. This is honest grief — naming what was consumed so that the remaining life can be given to something that does not consume it.

What were the years when you could have been present that you were absent? What relationships were available to you that the addiction made unavailable? What version of yourself — the parent, the spouse, the child, the worker, the person — did not exist because the addiction was existing in that space?

Write it. Not to punish yourself. To grieve it honestly — because the grief that is named before God is the grief that receives the promise of Joel 2:25: I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.

The restoration cannot reach what has not been honestly grieved. Grieve it. Then receive what comes after.

THE NAME THAT WAS ALWAYS IN THE PROMISE

The inventory of Step 4 traces what has lived in the life. The covenant traces what God placed in history from the beginning — and what He called it.

"For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace." — Isaiah 9:6 KJV

The prophet Isaiah, seven centuries before the manger, named the child who would be born and called Him the mighty God — the everlasting Father. Not a representative of the Father. The Father. The same God who made all things, arriving as a child, carrying in one person the complete identity of the One who has always been.

The inventory the student is writing in Step 4 is being made before that God — the One who Isaiah saw coming, the One John identified as the Word made flesh, the One Paul called the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The honest accounting of Step 4 is not made before an idea. It is made before the God who put His name on the promise seven hundred years before the promise arrived.

What does it mean that the God before whom you are making this inventory knew your name before Isaiah wrote His?

THE ROAD FORWARD

The inventory is now complete — resentments, fears, harms, and defects all on paper. Lesson 4 closes Step 4 by processing what the inventory shows and preparing the ground for Step 5.

The person who emerges from an honest Step 4 knows themselves differently. Not more harshly — more accurately. And the person who knows themselves accurately before God is the person God can actually work with. The inventory is not the end. It is the clearing that makes the next step possible.

What is written on these pages does not yet have its full power. There is something the next step requires that this one alone cannot accomplish.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 4 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. This is the hardest writing session of the inventory. The harms column requires honesty about what the person did — not what was done to them. The character defects column requires the student to see the pattern rather than the isolated incidents. Both require pastoral support. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER Matthew 5:23-24 is in the Sermon on the Mount — Jesus speaking to people under the old covenant who are about to watch Him establish the new one. The princ...

ASSIGNMENT

Harms and defects columns 1. Write the harms column: who has something against you? Write every name and what happened. 2. Look across the harms column and name the character defects — the repeated traits that kept producing the same result. 3. Sort your defects into 1 John 2:16 categories: flesh, eyes, or pride. Which category is largest? 4. Bring the completed inventory to your mentor. All four ...

lessons.title: What the inventory reveals — completing Step 4 and receiving what God shows
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When Solomon completed the temple and the cloud filled the house of the LORD, the priests could not stand to minister. The presence of God occupies what has been prepared for Him and made available to Him. Step 4 is the preparation — the honest clearing of what has been accumulating in the inner life. What the inventory reveals is not condemnation. It is the accurate picture of what needs to be moved before the filling can happen.

Step 3 was a decision. What follows now is the evidence of whether that decision was real — or only the intention of one.

The inventory is honest accounting before God. It is not coincidental that this follows surrender — it is the natural next movement of genuine repentance. The person who has truly turned does not fear looking at what the turning is leaving behind.

WHAT THE INVENTORY REVEALS

The inventory is now written. Look at it honestly — not with shame, not with self-contempt, but with the same honest attention a physician brings to an accurate diagnosis. What does it show? Most inventories reveal one or more of the following patterns: The resentment pattern: specific relationships or institutions that have been held in resentment for years — producing decisions, behaviors, and damage that extended far beyond the original wound. The fear pattern: a specific fear — usually of abandonment, inadequacy, or loss of control — that has been the actual governing principle of decisions the person believed were made for other reasons. The harm pattern: a consistent way of harming others that appears across different relationships and different circumstances — showing that the issue is not the situations but the character defect producing the same result in each one. The hiding pattern: the long-term management of what is seen — the consistent gap between the person presented to the world and the person that the inventory has now described on paper. Name what you see. Not to condemn it. To see it clearly enough that Step 5 can share it and Steps 6 and 7 can address it.

David wrote Psalm 139 — Search me, O God — after the worst failure of his life. The inventory does not require a clean record. It requires an honest one.

WALKING IN THE LIGHT

"But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." — 1 John 1:7 KJV Walking in the light does not mean living without sin. It means living without hiding. The person who walks in the light brings what is actually there into the open — before God and, in Step 5, before another human being. The blood cleanses what is brought into the light. It cannot reach what is kept in the dark. The inventory is the act of walking in the light. It is the willingness to let what has been hidden be seen — by God first, by the self through the writing, and by another person in Step 5.

THE RELIEF THAT FOLLOWS HONESTY

"Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is he unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile." — Psalm 32:1-2 KJV

David wrote Psalm 32 after the experience of both hiding and honesty — describing the physical and spiritual cost of the covering and the relief of the open acknowledgment. No guile. No hidden thing requiring management. The person described in Psalm 32:2 is not a person who has never sinned. It is a person in whose spirit there is no longer any guile — no hidden management, no gap between the inner reality and what is presented. That is the destination the inventory is pointed toward. Not the absence of a past — but a present in which what the past produced is no longer hidden.

THE ROAD TO STEP 5

The inventory is complete. Do not sit with it alone. The design of the program places another human being in Step 5 — not because God requires the witness but because the human being carrying the inventory requires it. The shame that protected the darkest entries from being written cannot survive a second reading — this time out loud, to someone who receives what is shared without condemnation. Take the inventory to your mentor within the week. Do not revise it. Do not add what seems more acceptable. Read what you wrote.

Scripture shows consistently that honest examination before God precedes restoration. David examined. Job examined. Paul examined. The inventory is not novel — it is the ancient practice of the person who takes God's governance seriously.

PENIEL — YOU DO NOT LEAVE THE SAME WAY YOU ENTERED

Jacob did not go looking for a fight that night at the ford of Jabbok. He sent everyone and everything ahead of him and stayed alone — which is often the posture of the person who is about to encounter God most directly. And something met him. Something he wrestled with through the entire night, until the breaking of the day. "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day... And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." — Genesis 32:24, 26 KJV Jacob held on. He came away limping — changed in his body, which is where all genuine change lands eventually. And he came away with a new name. Israel. No longer Jacob — the supplanter, the one who grabs and schemes. Israel — the one who has wrestled with God and prevailed. Peniel means the face of God. And Jacob named it that because he had looked at the face of God and lived — and what he saw had changed what he was called. The completed inventory is its own Peniel. The person who has wrestled honestly with what the inner life contained — who stayed in the examination when everything in the flesh wanted to send it across the river ahead of them — comes out of Step 4 with something they did not have when they entered: an honest account of who they actually are. The name the addiction had been calling them. The name the flesh had been ratifying. The process that began at the breaking of the day produces the new name. You do not leave the inventory the same way you entered it.

The person who emerges from an honest Step 4 knows themselves differently. Not more harshly — more accurately. And the person who knows themselves accurately before God is the person God can actually work with. The inventory is not the end. It is the clearing that makes the next step possible.

What is written on these pages does not yet have its full power. There is something the next step requires that this one alone cannot accomplish.

TEACHER NOTES

The goal is honest processing of what the inventory has shown — not emotional processing, not extensive discussion, but clear-eyed acknowledgment of the pattern and an immediate movement toward Step 5. lessons.title: Confess your faults one to another — admitted to God, to ourselves, and to another human being
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The covenant pattern of confession runs from the tabernacle to the New Testament. Under the old covenant, the priest laid the sins of the people on the head of the scapegoat — the act of transference required the naming, the acknowledgment, the public placement of what had been carried. The pattern was never private management. It was always the bringing of what was hidden into the presence of God. James 5:16 is written in the New Testament, to people already in the covenant community, describing the ongoing practice of the life that has genuinely entered it. The confession is mutual — one to another, not only upward. The prayer is mutual. And the healing follows. The healing. Not the feeling better. The healing — the actual addressing of what has been brought into the light. "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." — James 5:16 KJV The step that the inventory prepared for. The step that brings what was written into the presence of another person. Admitted — to God, to ourselves through the inventory, and now to another human being. The triple admission is the completion of the Step 4 honesty extended into relationship.

In Step 4 we looked honestly at what the unmanageable life had actually produced — not to condemn, but to name clearly what needed to change. Step 5 brings it into the light.

The God to whom this confession is made is not distant. He is one Spirit who has been present for everything being named — not approving, but present. Knowing.

Acts 22:16 records the instruction given to Paul after his encounter on the Damascus road. He had believed. He had seen. He had been fasting and praying for three days. And still Ananias said: "Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord." The calling on the name and the washing away of sins are one action described two ways. This is worth noticing.

There is a reason the Scripture connects confession and healing in the same sentence. What is confessed before God and another person is not merely acknowledged — it is brought into the light where repentance can complete its work. The confession of Step 5 is repentance made specific.

WHAT THE TEXT SHOWS

James wrote confess your faults — not your achievements, not your spiritual insights, your faults. The specific things that were wrong. The patterns the inventory revealed. The harms that were done. In the presence of another person who is also in the community of those who have received what God promises. And pray one for another. The confession is received in the context of prayer — not in the context of judgment, not in the context of advice, not in the context of assessment. The other person receives the confession and brings it to God in prayer. That is the posture Step 5 requires from both the person confessing and the person receiving. That ye may be healed. The healing is the promised result of the confession made in this context. Not the result of having told someone — but of having brought what was hidden into the light in the context of genuine covenant community.

The woman at the well had been through five marriages and was living with a sixth man when Jesus met her. He did not require her history to be different. He offered living water exactly where she was.

WHY ANOTHER PERSON IS REQUIRED

The confession to God alone — without the human witness — is real. But the experience of being known by another person and still received is a different kind of healing than the private prayer produces. The person who

has confessed everything to God alone has done something real. They have not yet experienced being known by a human witness and received without rejection. That experience is what the human heart needs — and what Step 5 provides. "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." — Matthew 18:20 KJV Jesus said this in the Gospels — describing the specific presence available in the gathered relationship. The presence of God in the Step 5 confession is not a metaphor. It is the promised reality of the covenant community gathered in His name around the specific, honest, brought-into-the-light disclosure of what was in the inventory.

THE WOMAN WHO COULD NOT STOP BLEEDING — WHAT COMES AFTER TWELVE YEARS OF HIDING

Mark 5 records the woman who had an issue of blood for twelve years. Twelve years. She had spent everything she had on physicians and was no better — she was worse. And she was ceremonially unclean, which meant she could not enter the temple, could not be in a crowd without contaminating those she touched, could not live a normal social life.

She came to Jesus in the crowd — which she was not supposed to do — and touched the hem of His garment from behind. She did not announce herself. She did not ask permission. She touched the hem and immediately the fountain of her blood was dried up.

And Jesus stopped and said: "Who touched my clothes?" — Mark 5:30 KJV

His disciples were baffled. A crowd was pressing against Him and He was asking who touched Him. But Jesus perceived that power had gone out of Him. He knew the difference between the crowd pressing against Him and a specific person reaching for Him in faith.

"But the woman fearing and trembling, knowing what was done in her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth." — Mark 5:33 KJV

She told him all the truth. The whole story. Twelve years. All the physicians. All the money. The failure of every other solution. In public, in front of a crowd, she told Him everything.

She had been hiding for twelve years. The hiding was over in one sentence of honest disclosure.

"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." — Mark 5:34 KJV

Daughter. He named her. The woman who had been unclean and untouchable for twelve years was named by Jesus as daughter in front of everyone who heard it.

Step 5 is the moment the hiding ends. It is the reaching through the crowd to tell the truth — all of it — to God and to another person. The fear and the trembling are not reasons to stay hidden. They are the condition in which the woman came forward. She was afraid and she told the truth anyway.

That is Step 5. And what follows the telling is the same thing that followed hers: go in peace.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern James records — confess your faults one to another and pray one for another, that ye may be healed — is not a suggestion. It is the God-ordained mechanics of how healing actually travels. It moves through relationship, not in isolation.

The nature and purpose of the confession have been established. Lesson 2 addresses what specifically happens when the confession is made — and what it produces in the person and the relationship. THE WITNESS "It is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth." — 1 John 5:6 KJV John wrote this to born-again believers — pointing to the Spirit as the One who bears witness to what is true. The confession of Step 5 is not only the human act of speaking what has been hidden. It is the moment of alignment between what the person says and what the Spirit has always known to be true. The Spirit bears witness to the honest confession — not as an outside observer but as the inner witness that confirms: this is true, this is what was there, this is the honest accounting. A witness is not a voice alone. A witness is the confirmation of truth by one who was present. The Spirit was present for all of it — the years, the hiding, the inventory entries, the pattern. When the honest confession is made, the Spirit who was present bears witness that it is true. And the witness that matters — the witness that produces the settled knowing — is not the self's own voice. It is the voice that confirms from outside the self. That is the witness of Step 5.

SPECIFICITY — VAGUENESS IS WHERE AVOIDANCE LIVES

One of the most important moments in Step 5 is when vague language becomes specific. Not "I had some problems" but naming exactly what happened and to whom. The vague version protects the person from the full weight of what is true. The specific version is what actually produces movement. Every sponsor who has sat with someone working Step 5 knows the moment when the inventory stops being a summary and becomes a name, a date, a specific act — and that is the moment something actually shifts. The same precision runs through the covenant. In the entire history of God's dealings with His people, He progressively revealed more of Himself as their needs required it. When Abraham needed provision, He revealed Himself as Jehovah-jireh. When Israel needed healing, He was Jehovah-rapha. When they needed victory, Jehovah-nissi. Sixteen compound names across the Old Testament — each one revealing a specific aspect, none of them revealing the saving name. The saving name was withheld. It was secret. When Jacob wrestled with the Angel of the LORD and asked for His name, the Angel would not tell him. What Jacob received instead was the thing wrestling always produces when it is done honestly — a new name for himself. The specificity of confession in Step 5 is its own form of wrestling: you hold on through the night, you come out limping, and you come out

named differently. When Manoah asked the same question, the answer was: "Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?" — Judges 13:18 KJV. The name was coming. The time had not arrived. "And thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." — Matthew 1:21 KJV When the fullness of time came, the name was given. Not a title. Not a category. Not Father, Son, and Holy Ghost as three separate names — one name. Jesus. The Hebrew roots reach back to Jehoshua — Jehovah and Yasha — meaning Jehovah is Salvation. Every compound name from the Old Testament collapses into this one: the Jehovah who provides, heals, gives victory, brings peace — revealed at last in the name that saves. The specificity the confession of Step 5 requires is the same specificity the covenant requires. Not a vague reaching toward God. The specific name. "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." — Acts 4:12 KJV Apply the discipline of Step 5 here: what name are you calling on?

The person who has completed Step 5 honestly is no longer carrying alone what was always too heavy to carry alone. The secrecy is broken. The isolation that fed the bondage has been interrupted. That is not a small thing. It is the condition the next steps require.

Naming it was the first movement. What comes next requires a different kind of willingness — not just to see it, but to let it go.

■ James 5:16 KJV — "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."

■ Matthew 18:20 KJV — "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."

The confession is mutual and specific. The prayer is the posture of reception. The healing is the result. But the experience of being known completely by a human witness — every specific fault, every pattern, every harm — and being received without rejection is a healing that private prayer alone does not produce.

lessons.title: And pray one for another — what confession produces and the community it builds
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Psalm 32 was written after confession — after David had stopped holding what was killing him from within and brought it into the open. The psalm begins at the end of the story: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. It then goes back and describes what the holding cost — the bones waxed old, the moisture turned to drought — and what the release produced. The psalm is the testimony of what Step 5 produces when it is done honestly.

In Step 4 we looked honestly at what the unmanageable life had actually produced — not to condemn, but to name clearly what needed to change. Step 5 brings it into the light.

The confession of Step 5 is an act of obedient faith. The person who tells the truth in Step 5 is not certain the truth will be received well. They confess because they believe that what God has said about confession — that it produces healing (James 5:16), that it breaks the power of secrecy — is more true than what the fear tells them. The act of confession is faith that has moved from belief to obedience.

The God to whom this confession is made is not distant. He is one Spirit who has been present for everything being named — not approving, but present. Knowing.

There is a reason the Scripture connects confession and healing in the same sentence. What is confessed before God and another person is not merely acknowledged — it is brought into the light where repentance can complete its work. The confession of Step 5 is repentance made specific.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS IN THE CONFESSION

The confession of Step 5 is not a recitation. It is the actual speaking aloud of what was written — every item, every pattern, every harm, every defect named in the inventory — in the presence of another person who receives it in the posture of prayer. What happens during the confession: the weight changes. Something that has been carried as a private burden, managed in isolation, shifts when it is spoken in the presence of a witness. The spoken word in the covenant context carries a different weight than the written word in the private journal. Not because the content has changed. Because the isolation has ended. "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." — James 5:16 KJV The healing that James describes is not the healing of shame alone — though shame is often part of what is healed. It is the healing of the separation that the unconfessed fault maintained. The fault between the person and God. The fault between the person and themselves. The fault between the person and the community. The confession addressed all three — because the triple admission of Step 5 restores what the triple separation of unconfessed sin had broken.

The woman at the well had been through five marriages and was living with a sixth man when Jesus met her. He did not require her history to be different. He offered living water exactly where she was.

WHAT CONFESSION PRODUCES

It produces relief. Not the false relief of continuing to manage — the genuine relief of the burden having been carried to the place it was designed to be deposited. The person who has completed Step 5 honestly typically reports feeling lighter — not because the circumstances changed but because the isolation that the unconfessed burden required is over.

It produces clarity. The patterns that were difficult to see while managing the story become clear when spoken aloud in the presence of a witness. The person hears themselves name what they had been protecting — and often for the first time sees it clearly enough to understand what Step 6 will present for removal. It produces connection. The experience of being fully known and fully received is the beginning of the genuine human community that the covenant has always been building toward. The person who has been fully known by their mentor — every fault named, every harm spoken — and received without rejection has experienced what the covenant community is designed to provide.

WHAT REMAINS AFTER THE CONFESSION

"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." — Romans 8:1 KJV Paul addressed this declaration to born-again believers — standing on the ground of what genuine obedience had produced. The confession of Step 5 is an act of walking in the light — walking not after the flesh but after the Spirit, in the posture of honesty that the Spirit sustains. The ground the person stands on after Step 5 is not the ground of performance. It is the ground of confession received — the ground that Romans 8:1 describes.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern James records — confess your faults one to another and pray one for another, that ye may be healed — is not a suggestion. It is the God-ordained mechanics of how healing actually travels. It moves through relationship, not in isolation.

The confession has been made. What it produced has been named. Lesson 3 addresses the ongoing practice of the honesty that Step 5 established — the life without secrets that the confession opened.

HANNAH — THE CRY THAT CAME OUT

"And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore... and Hannah prayed, and said, My heart rejoiceth in the LORD, mine horn is exalted in the LORD." — 1 Samuel 1:10, 2:1 KJV Hannah had been in her condition for years. Provoked by the woman who had what she lacked. Misunderstood by the priest who watched her lips moving without hearing her words and assumed she was drunk. Loved genuinely by her husband and still profoundly alone in the specific grief that her love could not reach. She prayed in such distress that Eli the priest approached her and said: put away thy wine. She answered: I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit: I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but have poured out my soul before the

LORD.

She poured out her soul before the LORD. The verb is specific — not spoken a prayer, not presented a request, but poured out. Like a vessel tipped over. What was in her, out. The full measure of the specific grief, the particular bitterness, the named sorrow she had been carrying without being able to fully articulate it even to the people who loved her — all of it, out before God. Eli then gave her his blessing and she went her way and her countenance was no more sad. The countenance changed before the answer came. She ate. She was no longer sad. Not because the condition had changed — it had not, not yet. Because the pouring out had produced something that the years of carrying had not. The honest, full, uninhibited confession before God — the pouring out that Step 5 requires — does not wait for the circumstances to change before it changes the person.

The person who has completed Step 5 honestly is no longer carrying alone what was always too heavy to carry alone. The secrecy is broken. The isolation that fed the bondage has been interrupted. That is not a small thing. It is the condition the next steps require.

Naming it was the first movement. What comes next requires a different kind of willingness — not just to see it, but to let it go.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 5 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson is taught after the Step 5 confession has been made. Many students will come to this session having experienced something they did not anticipate. Create space for that experience to be named. The lesson is not a lecture. It is a reflection on what actually happened. ASSIGNMENT

Is there anything in the inventory that was not said? If so, schedule a time with your mentor to complete the confession this week. 3. Read Romans 8:1-4 in full. choices: It cost him his health — showing that unconfessed sin produces physical illness
His bones waxed old and his moisture was turned to drought — showing that the holding of what should be confessed produces ongoing inner deterioration
It cost him his relationships — showing that unconfessed sin primarily damages the community

It cost him his sense of God's presence — showing that unconfessed sin produces spiritual distance Psalm 32:3-4 — bones waxing old, moisture as drought. The holding of the unconfessed inventory was producing ongoing deterioration — physical, emotional, spiritual. The cost of holding is the ongoing drain of the management. Step 5 ends the holding and the cost that comes with it.

quiz.question: What three specific things does an honest Step 5 confession produce according to this lesson?
choices: Resolution, accountability, and progress — the three outcomes of the Step 5 process
Relief, clarity, and connection — the burden is deposited, the patterns become visible, and the experience of being fully known and received produces genuine community

Freedom, confidence, and direction — the three results of completing the step Relief — the genuine deposit of the burden that had been carried in isolation. Clarity — the patterns that were difficult to see while managing become clear when spoken aloud. Connection — the experience of being fully known and fully received is the beginning of genuine covenant community.

quiz.question: According to Romans 8:1 KJV what is the ground the person stands on after the Step 5 confession — and what does no condemnation mean for the accusations the flesh still produces?
choices: The person stands on the ground of improved performance — no condemnation means the behavior is now acceptable
The person stands on the ground of confession received — no condemnation is the declaration of the covenant position, not a feeling that depends on the absence of accusation
The person stands on the ground of community approval — no condemnation means the group has accepted the confession

The person stands on the ground of emotional healing — no condemnation means the shame has been removed Romans 8:1 — there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit. The ground does not change when the accusation comes. The flesh may still produce condemnation. The declaration of the covenant position is no condemnation for the person walking in the honest posture that Step 5 represents.
