lessons.title: That ye may be healed — ongoing honesty and a life built without secrets
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The Day of Atonement under the old covenant required the high priest to confess the sins of all Israel over the head of the live goat — publicly, specifically, completely. The pattern was not private management followed by

In Step 4 we looked honestly at what the unmanageable life had actually produced — not to condemn, but to name clearly what needed to change. Step 5 brings it into the light.

There is a reason the Scripture connects confession and healing in the same sentence. What is confessed before God and another person is not merely acknowledged — it is brought into the light where repentance can complete its work. The confession of Step 5 is repentance made specific.

annual cleanup. It was the consistent, structured, communal practice of bringing what was carried into the presence of God. The new covenant fulfills and deepens this pattern — not with an annual day but with the ongoing posture of the person walking in the light daily. Step 5 was not a one-time event. It was the beginning of a way of living. The life without secrets that the confession opened is the life that Step 5 is building toward — not the absence of struggle, but the absence of the isolation that makes the struggle unmanageable.

THE ONGOING HONESTY

"Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed." — James 5:16 KJV The instruction is ongoing — not a past event to be completed but a present practice to be maintained. The person who completed the formal Step 5 confession has done something important. They have not completed the practice the verse describes. The ongoing confession — the daily or weekly honesty with the mentor or sponsor about what the daily inventory is surfacing — is the continuation of what Step 5 began. The life without secrets is not a life without sin. It is a life in which what surfaces is brought into the light rather than managed in the dark. The difference between those two lives is not the presence or absence of struggle. It is the presence or absence of the isolation that makes the struggle dangerous.

The woman at the well had been through five marriages and was living with a sixth man when Jesus met her. He did not require her history to be different. He offered living water exactly where she was.

BUILDING A LIFE WITHOUT SECRETS

A secret is not simply information that others do not have. A secret is information that the person is protecting from exposure because exposure would cost something. The addict in active addiction maintains elaborate secret systems — the storage, the money, the conversations, the stories. The recovery that does not address the secret-keeping capacity of the person has addressed the behavior without addressing the mechanism. "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret." — Ephesians 5:11-12 KJV Paul wrote this to the Ephesians — born-again believers — describing the posture of the community that has genuinely received the light. No fellowship with the works of darkness. Not tolerance. Not management. Not the quiet maintenance of the secret alongside the public recovery. The reproof — the bringing into the light of what is done in secret — is the ongoing practice of the covenant community.

THE MENTOR RELATIONSHIP AS THE ONGOING LIGHT

The mentor is not a one-time witness for the Step 5 confession. They are the ongoing human presence in which the practice of James 5:16 continues. The weekly meeting with the mentor is not a check-in. It is the ongoing context for the confession and prayer that produces the ongoing healing the verse describes. The person who has nothing to bring to the mentor meeting — who reports that everything is fine with nothing specific — is either genuinely well or has returned to the management posture that Step 5 was designed to end. The distinguishing question is: what did the daily inventory surface this week that I have not yet said out loud?

THE FATHER SEEN IN THE SON — THE GOD PRESENT IN THE CONFESSION

The confession of Step 5 is made before the God who has always known what is being confessed — and has never turned away. That God has a specific identity that the New Testament makes plain.

"Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?" — John 14:9 KJV

Philip asked to see the Father. Jesus answered by pointing to Himself. The Father is not hidden behind the Son, accessible through the Son — the Father is seen in the Son, present in the Son, dwelling fully in the Son. "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father."

The God before whom the confession of Step 5 is made is the God who said this. Not a mediator standing between the person and the Father. The God who contains the Father — who contains all the fulness of what God is — present in the confession, hearing every word, having already known every word before it was spoken.

This is not a distant God approving a transaction. This is the God who said "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" — present, known, and utterly capable of receiving what is being confessed and doing with it what only He can do.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern James records — confess your faults one to another and pray one for another, that ye may be healed — is not a suggestion. It is the God-ordained mechanics of how healing actually travels. It moves through relationship, not in isolation.

The ongoing practice of honesty has been established. Lesson 4 is the completion of Step 5 — the honest accounting of what the confession produced and the beginning of Step 6.

THE FAMILY THAT DOES NOT END

One of the things addiction dismantles most reliably is belonging. Not immediately — at first the substance or behavior creates a feeling of belonging, a community of people who understand, a place where the ordinary world's rules do not apply. But over time it isolates. The thing that offered belonging becomes the thing that destroys it. And the person who arrives at Step 1 has usually lost most of the legitimate belonging they had — family relationships strained or severed, friendships that could not survive what the addiction required, a community that no longer knows what to do with them. The hunger for belonging does not go away when the addiction is addressed. It intensifies. Because the false community is gone and the genuine community has not yet been found. This is one of the most dangerous seasons in early recovery — the person is honest and clean, and also alone in a way they have not been before. The Scripture describes a family that is not built on performance or proximity or shared history of damage. "Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named." — Ephesians 3:14-15 KJV Not a program. Not a meeting schedule. A family — with a family name, a lineage that runs from earth into heaven, a belonging that does not end when the circumstances change. Every person who has entered through the covenant the last Adam established bears that family name. The belonging is not earned. It is received through entry. And the family name is a name with a history. Revelation 3:4 speaks of "a few names even in Sardis" — referring not to labels but to people. In Scripture, a name is the person. To bear His name is to be identified with Him — His character, His authority, His ownership. "And all people of the earth shall see that thou art called by the name of the LORD." — Deuteronomy 28:10 KJV The community this program builds is real. But it points toward something larger than the program — the family of everyone, in every generation, who has received the name and entered the inheritance. That family has no graduation date and no expiration.

The person who has completed Step 5 honestly is no longer carrying alone what was always too heavy to carry alone. The secrecy is broken. The isolation that fed the bondage has been interrupted. That is not a small thing. It is the condition the next steps require.

Naming it was the first movement. What comes next requires a different kind of willingness — not just to see it, but to let it go.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 5 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson is about maintenance — the ongoing practice of what Step 5 began. The most common failure point after a successful Step 5 confession is the belief that the honesty practiced then covers what is being managed now. Address this directly. quiz.question: According to Ephesians 5:11-12 KJV what is the posture of the covenant community toward the works of darkness — and what does this mean for the secret-keeping that addiction produced?
choices: Tolerance — the community extends grace to those still struggling with hidden sin
Have no fellowship — the ongoing practice of bringing what is done in secret into the light rather than quietly maintaining the secret alongside the public recovery
Accountability — the community checks on one another to ensure the secret-keeping has stopped

Confrontation — the community actively exposes what is being managed in secret Ephesians 5:11-12 — have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness but rather reprove them. The fellowship is the participation, the quiet maintenance of the secret alongside the public life. The reproof is the ongoing bringing into the light of what is done in secret. Not a one-time event — the posture of the covenant life.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a life without sin and a life without secrets — and why does this distinction matter for ongoing recovery?
choices: There is no meaningful difference — sin produces secrets and the elimination of sin eliminates the secrets

A life without secrets is not the absence of struggle but the absence of the isolation that makes the struggle unmanageable — the ongoing practice of bringing what surfaces into the light rather than managing it in the dark
A life without secrets is the higher standard — the life without sin is the starting point

A life without secrets requires a particular personality type — people who are naturally open find it easier The life without secrets is not the absence of sin — it is the absence of the isolation that makes the sin unmanageable. The person who struggles and brings the struggle into the light has no secret. The person who struggles and manages the story has a secret. Recovery is not the absence of struggle. It is the presence of honest ongoing light.

quiz.question: According to James 5:16 KJV what does the ongoing confession produce — and what does this mean for the mentor relationship?
choices: Forgiveness — the ongoing confession provides ongoing forgiveness for ongoing failure
Ongoing healing — the ongoing confession in the context of prayer produces the continuous healing that the verse describes, making the weekly mentor meeting the ongoing context of the practice
Accountability — the ongoing confession provides the accountability that prevents relapse

Community — the ongoing confession builds the relationships that sustain recovery James 5:16 — confess your faults one to another and pray one for another that ye may be healed. The healing is ongoing because the practice is ongoing. The weekly mentor meeting is the ongoing context for the confession-and-prayer practice that produces the ongoing healing. It is not a check-in. It is the continuation of Step 5.

lessons.title: Received and moving forward — completing Step 5 and what it opened
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When the people of Israel returned from captivity in Babylon, the first thing Ezra did when he read the Law publicly was lead them in a comprehensive confession — a naming of what had been, an honest accounting before God and before one another. The confession was not the end. It was the clearing of the ground for what God was going to build next. Step 5 has done the same thing. The inventory has been shared. The ground is cleared. Now the step is complete — and what it opened is more significant than what it closed.

WHAT WAS RECEIVED IN STEP 5

There is a reason the Scripture connects confession and healing in the same sentence. What is confessed before God and another person is not merely acknowledged — it is brought into the light where repentance can complete its work. The confession of Step 5 is repentance made specific.

In Step 4 we looked honestly at what the unmanageable life had actually produced — not to condemn, but to name clearly what needed to change. Step 5 brings it into the light.

"Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is he unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no guile." — Psalm 32:1-2 KJV David wrote this after the experience of both hiding and confession — knowing the weight of the unspoken thing and then knowing the relief of having spoken it. Read Psalm 32:1-2 as a description of what Step 5 produced. Not a future hope. A present reality for the person who has walked through the honest accounting. Three things were received in Step 5: First: the experience of being fully known and not rejected. The inventory contained what the person was most certain would disqualify them. It was heard. The person sharing it is still here. What the self most feared would cause abandonment did not. This is the beginning of the capacity for genuine relationship — because the person who has been fully known and not rejected no longer needs to manage what is seen. Second: the beginning of the end of shame. Shame requires hiding. The thing brought into the light is no longer a secret. The power it had over the person — the power of the unspoken thing — has been broken by the speaking of it.

Third: clarity about the defects that Step 6 will address. The sharing of the inventory in Step 5 almost always reveals which defect is the deepest root. Not the largest harm — the trait that produced the most consistent harm across the most different situations. That is the primary defect. Name it clearly. It is the target of Step 6.

NO CONDEMNATION

"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." — Romans 8:1 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Rome — describing the condition of the person who has been born again through obedience and is now walking in the Spirit rather than the flesh. No condemnation. Not reduced condemnation. None. The inventory contained what it contained. The confession was honest. The blood of 1 John 1:7 cleanses what was brought into the light. The person who walked through Step 5 honestly stands in the position Romans 8:1 describes.

The woman at the well had been through five marriages and was living with a sixth man when Jesus met her. He did not require her history to be different. He offered living water exactly where she was.

The person who has confessed and then fallen again is not disqualified from this road.

The confession of Step 5 is not nullified by a subsequent failure. The work that was done in Steps 1 through 5 is not undone by what happens next. The foundation was laid. A foundation that has been laid and then covered by rubble is still a foundation — and the rubble can be cleared again, faster than the foundation was laid the first time.

"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9 KJV

He is faithful — meaning His response to the confession does not depend on the confessor's track record. It depends on His character. His character does not change based on how many times the person has returned.

The person returning to the program after a fall does not need to perform remorse for the community. They need to return. The return is the act that matters — not its emotional quality, not its speech, not how convincingly the person can demonstrate that they mean it this time.

What is required is what was required at the beginning: honesty about what is actually true. That is always the door. It has never stopped being the door.

The mentor who receives the returning person does not require the performance of shame. They require the return. And they welcome it. Because the person doing the welcoming was once the person returning.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern James records — confess your faults one to another and pray one for another, that ye may be healed — is not a suggestion. It is the God-ordained mechanics of how healing actually travels. It moves through relationship, not in isolation.

Step 5 is complete. Do not stay here. The relief that Step 5 produces is real — and it can produce a temptation to rest in the relief rather than continuing toward what the relief is pointed at. Step 6 asks whether the person is entirely ready for God to remove what the inventory revealed. It is a harder question than it sounds. The defects named in Step 4 have been useful — they were developed as survival tools, as ways of managing what could not otherwise be managed. Entirely ready means willing to release even the tools that worked. That is the question Step 6 opens.

The person who has completed Step 5 honestly is no longer carrying alone what was always too heavy to carry alone. The secrecy is broken. The isolation that fed the bondage has been interrupted. That is not a small thing. It is the condition the next steps require.

Naming it was the first movement. What comes next requires a different kind of willingness — not just to see it, but to let it go.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 5 Lesson 4 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson does the completion and transition work of Step 5. Most students arrive at this lesson with the inventory already shared — the task is processing what the experience produced and positioning them for Step 6. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER Ezra 9-10 and Nehemiah 9 both record the comprehensive public confession that preceded the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The confession is not the destination — it is the clearing of the ground for what God builds next....

No condemnation is not the feeling — it is the position. The feeling often follows the position rather than preceding it.

lessons.title: Create in me a clean heart O God — were entirely ready and what that actually requires
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
David prayed Psalm 51 after Nathan the prophet came to him — after the full weight of what David had done had been named, seen, and stood in. The prayer was not the prayer of a person who had improved sufficiently to ask for the blessing. It was the prayer of a person who had seen clearly what was there and understood that what was there could not be removed by human effort. Create in me a clean heart — not: I will work on cleaning my heart. Create. Do what I cannot do. Give what I cannot manufacture. This is the prayer of Step 6. "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." — Psalm 51:10 KJV The Step 5 confession showed what the heart contained. Step 6 is the willingness — the entirely ready posture — for God to create what the confession revealed cannot be produced from within. Not the management of the defects. Not the reduction of the most visible ones. The creation of what was not there before: a clean heart, a right spirit.

In Step 5 we saw that what had been kept hidden had power precisely because it was hidden. Step 6 asks a different kind of willingness entirely.

The God who is being asked to remove what self-effort cannot remove is one Spirit, one LORD — and the Scripture does not record a single instance of God refusing the request of a person who came to Him in genuine readiness.

The vessel cleared in Step 6 is not cleared so that it remains empty. An empty vessel waiting is the condition described by Jesus when He spoke of the swept house — cleaned but unoccupied, and therefore vulnerable to what returns. The clearing of Step 6 is preparation for what belongs in the vessel. And what belongs in the cleared vessel is not a concept — it is a person, who comes in a name.

Readiness to have the defects removed is the inner posture of genuine repentance. It is not enough to name what is wrong and carry it. Repentance that stops at naming has not completed its movement. Step 6 is the turning that makes the request of Step 7 honest.

WHAT ENTIRELY READY ACTUALLY MEANS

Entirely ready does not mean eager. It means willing — genuinely, completely, without protected reservations. The person who is entirely ready for God to remove their defects has examined each defect and is holding none of them back from the removal. The surprise of Step 6 is that the entirely ready is harder than it looks. The defects the inventory named have been serving a function. The resentment protected from further hurt. The pride prevented the experience of shame. The selfishness ensured the self got what it needed. The dishonesty kept the story manageable. Removing the defect also removes the function the defect was serving — and the flesh does not release functions voluntarily. "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." — Matthew 5:6 KJV Jesus said this in the Gospels — in the Sermon on the Mount, to the crowd gathered at the beginning of His ministry. The hungering and thirsting describes the intensity of the entirely ready — the person who does not merely prefer to be free of the defects but hungers for it the way a person who has not eaten hungers for food. That intensity is what Step 6 is asking for.

Jacob wrestled with God through the night — broken, exhausted, holding on — and received both the wound and the blessing in the same encounter. Readiness does not require strength. It requires surrender.

WHY WILLPOWER CANNOT PRODUCE IT

The defects named in the inventory are not defects the person can simply decide to stop having. The resentment does not resolve because the person decides it should. The selfishness does not disappear because the person

identifies it as a problem. The inventory showed the pattern. The pattern runs deeper than decision. "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." — Philippians 4:13 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers — describing the strength that operates in the person who has genuinely received what God promises the obedient. The all things includes the removal of what willpower cannot reach. The strengthening is the work of Christ in the person who is entirely ready — not instead of human effort, but as the power that makes possible what human effort cannot produce alone.

GIDEON — THE THRESHING FLOOR AND THE READINESS HE DID NOT FEEL

Gideon was in a winepress, threshing wheat in hiding, when the angel of the LORD appeared and said: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." — Judges 6:12 KJV

The name Gideon means one who cuts down or great warrior. He was not living up to either. He was hiding from the Midianites, doing the work of harvest in a place designed for something else, because he was afraid of what would happen if he was seen.

And the angel called him mighty. Not because of what he was doing. Because of what God was going to do with his willingness.

Gideon's first response was not enthusiasm. It was: "Oh my Lord, if the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?" — Judges 6:13 KJV

Why has everything gone wrong if God is present? It is the question every person in this program has asked. If God is real, why is my life in this condition?

What Gideon did not know, in the winepress, was that his readiness — his willingness to step out of hiding and trust the God who had called him — was the precise thing that God was going to use to defeat an army of 135,000 with 300 men.

Step 6 does not ask whether you feel ready. It asks whether you are willing. Entirely willing — not partially, not conditionally, not when the situation improves. Entirely. The readiness that Step 6 describes is not confidence. It is surrender. The person who says I am entirely ready is not saying I believe I can do this. They are saying I am willing for God to do what I cannot.

Gideon was not confident in the winepress. He was willing to come out of it. That willingness — that step from hiding into the open — was what everything else required.

You are not being asked to feel ready. You are being asked to be willing.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every story of genuine transformation in Scripture: the person brings what they have — the willingness — and God does what only He can do. Human readiness and divine action. Both are required. Neither alone is sufficient.

The nature of entirely ready has been established. Lesson 2 addresses the specific dynamics of the flesh and the Spirit in the context of Step 6 — why the willingness requires what it requires and what the Spirit produces when the willingness is genuine.

Readiness is itself a form of identity. The person who is entirely ready has made a declaration about who they are becoming — a person whose character is no longer self-governed, but yielded. That posture is what Step 7 walks into.

Readiness leads directly to the request. Steps 6 and 7 are two halves of one movement — and what Step 7 asks for is what makes everything prior sustainable.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Psalm 51:10 KJV — "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."

■ Matthew 5:6 KJV — "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled."

ASSIGNMENT

Examining the readiness 1. List the five defects most identified in the Step 4 inventory. For each one: (a) what function was it serving? (b) are you entirely ready for it to be removed, including the loss of the function? 2. Name the one defect you are least ready to surrender. Write specifically: what would the removal of this defect cost you — what function would be gone? Is the cost worth the ...

He asks God to create a clean heart and renew a right spirit — the word create implies what is being asked for does not exist yet, it must be made new not improved
He asks God to cleanse — showing that Step 6 is about the removal of specific sins

He asks God to strengthen — showing that Step 6 is about developing the capacity to resist the defects Psalm 51:10 — create in me a clean heart. Create — not improve, not restore, not help develop. The word implies that what is being asked for does not exist yet in the person asking. A clean heart is not an improved version of the existing heart. It is a new creation. David prayed create because he understood that was what was needed.

choices: An interest in righteousness — showing Step 6 requires the general preference for right behavior

Because the defects have been serving functions — protecting from hurt, preventing shame, ensuring the self gets what it needs — and the readiness requires surrendering the function as well as the pattern

Because the entirely ready requires the approval of the community before the individual readiness is complete The defects named in the inventory have been serving functions. The resentment protected from further hurt. The pride prevented shame. The selfishness ensured the self got what it needed. Removing the defect also removes the function it served. The entirely ready requires surrendering the function as well as the pattern — which is why the step is harder than it initially appears.

lessons.title: Renew a right spirit within me — the flesh and the Spirit and why readiness is not effort
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The new covenant that the prophets pointed toward was always described as the covenant of the Spirit — not the law written on stone but the law written on the heart, not the external requirement but the internal transformation. Ezekiel 36:26-27 described it: a new heart, a new spirit, the Spirit of God causing the person to walk in His statutes. The causing is significant. Not helping. Not enabling. Causing — the Spirit doing what the flesh cannot do, in the person who has received what only the Spirit can give. Step 6 is the willingness for this to happen. Not the performance of it. The willingness.

In Step 5 we saw that what had been kept hidden had power precisely because it was hidden. Step 6 asks a different kind of willingness entirely.

Readiness is faith presented to God before the change has occurred. The person who is entirely ready is not the person who has already been changed — they are the person who believes the change is possible and has presented themselves to receive it. That presentation — the willingness before the evidence — is exactly what Hebrews 11 describes as faith: the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

The God who is being asked to remove what self-effort cannot remove is one Spirit, one LORD — and the Scripture does not record a single instance of God refusing the request of a person who came to Him in genuine readiness.

Readiness to have the defects removed is the inner posture of genuine repentance. It is not enough to name what is wrong and carry it. Repentance that stops at naming has not completed its movement. Step 6 is the turning that makes the request of Step 7 honest.

WHY READINESS IS NOT EFFORT

The defects identified in the inventory are not removed by effort. They are removed by the work of the Spirit in a person who has become entirely willing to have them removed. The difference between effort and willingness is the difference between a person trying to pull weeds by the top — producing temporary results as the root remains — and a person presenting the garden to the One who removes the root. "For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace." — Romans 8:6 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers — describing the nature of the two orientations available to the person. The carnal mind and the spiritual mind are not two different intellectual capacities. They are two different centers of governance. The carnal mind is the flesh in governance — applying effort, managing, performing. The spiritual mind is the Spirit in governance — receiving, abiding, being led. Step 6 is the transition from the effort of the carnal mind to the readiness of the spiritual.

Jacob wrestled with God through the night — broken, exhausted, holding on — and received both the wound and the blessing in the same encounter. Readiness does not require strength. It requires surrender.

THE DEFECTS AND THE SPIRIT

"But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance." — Galatians 5:22-23 KJV Paul wrote this to the Galatians — people who had received the Spirit — describing not what they were working toward but what the Spirit produces in a person in whom He dwells and governs. The fruit is the natural production of the indwelling Spirit. It is not manufactured. It is grown. What the Spirit produces is the replacement for what the defects were providing. The love of the Spirit replaces the selfishness that was managing the lack of it. The peace of the Spirit replaces the anxiety that drove the control. The temperance of the Spirit replaces the excess that the flesh was using to manage the pain. The entirely ready of

Step 6 is the willingness to receive the Spirit's fruit in the place of the flesh's defects.

WHAT THE READINESS LOOKS LIKE

The entirely ready person has examined each defect and is holding none of them back from God's work. They have named the function each defect was serving and have surrendered the function alongside the defect. They have brought the specific resistance — the one defect they are not yet ready to surrender — to God and asked for the willingness to become willing. Willingness to become willing is not hypocrisy. It is the honest posture of a person who sees the defect clearly, recognizes they are not yet entirely ready, and asks God to produce the readiness they cannot manufacture themselves.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every story of genuine transformation in Scripture: the person brings what they have — the willingness — and God does what only He can do. Human readiness and divine action. Both are required. Neither alone is sufficient.

The dynamics of flesh and Spirit have been examined. Lesson 3 addresses the specific defects that are still being protected — and what to do when the entirely ready is not complete. WHAT FILLS THE CLEARED VESSEL "Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." — 2 Corinthians 3:17 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Corinth — identifying what the presence of the Spirit of the Lord produces: liberty. Not managed behavior. Not sustained effort. Liberty — the freedom that belongs to the person whose inner life is genuinely governed by the Spirit rather than by the flesh, the fear, and the patterns the inventory revealed. The defects being removed in Step 6 are being removed to make space for the liberty that 2 Corinthians 3:17 describes. The vessel is not being cleared for the sake of emptiness. It is being cleared for the filling. The liberty does not come with the clearing — it comes with what occupies the cleared space. And what was always designed to occupy it is the Spirit of the Lord. The person entirely ready in Step 6 is not only the person ready for removal. They are the person ready for what the removal makes possible — the liberty that the Spirit brings when the vessel has genuinely been made available.

CALVARY — THERE IS NO NEW LIFE WITHOUT DEATH TO THE OLD ONE

The cross is not the program's inspiration or its mascot. It is its foundation. Everything in the twelve steps is built on what Calvary accomplished — and the pattern of Calvary runs through every step that requires the death of something the flesh was protecting. "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me." — Galatians 2:20 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Galatia — describing his own experience of the death that preceded the life. Not I, but Christ. The self that was running the life before — the self that had plans, strategies, positions to protect, defects to maintain because they had been useful — that self went to the cross with Christ. What remained was the life that Christ produces, lived through the vessel that had been surrendered.

The defects that Step 6 examines are the things the flesh has kept alive past their useful date. They were survival tools — developed under pressure, maintained because they worked, protected because releasing them felt like death. That feeling is not wrong. Releasing what the self has used to survive is a form of death. The cross does not minimize that. It validates it — and then shows what comes after. There is no resurrection without crucifixion. There is no new life in recovery without the death of what the old life was built on. Step 6 is standing at the foot of the cross with the list of what has not yet died. Entirely ready means willing for the dying to be complete.

Readiness is itself a form of identity. The person who is entirely ready has made a declaration about who they are becoming — a person whose character is no longer self-governed, but yielded. That posture is what Step 7 walks into.

Readiness leads directly to the request. Steps 6 and 7 are two halves of one movement — and what Step 7 asks for is what makes everything prior sustainable.

lessons.title: The defects God is removing and the ones still being protected
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The covenant consistently shows a God who works in stages. The Israelites did not enter the promised land and immediately possess all of it — the land was cleared bit by bit, enemy by enemy, as the obedience was sustained. Deuteronomy 7:22 — the LORD thy God will put out those nations before thee by little and little. The removal of what occupied the land was progressive. So is the removal of what the inventory identified. Step 6 does not promise immediate or total removal. It asks for the entirely ready posture — and the God who receives that posture works in the yielded life progressively, removing what is presented with the willingness that actually enables the removal.

In Step 5 we saw that what had been kept hidden had power precisely because it was hidden. Step 6 asks a different kind of willingness entirely.

Readiness to have the defects removed is the inner posture of genuine repentance. It is not enough to name what is wrong and carry it. Repentance that stops at naming has not completed its movement. Step 6 is the turning that makes the request of Step 7 honest.

THE DEFECTS BEING REMOVED

Some defects yield relatively quickly after the inventory and the Step 7 prayer. The ones the person has been most transparent about — the ones confessed most fully in Step 5, the ones presented with genuine willingness in Step 6 — often show visible change first. Not because they were less severe. Because the willingness regarding them was more complete. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9 KJV John wrote this to born-again believers — describing the faithful response of God to the honest, ongoing confession. He is faithful and just to forgive and to cleanse. The cleansing follows the confession. And the cleansing is His work — not the result of the person having worked hard enough on the defect to deserve the removal.

Jacob wrestled with God through the night — broken, exhausted, holding on — and received both the wound and the blessing in the same encounter. Readiness does not require strength. It requires surrender.

THE DEFECTS STILL BEING PROTECTED

Some defects will not yield in the first round of Steps 6 and 7. The most deeply rooted ones — the ones that have been serving the most important functions, the ones that the person has been most reluctant to see clearly — may require returning to this step more than once. This is not failure. This is the honest description of progressive sanctification. The defect still being protected is identifiable. It is the one the person has the most elaborate justification for. It is the one they have the best reasons for keeping. It is the one they are most articulate about why the circumstances

make it necessary. "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ." — 2 Corinthians 10:5 KJV Paul wrote this to the Corinthians — born-again believers — naming the specific work of bringing into captivity what the mind has been building arguments for. The imagination that exalts itself is the elaborate justification the flesh constructs to protect the defect it is not yet willing to surrender. Step 6 names it. Step 7 asks for its removal. The captivity is the beginning of the freedom.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every story of genuine transformation in Scripture: the person brings what they have — the willingness — and God does what only He can do. Human readiness and divine action. Both are required. Neither alone is sufficient.

The defects being removed and those still being protected have been named. Lesson 4 is the Step 6 completion — the entirely ready examination and the beginning of Step 7.

Readiness is itself a form of identity. The person who is entirely ready has made a declaration about who they are becoming — a person whose character is no longer self-governed, but yielded. That posture is what Step 7 walks into.

Readiness leads directly to the request. Steps 6 and 7 are two halves of one movement — and what Step 7 asks for is what makes everything prior sustainable.

Name the protected defect without shame and help the person move toward the willingness they do not yet have. lessons.title: Entirely ready — completing Step 6 and presenting the cleared vessel
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When Elisha sent his servant to lay his staff on the child who had died, nothing happened. When Elisha himself came and lay upon the child — gave his full presence, his full contact, his full attention — the child's flesh grew warm and the child sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. The partial offering produced nothing. The full presence produced the result. Step 6 is the question of full presence: is the person entirely ready, or presenting the appearance of readiness while holding something in reserve?

In Step 5 we saw that what had been kept hidden had power precisely because it was hidden. Step 6 asks a different kind of willingness entirely.

Readiness to have the defects removed is the inner posture of genuine repentance. It is not enough to name what is wrong and carry it. Repentance that stops at naming has not completed its movement. Step 6 is the turning that makes the request of Step 7 honest.

ENTIRELY READY — WHAT THE EXAMINATION SHOWS

Return to the four areas named in Step 3 L4: time, relationships, money, future. Now add the defects named in Step 4. Ask the question of each one: Is there a defect I am not ready to release because I am still using it? Pride that keeps a relationship intact because it avoids the vulnerability of honest need. Dishonesty that maintains a comfort level that honesty would disrupt. Self-seeking that protects an opportunity the person is not ready to surrender. Fear that is still governing a decision the person knows should be surrendered. Entirely ready does not mean the defect is already gone. It means the person is genuinely willing for God to remove it — not willing if the conditions are right, not willing as long as it is convenient, but willing.

Jacob wrestled with God through the night — broken, exhausted, holding on — and received both the wound and the blessing in the same encounter. Readiness does not require strength. It requires surrender.

THE VESSEL PRESENTED

"If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work." — 2 Timothy 2:21 KJV Paul wrote this to Timothy — describing what the purged vessel becomes. Meet for the master's use. Prepared for every good work. The defects are not only harmful to the person carrying them — they make the vessel less available for what God intends to do through it. The person who has purged what Step 6 identifies is not only a freer person. They are a more useful vessel.

THE CLOSING COMMITMENT

Step 6 closes with a specific prayer — not a formula but a genuine expression of readiness. It says three things:

I have named the defects honestly. I am willing for God to remove them. I am not placing conditions on the removal. Pray this prayer with your mentor. Not after you feel ready. Now. The feeling of readiness often follows the act of willingness — it does not precede it.

GOD MANIFEST IN THE FLESH — WHAT THE CLEARED VESSEL IS PREPARED FOR

The vessel cleared in Step 6 is not cleared to remain empty. It is cleared in preparation for the presence of the God who entered His own creation in a way the whole of Scripture was building toward.

"And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory." — 1 Timothy 3:16 KJV

God was manifest in the flesh. Not a man who became divine. God — the same God who spoke creation into existence, who covenanted with Abraham, who appeared to Moses in the burning bush — was manifest in the flesh. The manifestation was complete. The mystery is great. And the result of that manifestation is the same Spirit that powered the ministry of Jesus, raised Him from the dead, and came upon the disciples in the upper room.

The vessel cleared in Steps 6 and 7 is being prepared for that Spirit. The same Spirit that raised Christ from the dead — the Spirit of the God who was manifest in the flesh — is what the humble request of Step 7 is approaching.

What does it mean to be entirely ready to receive the Spirit of the God who was manifest in the flesh? That readiness is what Step 6 is asking for.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This reveals a pattern that runs through every story of genuine transformation in Scripture: the person brings what they have — the willingness — and God does what only He can do. Human readiness and divine action. Both are required. Neither alone is sufficient.

Step 7 is the humble asking — the specific request for the removal that Step 6 expressed willingness for. Step 6 is the readiness. Step 7 is the petition. Together they complete the submission of the will that began in Step 3.

THE PETITION OF STEP 7 BEGINS HERE

"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." — Psalm 51:10 KJV David prayed this after the honest confrontation with what he had done. He did not pray it after he had already cleaned himself up. He prayed it as the expression of the readiness — the entirely ready posture that presents what is there to the God who can do what the person cannot do for themselves. This is the closing prayer of Step 6. Not the prayer of the person who has already achieved cleanliness. The prayer of the person who is entirely ready for God to create what they cannot create — a clean heart. A right spirit. Not restored. Created anew. Step 7 begins immediately with the humble asking that Step 6 has prepared for. The readiness expressed here is the ground from which the petition of Step 7 rises.

Readiness is itself a form of identity. The person who is entirely ready has made a declaration about who they are becoming — a person whose character is no longer self-governed, but yielded. That posture is what Step 7 walks into.

Readiness leads directly to the request. Steps 6 and 7 are two halves of one movement — and what Step 7 asks for is what makes everything prior sustainable.

TEACHER NOTES

Its function is accountability to the readiness question — not emotional processing but honest examination of whether the willingness expressed is genuine or conditional. lessons.title: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord — and He shall lift you up
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Throughout the covenant history, the people who received the most from God were consistently the people who came to Him with the least reliance on their own position. Abraham left everything he knew. Moses argued that he was not sufficient. Gideon was the least in his father's house. David was the youngest and was left in the field when Samuel came. The pattern is not coincidence. It is the consistent expression of what James states plainly: God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble. Step 7 is the step that takes what Step 6 prepared and brings it before God with nothing added — no performance, no augmentation, no presentation of the self as deserving of the removal. Just the asking.

Step 6 established something important: there are things in the character that human effort named but could not remove. That is not failure — it is the honest prerequisite for what this step asks.

The God who lifts the humble is one Spirit, one LORD — James 4:10 KJV — and the promise has never changed across the full arc of the covenant.

Peter's instruction in the apostolic record begins with one word: Repent. Then baptism. Then the gift. But the sequence begins with the humble turning — which is exactly what Step 7 is. The person who humbles himself before God and asks for what only God can give is doing precisely what the apostolic record shows happening before the name is applied and the Spirit is received.

When Peter stood on the day of Pentecost and told the crowd what to do, the first word he spoke was repent. Not believe harder. Not try again. Repent — and be baptized every one of you in the name the Scripture identifies Christ for the remission of sins. The remission — the sending away — of sin is not accomplished by the decision of Step 3 alone. It is accomplished by the full covenant response: repentance, the name, and the Spirit. This is what the steps have been preparing the road toward.

HUMBLE YOURSELVES IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD

"Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up." — James 4:10 KJV James wrote this to born-again believers — people who had received the Spirit and were being instructed in the posture that maintains availability to God's ongoing work. Humble yourselves. The humbling is the action of the person. The lifting is the action of God. The sequence is fixed. The lifting does not precede the humbling. It follows it. Humility in Step 7 is not self-contempt. It is accurate assessment — knowing what the self can produce and what only God can produce, and placing what only God can produce in His hands without managing the delivery.

The tax collector in the temple did not lift his eyes toward heaven. He beat his breast and said: God be merciful to me a sinner. Jesus said he went home justified. Humility is not a performance. It is the honest posture of the person who knows what they are.

THE PROUD AND THE HUMBLE

"God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." — James 4:6 KJV Resisteth. Not ignores. Not passes over. Actively opposes. The proud person — the person who approaches God with what they have already accomplished, with the inventory of their effort and their progress and their willingness — meets resistance. Not because God is harsh but because the proud posture has already placed something between the person and the grace that is being offered. The humble person — the person who comes with nothing to offer but the honest naming of what they need — receives grace. Not because they earned it by being sufficiently humble. Because the posture of genuine humility removes the obstacle that the proud posture erected.

WHAT HUMILITY IS NOT

Humility is not the performance of lowliness. The person who has learned that appearing humble produces approval has developed a sophisticated form of pride. True humility is not managed. It is the honest accounting of

what the self is and what the self is not — without embellishment in either direction. "For I say, through the grace given unto me, to every man that is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly, as God hath dealt to every man the measure of faith." — Romans 12:3 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Rome — instructing them in the sober self-assessment that genuine humility produces. Not lower than accurate. Not higher than accurate. Sober. The person in Step 7 does not arrive with a list of what they have accomplished. They arrive with an honest accounting of what they have been unable to produce and a genuine request for the removal of what they are unable to remove on their own.

THE BROKEN AND CONTRITE HEART

"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." — Psalm 34:18 KJV Broken does not mean destroyed. It means no longer relying on its own structural integrity. The broken heart is the one that has stopped trusting its own capacity to hold itself together and has placed its weight on what God provides instead. That is the posture of Step 7. The contrite spirit — the crushed, ground-down acknowledgment of what the self has produced — is not the destination. It is the condition that opens the person to what God gives to those who come that way. He is nigh. He saves. Not to the performance of seeking without the substance. To the broken heart that has genuinely arrived.

The pattern is consistent across the whole of Scripture: God lifts those who humble themselves. Not those who perform humility — those who actually occupy the low place honestly. The lifting is always in response to the genuine posture, never to the performance of it.

THE CRY — WHAT THE SPIRIT PRODUCES WHEN IT ENTERS

"And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father." — Galatians 4:6 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Galatia — describing what happens when the Spirit enters the heart. A cry. Not a private internal impression. A cry — the Spirit of God within producing a voiced expression of the relationship that has been established. Romans confirms it: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." — Romans 8:15-16 KJV The Spirit bears witness. And it does so with a cry — something that comes from within but is not manufactured by the person. Something that arrives with the Spirit's arrival. The person who has received the Spirit of adoption knows the difference between the cry that was produced and the prayer that was composed. One is the work of the self. The other is the work of the Spirit bearing witness. Carry this question through the coming steps: what does it mean that the Spirit bears witness with your spirit? What would that witness look like? What would it sound like?

The person who has genuinely asked God to remove what they could not remove has done something they could not undo. They have acknowledged in the most specific possible way what is true: they cannot complete themselves. And God, who is faithful to that kind of honesty, lifts what is brought to Him.

The prayer established in this step becomes the ongoing contact of Step 11. What begins here as a request becomes a relationship.

THE TAX COLLECTOR IN THE TEMPLE — THE PRAYER THAT WAS HEARD

Jesus told the story of two men who went to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee — educated, observant, respected. The other was a tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a man whose profession made him ritually unclean and socially despised.

The Pharisee's prayer: "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess." — Luke 18:11-12 KJV

The tax collector's prayer: "God be merciful to me a sinner." — Luke 18:13 KJV

The tax collector did not look up. He did not list his qualifications. He did not compare himself to anyone else. He stood at a distance, beat his breast — the physical posture of genuine grief — and said the only thing he had to say: God be merciful to me a sinner.

"I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." — Luke 18:14 KJV

Justified. The legal term. The account settled. The standing before God established. Not because he performed the right ritual. Not because he had sufficient credentials. Because he came in the only posture that the God of the covenant responds to: honest humility.

The Pharisee left the temple the same man who entered it. The tax collector left justified.

The name publican carried shame in the first century. Tax collectors were ranked with sinners in every list that named them — "publicans and sinners" as a single category. And it was a publican — not a Pharisee, not a scribe, not a religious leader — who left the temple justified.

The prayer of Step 7 does not require credentials. It does not require a clean record. It requires the posture the tax collector had: beating the breast, standing at a distance, and saying the honest thing. God be merciful to me. Remove what I cannot remove. Do what I cannot do.

That prayer — in that posture — is the prayer that goes home justified.

■ Psalm 34:18 KJV — "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."

Identify one area where you stopped trusting your own capacity to hold things together. Write what it was like to stop. That is the broken heart Psalm 34:18 describe...

The sequence is fixed — the lifting does not precede the humbling. Step 7 is fully within the person's capacity because the humbling belongs to them. The lifting belongs to God.

The proud posture produces active resistance. The humble posture removes the obstacle and makes grace available. The posture is not about performance — it is about whether the obstacle is in place.

lessons.title: Humility as the daily posture — what a life looks like when self-will is not running it
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The Old Testament wisdom tradition — Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Job — consistently returns to the same theme: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and humility is what that fear produces in the daily life. Not the fear of punishment. The reverent awe of the person who has genuinely encountered who God is and consequently sees themselves with accurate vision. That vision — the God's-eye view of the self — is humility. And the person who lives from that vision lives differently than the person who is running their life from the self's own assessment. Step 7 was the humble asking. The daily posture of Step 7 is the life that maintains that humility — not as a spiritual accomplishment to be achieved once but as the orientation that governs the daily decisions. "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." — Proverbs 16:18 KJV The wisdom literature of the Old Testament did not see pride as a minor personal failing. It saw it as the orientation that produces destruction and the fall that precedes it. The haughty spirit is the spirit running its own operation — convinced of its own adequacy, resistant to correction, maintaining the appearance of having things under control. That spirit goes before a fall not as punishment but as natural consequence. What is not under

Step 6 established something important: there are things in the character that human effort named but could not remove. That is not failure — it is the honest prerequisite for what this step asks.

The God who lifts the humble is one Spirit, one LORD — James 4:10 KJV — and the promise has never changed across the full arc of the covenant.

When Peter stood on the day of Pentecost and told the crowd what to do, the first word he spoke was repent. Not believe harder. Not try again. Repent — and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins. The remission — the sending away — of sin is not accomplished by the decision of Step 3 alone. It is accomplished by the full covenant response: repentance, the name, and the Spirit. This is what the steps have been preparing the road toward.

God's governance eventually produces what self-governance always produces.

WHAT THE HUMBLE LIFE LOOKS LIKE

The humble life is not the life of the person who thinks poorly of themselves. It is the life of the person who thinks accurately of themselves — who has the God's-eye view of their capacities, their limitations, their actual condition, and who makes decisions from that honest assessment rather than from the inflated or deflated self-assessment the flesh maintains. "By humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life." — Proverbs 22:4 KJV The wisdom tradition associated humility not with weakness but with the specific conditions that produce what the prideful life is actually pursuing. The prideful life is pursuing riches, honor, and life. The humble life is the one that actually receives them — because it is positioned under the governance that is able to provide what the self-governed life cannot secure for itself.

The tax collector in the temple did not lift his eyes toward heaven. He beat his breast and said: God be merciful to me a sinner. Jesus said he went home justified. Humility is not a performance. It is the honest posture of the person who knows what they are.

THE OPPOSITE OF SELF-WILL

The person whose self-will is no longer running the operation does not become passive. They become rightly active — doing what God directs rather than what the self has decided, receiving guidance rather than insisting on the plan, correctable rather than defensive, honest about limitations rather than performing adequacy. This is the practical content of the daily humble posture. In the relationships — the humble person receives feedback without defense. In the work — the humble person asks for help without shame. In the recovery — the humble person names what they are struggling with before it becomes a crisis. In the spiritual life — the humble person maintains the daily seeking rather than assuming they have arrived.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern is consistent across the whole of Scripture: God lifts those who humble themselves. Not those who perform humility — those who actually occupy the low place honestly. The lifting is always in response to the genuine posture, never to the performance of it.

The daily humble posture has been described. Lesson 3 addresses what happens when that posture is challenged — the adversary who opposes the humble life and the armor the covenant provides. THE CRY THAT

CONFIRMS

"And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father." — Galatians 4:6 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Galatia — describing what the Spirit produces in the heart of the person who has entered the covenant relationship. The Spirit cries. Not the person manufacturing an emotional response — the Spirit Himself, within the heart of the person who has received Him, producing the cry: Abba, Father. Every genuine birth produces a cry. The physical birth announces itself. The birth of the Spirit announces itself in the same way — not in silence, not in a quiet internal decision, but in the cry that the Spirit produces from within the person who receives Him. The humility of Step 7 — the posture of the person who has placed what they cannot carry in the hands of the One who can — is the posture that makes the heart available for what Galatians 4:6 describes. The cry of Abba Father is not manufactured by effort. It is the evidence that something has arrived. And the something that arrives does not arrive silently. Is the step toward humility also a step toward the threshold where that cry becomes possible? The road is pointing toward something. Keep walking.

BARTIMAEUS — PERSISTENT FAITH THAT WOULD NOT BE SILENCED

Bartimaeus was sitting by the roadside at Jericho — blind, begging, in the position of absolute social limitation. When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he cried out: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." "And many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal." — Mark 10:48 KJV The crowd told him to be quiet. The people around him — the people with standing and position and the ability to see — told him his voice was inappropriate. And he cried the more a great deal. Jesus stopped. He called him. He asked: what wilt thou that I should do unto thee? And Bartimaeus said: Lord, that I might receive my sight. And Jesus said: thy faith hath made thee whole. The person in recovery who has been silenced — by the people who knew what they had done, by the shame that said their voice did not have the right to be heard in the presence of God, by the crowd that moved confidently through the world while they sat at the side of the road — Bartimaeus is their example. He did not have the right credentials. He did not have the standing the crowd had. He had one thing: the knowledge of who was passing and the willingness to cry out regardless of who told him to stop. The humble posture of Step 7 is not the posture of the person who does not speak. It is the posture of the person who does not let the crowd's assessment of their worthiness determine whether they cry out to the One who stopped for the blind man at Jericho.

The person who has genuinely asked God to remove what they could not remove has done something they could not undo. They have acknowledged in the most specific possible way what is true: they cannot complete themselves. And God, who is faithful to that kind of honesty, lifts what is brought to Him.

The prayer established in this step becomes the ongoing contact of Step 11. What begins here as a request becomes a relationship.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 7 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. Help students distinguish between the false humility of low self-assessment and the genuine humility of accurate self-assessment. The humble person does not think poorly of themselves — they think accurately. That accuracy is what makes them correctable, what makes them honest about limitations, and what makes them genuinely open to the God who is able to do what they cannot. SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Proverbs 16:18 KJV — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

■ Proverbs 22:4 KJV — "By humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life."

ASSIGNMENT

Write what it looks like — the specific decisions, the specific resistance to correction, the specific performance of adequacy. Then write what the humble posture would look like in that same area this week. 2. Read Proverbs 11:2 — with the lowly is wisdom. Write: where has the prideful approa...

Not: pride causes God to punish. Pride produces destruction as the natural consequence of the self-governed life encountering what it is not equipped to handle.

choices: It produces contentment — the humble person stops wanting what pride pursued
It produces riches honor and life — the same things the prideful life was pursuing but could not secure through self-governance
It produces spiritual insight — the humble person understands what the proud person cannot see

It produces relationships — the humble person receives the community that self-sufficiency prevented Proverbs 22:4 — by humility and the fear of the LORD are riches and honour and life. Counter-intuitive because those are precisely what the prideful life was pursuing. The humble life receives what the self-governed life was trying to produce. The position under God's governance provides what the self-governance could not secure for itself.

choices: It looks like avoiding assertiveness and deferring to others in all decisions

It looks like constantly diminishing personal achievements and denying capability

It looks like waiting for clear divine direction before making any decision The humble life is rightly active — not passive. The humble person does what God directs, receives feedback without defense, asks for help without shame, names what they are struggling with before it becomes a crisis, and maintains the daily seeking rather than assuming arrival. The humble person does not think poorly of themselves. They think accurately.

lessons.title: The adversary and the armor — spiritual warfare and why recovery is more than behavior
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The spiritual warfare addressed in the New Testament epistles is not a new development in the covenant story. The adversary who opposes the people of God appears across the Old Testament — in the garden, in the accusations against Job, in the temptation narratives of the Gospels. What the epistles add is the specific instruction to people who have entered the covenant life about how to stand — and the specific provision that makes standing possible. Paul wrote to born-again believers at Ephesus — people who had genuinely received what God promises the obedient — showing them the reality they were now living inside and the provision that God had made for it. The instruction is not for people outside the covenant. It is for people who have entered it and need to understand what they are in the middle of. "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places." — Ephesians 6:12 KJV The wrestling is real. The adversary is real. And the recovery that addresses only the behavioral dimension of the addiction — the managing of the use, the changing of the environment, the building of new habits — has not addressed what Ephesians 6:12 describes. The person who is sober but unguarded is not safe. The person who is sober and standing in the armor is standing in something that sobriety alone cannot provide.

Step 6 established something important: there are things in the character that human effort named but could not remove. That is not failure — it is the honest prerequisite for what this step asks.

When Peter stood on the day of Pentecost and told the crowd what to do, the first word he spoke was repent. Not believe harder. Not try again. Repent — and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins. The remission — the sending away — of sin is not accomplished by the decision of Step 3 alone. It is accomplished by the full covenant response: repentance, the name, and the Spirit. This is what the steps have been preparing the road toward.

THE ARMOR

"Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil." — Ephesians 6:11 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers — describing the specific provision available to the person who has received what God promises. The whole armor is not a metaphor for trying harder. It is the description of what the covenant life provides: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, prayer. Each piece is real. Each piece protects against the specific strategies the adversary uses against the person in recovery. The wiles — the strategies, the schemes. The adversary does not attack only with the obvious. He attacks through the subtle: the thought that the person is not good enough, the lie that they are too far gone, the suggestion that the defects are too deep for the removal, the accusation that the progress is not real, the temptation disguised as something the person deserves after sustained effort. The armor is the covenant defense against every form of the attack.

The tax collector in the temple did not lift his eyes toward heaven. He beat his breast and said: God be merciful to me a sinner. Jesus said he went home justified. Humility is not a performance. It is the honest posture of the person who knows what they are.

SOBRIETY IS NOT SECURITY

The person who has gotten behaviorally clean but has not entered the covenant protection is a house swept and garnished — the strong man has been removed but the house stands empty. Matthew 12:44-45 describes what fills the empty house. Recovery that is only behavioral is not the same as the armor of Ephesians 6. The armor is worn by the person who has genuinely received what God promises — and who is standing in that reception daily.

The armor of Ephesians 6 is not abstract spiritual equipment. It is the specific provision for specific attacks — and the person who names their specific attacks is the person who puts on the armor with intention rather than habit.

THE FOUR CATEGORIES OF ATTACK IN RECOVERY:

Relational triggers — specific people who destabilize. Not all people from the old life are equally dangerous. Some are. The person who leaves a conversation with them feeling the pull has identified a relational trigger. This is not judgment of the other person — it is honest assessment of the self.

Environmental triggers — specific places. The bar where you drank. The neighborhood where you used. The house where it happened. The armor of Ephesians 6 does not require you to walk back into the place that defeated you. Proverbs 4:15 KJV: "Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away." Avoidance is not weakness. It is wisdom.

Emotional triggers — specific internal states. Loneliness, boredom, anger, resentment, celebration, and exhaustion are the emotional environments where the flesh has historically found its opening. The daily examination of Step 10 is designed to catch these states before they become situations.

Spiritual triggers — the moment the maintenance practices slip. When the morning Word stops, when the mentor relationship goes quiet, when the daily examination becomes occasional — the armor is being removed piece by piece. The adversary does not need an external attack when the person has stopped suiting up.

Name your specific triggers in each category. Write them. Give the list to your mentor. The person who knows specifically what they are defending against puts on the armor with a different kind of intentionality than the person who only knows that armor exists.

THE ROAD FORWARD

The pattern is consistent across the whole of Scripture: God lifts those who humble themselves. Not those who perform humility — those who actually occupy the low place honestly. The lifting is always in response to the genuine posture, never to the performance of it.

The adversary and the armor have been identified. Lesson 4 is the Step 7 completion — what has been received through the humble asking, and the beginning of Step 8.

THE PATTERN — ACTS AND THE COVENANT RESPONSE

Here is the pattern the Scripture records without variation: every time the Spirit fell upon people in the book of Acts, the same sequence occurred. Not a similar sequence. The same one.

On the day of Pentecost — Acts 2:38: repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, receive the Holy Ghost. At the house of Cornelius — Acts 10:44-48: the Holy Ghost fell, they spoke in tongues, Peter commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. At Ephesus — Acts 19:1-6: Paul asked if they had received the Holy Ghost since they believed. They had not. He baptized them in the name of the Lord Jesus. The Holy Ghost came, they spoke in tongues.

The question is not whether this pattern exists. It exists. The question is what a person does with it.

The remission of sins — the actual clearing of the debt that the life under bondage accumulated — is not accomplished by the decision of Step 3, by the inventory of Step 4, or by the confession of Step 5. Those steps are the honest preparation. The remission is the covenant gift that comes through the covenant response: repentance, the name of Jesus in baptism, and the entrance of the Spirit.

This is what Step 7 has been building toward. The humble request. The vessel cleared. And the provision that actually answers the question all the prior steps have been asking.

Scripture uses a phrase that is worth naming directly here: obeying the gospel.

"And to you who are troubled rest with us, when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, In flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God, and that obey not the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ." — 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8 KJV
"For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God?" — 1 Peter 4:17 KJV

The gospel must be obeyed, not merely acknowledged. Paul the apostle defines the gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 KJV as three events: the death of Christ, His burial, and His resurrection. These are not merely historical facts to believe — they are a pattern to obey. Repentance corresponds to death. Baptism corresponds to burial. Receiving the Holy Ghost corresponds to resurrection. The gospel is not only proclaimed — it is entered.

JERICHO — STRONGHOLDS FALL DIFFERENTLY THAN YOU EXPECT

The walls of Jericho were not taken by force. The Israelites did not build siege engines or attack the gates. They walked. Every day for six days they walked around the city in silence. On the seventh day they walked seven times, and then they shouted, and the walls fell. "By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days." — Hebrews 11:30 KJV The writer of Hebrews does not say the walls fell by military strategy. He says they fell by faith — expressed as sustained, consistent, obedient action that looked nothing like how walls are supposed to fall. Some of the strongholds in recovery do not respond to direct assault. The person who tries to break a particular bondage through concentrated effort — treating it as a problem to be solved by sufficient force of will — often finds that the wall is still standing and they are exhausted. The pattern this program teaches is not force. It is consistency. Obedience sustained past the point where results are visible. The daily surrender of Step 3. The daily inventory of Step 10. The daily prayer and Word of Step 11. Six days of walking around the wall in silence. Then the seventh day. The stronghold does not fall on your timeline or by your method. It falls when the obedience is complete. And when it falls — like Jericho — it falls completely.

The person who has genuinely asked God to remove what they could not remove has done something they could not undo. They have acknowledged in the most specific possible way what is true: they cannot complete themselves. And God, who is faithful to that kind of honesty, lifts what is brought to Him.

The prayer established in this step becomes the ongoing contact of Step 11. What begins here as a request becomes a relationship.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 7 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson must be taught with epistle-framing. Paul wrote to born-again believers. The armor is available to and describing the posture of people who have genuinely entered the covenant. Do not present this lesson as armor available to everyone regardless of covenant position. Show it in its covenant position. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER Ephesians 6:11-12 is an epistle — written to born-again believers at Ephesus, describing the spiritual reality they were...

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Ephesians 6:11 KJV — "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."

■ Ephesians 6:12 KJV — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world."

■ 1 Peter 5:8 KJV — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour."

ASSIGNMENT

The armor and the adversary 1. Identify the three most active attacks on your recovery that are non-behavioral — the thoughts, the lies, the disguised suggestions. For each: name it specifically, identify which piece of the armor addresses it, and write what applying that piece looks like this week. 2. Read Ephesians 6:13-18 in full. For each piece of the armor, write: what does this look like spe...

choices: The armor is for spiritual advancement — enabling the person to grow beyond basic recovery into leadership
