lessons.title: Daily examination — the four areas of inventory and how to work them every day
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
When God established the daily rhythm of the tabernacle — the morning sacrifice and the evening sacrifice, the daily burning of incense, the weekly setting of the showbread — the pattern was not arbitrary. The daily return to the appointed practice was the maintenance of the relationship that the practice expressed. Step 10 establishes the same daily rhythm: not because the relationship is in danger every day but because the daily practice is what keeps the relational ground clear that Steps 4 through 9 cleared.

Step 9 cleared the ground of the past. Step 10 is the daily practice that keeps it clear.

The God before whom the daily examination takes place is one Spirit, one LORD — who knows the heart before the examination begins and is not surprised by what the inventory finds.

Daily inventory is daily repentance made practical. The person who takes a daily inventory and promptly admits when wrong is practicing what Paul the apostle described as dying daily — the ongoing posture of a life that continues to turn toward God rather than toward self.

THE FOUR DAILY INVENTORY AREAS

"Lamentations 3:40 — Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." — Lamentations 3:40 KJV Jeremiah wrote Lamentations in the aftermath of Jerusalem's destruction — describing the return to the LORD as beginning with searching and trying the ways. The daily inventory is the same search applied not to the accumulated years but to today.

Paul the apostle wrote about dying daily — not from a position of arrival, but from the ongoing practice of a person who knew that the flesh does not retire. The daily examination is not evidence of failure. It is the practice of the person who has understood.

TODAY'S CRAVING CHECK

If a craving came today: when? what preceded it? what did you do? how long did it last?

The craving log is not evidence of failure in the program. It is the most honest data the daily examination can produce. The person who tracks cravings is doing exactly what Step 10 requires — examining, naming, not hiding. Report it to your mentor.

RESENTMENT — TODAY'S CHECK

Did anything today produce the familiar re-feeling — the resurfacing of an old wound in a new situation? Name it. Is it an old resentment surfacing in a new context, or a new resentment beginning? Either way: name it, examine my part in it, and address it today before it sits overnight. The question: what produced a reaction in me today that was larger than the situation warranted? The disproportionate reaction is often the surface of a resentment — old or new.

FEAR — TODAY'S CHECK

What decision did I make today from fear rather than faith? What conversation did I avoid? What did I manage rather than address honestly? Fear in the daily inventory is often more subtle than the fears that appeared in Step 4 — it shows up in small daily avoidances rather than major life decisions. The question: where did I manage a situation today instead of engaging it honestly? That is usually fear.

HARM — TODAY'S CHECK

Who has something against me as a result of today? Not the accumulated list from years — today's. Did I speak carelessly? Did I fail to keep a commitment? Did I use someone for my own ends? Did I leave something undone that I had agreed to do? The question: who did I put into the position of having something against me today?

OMISSION — TODAY'S CHECK

What did I know to do today and not do? James 4:17 is the governing passage. The omission is the daily version of the fourth column in Step 4 — what I knew and did not act on. The question: what did I know today and not do?

This is the pattern Paul the apostle described as dying daily — not a single event, but a practice. The ongoing inventory is not the evidence of a person who has not arrived. It is the practice of a person who understands that the flesh does not retire, and has stopped pretending otherwise.

THE PROMPTLY PRINCIPLE IN PRACTICE

For every entry in the daily inventory: address it today where it can be addressed today. The person who is wrong today and addresses it today has nothing to carry into to morrow. The person who defers carries it — and the deferred thing begins to behave like the unaddressed inventory of Steps 4 and 5 behaved. "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit." — Ephesians 5:18 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Ephesus — describing the two options available to the person who has yielded their life. The daily inventory is one of the practices that keeps the person in the filling rather than drifting toward what the filling was meant to replace. The person who examines daily and addresses promptly is the person who maintains the available posture that the Spirit fills.

The person who maintains a daily inventory is not performing accountability — they are living as someone for whom honesty has become the default. That is transformation at the level of character, not behavior. That is what the steps have been building.

The examined life and the prayerful life are the two disciplines that sustain everything the prior steps built. Step 11 is where the examined life finds its source.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 10 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson gives the practical daily structure. The four areas should be taught as a checklist that takes minutes, not hours. The goal is the establishment of a sustainable daily practice, not an elaborate ritual. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER The daily sacrifice of the tabernacle — morning and evening, without exception — is the covenant picture of the daily inventory. The rhythm is the maintenance of the relationship. Help students see: Step 10 is not reme...

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ Lamentations 3:40 KJV — "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD."

ASSIGNMENT

The daily inventory practice 1. Use the four-area format every evening this week: resentment, fear, harm, omission. 2. For every entry: address it promptly before the next day where possible. 3. Track which area produces the most entries. At the end of the week: name the pattern. 4. Bring the week's record and the pattern to your mentor. Due: Before Lesson 3

Jeremiah wrote this in the worst of circumstances. The examination comes first, then the turning. Step 10 is the daily version of the same sequence applied to the ordinary day rather than the crisis.

lessons.title: When wrong promptly admit it — what prompt admission does for the life and the relationships
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
David was called a man after God's own heart — not because he did not sin grievously but because when confronted with what he had done, his response was immediate and unqualified: "I have sinned against the LORD." When Nathan said "Thou art the man," David did not deflect. He did not qualify. He did not reference Bathsheba's part or Uriah's circumstances or the pressures of the season. He said: I have sinned against the LORD. That is prompt admission.

Step 9 cleared the ground of the past. Step 10 is the daily practice that keeps it clear.

Daily inventory is daily repentance made practical. The person who takes a daily inventory and promptly admits when wrong is practicing what Paul the apostle described as dying daily — the ongoing posture of a life that continues to turn toward God rather than toward self.

WHEN WRONG PROMPTLY ADMIT IT

"Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled." — Matthew 5:23-24 KJV The pattern is the same one Step 9 walked through — but now in real time, in the daily life, at the moment it surfaces rather than after it has accumulated for years. When the daily inventory reveals that something happened today that left a brother with something against you — the instruction is the same: go. Address it. Today.

Paul the apostle wrote about dying daily — not from a position of arrival, but from the ongoing practice of a person who knew that the flesh does not retire. The daily examination is not evidence of failure. It is the practice of the person who has understood.

HOW TO SAY YOU ARE WRONG

The prompt admission has no qualifications attached. It does not begin with what the other person did. It does not explain the circumstances that contributed. It does not minimize what happened. It says: "I was wrong. I said [the specific thing]. I am sorry. I will [the specific change]." That is complete. Four parts. The specific wrong, the acknowledgment, the apology, and the change. Anything added to this formula is usually the self protecting its position — explaining the context, referencing the other person's contribution, minimizing the severity. Additions are the signal that the self is managing rather than admitting.

THE CHARACTER OF PROMPT ADMISSION

"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." — James 5:16 KJV The person who can say they are wrong without qualification — promptly, specifically, and without management — has developed the character that Step 9 began forming. The prompt admission is the daily practice of the same character. It is not easier than the amends of Step 9. It is the same skill applied to smaller daily material — which is how the skill becomes automatic rather than effortful. The person who practices prompt admission daily for a year is a different person than the one who made the amends list once and returned to deferred acknowledgment in the daily life. The character is formed in the daily practice, not in the single event.

WHEN WRONG AND NO ONE KNOWS

Some daily inventory entries will involve wrongs that only the person and God are aware of — the internal resentment, the private fear-based decision, the omission no one observed. The prompt admission in these cases is to God, in the daily prayer. The same unqualified acknowledgment: I was wrong. I did this. I am returning to the truth of what You showed me in the inventory. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9 KJV The promise is not conditional on the severity. It is conditional on the honesty. The daily prompt admission to God of what the daily inventory revealed is the daily application of 1 John 1:9 — the daily walking in the light that the verse describes. THE TONGUE IN THE DAILY INVENTORY "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh." — Luke 6:45 KJV

The daily inventory of Step 10 includes what the mouth produced today. Not as a separate category — but as the diagnostic instrument that shows what the heart contains. The tongue is not an independent problem to be managed. It is the report of the heart's current contents. What did the mouth produce today that the honest examination shows came from a place the inventory has already named? The resentment that found its way into a sarcastic comment. The fear that produced a controlling conversation. The pride that could not acknowledge being wrong until the accumulation made it unavoidable. The prompt admission of Step 10 often begins with the tongue — because the mouth spoke what the heart held before the examination reached it. The honest examination works backward from what was said to what must still be present in the heart. That is the candle of Proverbs 20:27 in daily operation: the spirit of man illuminating what the mouth reported before the mind examined it. What did your mouth say today that your heart was carrying?

This is the pattern Paul the apostle described as dying daily — not a single event, but a practice. The ongoing inventory is not the evidence of a person who has not arrived. It is the practice of a person who understands that the flesh does not retire, and has stopped pretending otherwise.

GAZA — SAMSON AND THE DANGER OF RETURNING

Samson was the strongest man the Scripture records. His strength was genuine — the gift of God operating in a man set apart from birth. And he lost it not through a single catastrophic decision but through a pattern of returning to the wrong places. Gaza was Philistine territory. It was where his enemies lived, where the temptations that governed his weakness operated, where every significant compromise of his life had its geography. And he kept going back. "Then went Samson to Gaza, and saw there an harlot, and went in unto her." — Judges 16:1 KJV The strength that could kill a lion and tear the gates of a city off their posts could not overcome the pull of the wrong geography. Samson's fall was not primarily about Delilah. It was about Gaza. The return to the place, the environment, the relational field where the pattern had always operated. The promptly principle of Step 10 includes the geography of the daily life. The person who addresses the substance but returns to the environment — the people, the places, the situations where the pattern lived — is in Gaza. The prompt admission when wrong must include the honest accounting of where wrong was invited in. What places are you still visiting that have not yet been surrendered? What environments are you returning to that are Philistine territory? The daily examination of Step 10 asks this as surely as it asks about resentment and fear.

The person who maintains a daily inventory is not performing accountability — they are living as someone for whom honesty has become the default. That is transformation at the level of character, not behavior. That is what the steps have been building.

The examined life and the prayerful life are the two disciplines that sustain everything the prior steps built. Step 11 is where the examined life finds its source.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 10 Lesson 3 MEMBER LESSON. The focus of this lesson is the specific skill of prompt admission — how to say you are wrong without qualification. Most students have a version of the qualified admission they have been using — the admission with the explanation attached, the acknowledgment with the contribution of the other person referenced. Help them see the qualifier as the self managing its position. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER 2 Samuel 12:13 — David said: I have sinned against the L...

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ 1 John 1:9 KJV — "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

ASSIGNMENT

Prompt admission practice 1. This week: every time the daily inventory reveals a wrong — deliver the four-part admission before the day ends. 2. Track the qualifiers you tried to attach. Write them down and then remove them from the actual admission. 3. For private wrongs — bring them to the daily prayer in the same four-part honesty. 4. Report to your mentor: how many prompt admissions this week,...

Acknowledgment apology explanation and plan — the explanation is part of the complete admission

Confession witness accountability and amendment — all four require another person to be present The complete prompt admission: I was wrong / I said or did [the specific thing] / I am sorry / I will [the specific change]. Qualifiers — the but, the because, the context, the other person's contribution — are the self managing its position. Remove them. The four parts without additions are the complete admission.

lessons.title: A life lived in daily maintenance — completing Step 10 and carrying it forward
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
The daily rhythm of the tabernacle did not end because the tabernacle was completed. The daily sacrifice continued as long as the tabernacle stood — and then continued in the temple — because the relationship it maintained required the daily practice, not the single event of dedication. Step 10 is the same. It does not complete with a graduation. It continues as the daily discipline of the person who has committed to a life in which the ground cleared by Steps 4-9 stays clear.

Step 9 cleared the ground of the past. Step 10 is the daily practice that keeps it clear.

Daily inventory is daily repentance made practical. The person who takes a daily inventory and promptly admits when wrong is practicing what Paul the apostle described as dying daily — the ongoing posture of a life that continues to turn toward God rather than toward self.

A LIFE LIVED IN DAILY MAINTENANCE

"Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." — 1 Corinthians 10:12 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers at Corinth — the people who believed their progress was sufficient security. The warning is not to the person in visible failure. It is to the person who thinks they stand — who has reached a level of recovery that feels secure enough to reduce the vigilance. The daily inventory is not a discipline for the struggling. It is the discipline of the person who has learned what happens when the discipline is removed. The maintenance of what Steps 4-9 produced requires the same honest daily attention that the building required.

Paul the apostle wrote about dying daily — not from a position of arrival, but from the ongoing practice of a person who knew that the flesh does not retire. The daily examination is not evidence of failure. It is the practice of the person who has understood.

WHAT DAILY MAINTENANCE LOOKS LIKE

The person who has established the daily inventory as a genuine practice — not a formal session but the ongoing posture of the day — carries less into each week than the person who reviews monthly or only in crisis. The daily examination keeps the pile small. The promptly principle keeps it addressed. The combination produces a life in which the accumulated inventory of Step 4 does not need to happen again — because what would become that inventory is addressed daily before it accumulates. This is the daily life of the person who has worked the steps honestly: not the absence of resentment, fear, harm, and omission — but the consistent daily addressing of whatever appears, so that it does not stay.

NEHEMIAH'S WORKERS — BUILDING AND WATCHING SIMULTANEOUSLY

"They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon." — Nehemiah 4:17 KJV Step 10 is the weapon in the other hand. The new life is being built in Step 11 — the deepening of the relationship with God, the drawing nigh that produces the drawing nigh of God toward you. Step 10 is the watching that allows the building to continue without the enemy reclaiming what was cleared. The person who drops the weapon — who stops the daily examination because the life is going well — is the person Corinthians warns: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed. The stability of the good season is the season the vigilance is most important to maintain.

THE ROAD FORWARD

This is the pattern Paul the apostle described as dying daily — not a single event, but a practice. The ongoing inventory is not the evidence of a person who has not arrived. It is the practice of a person who understands that the flesh does not retire, and has stopped pretending otherwise.

Step 10 continues permanently. Step 11 deepens the relationship with God that all of the preceding steps have been preparing for. The person who has cleared the ground through Steps 4-9 and maintains it through Step 10 is the person positioned for what Step 11 opens.

LAODICEA — COMPLACENCY IS AS DANGEROUS AS BONDAGE

Of all the churches Jesus addressed in Revelation, the one He described most severely was not the one in obvious sin. It was the one that was comfortable. "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth. Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked." — Revelation 3:15-17 KJV Laodicea was prosperous. It had a banking center, a medical school famous for eye salve, and a textile industry. The church there had absorbed the values of the city — it had need of nothing. And Jesus said it was wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. The very things the city was known for — wealth, medicine for the eyes, clothing — Jesus said the church lacked, because it believed its comfort was evidence of its health. The person who has been in recovery long enough to feel stable, whose worst days are far enough behind them that the urgency of early recovery has settled, who has built a life that functions and no longer feels the pressing need of the first months — that person is in Laodicea. The stability is real. The danger is also real. The temperature of the early recovery — the desperate daily hunger for what the program pointed toward — must be maintained as a discipline when the desperation is no longer driving it. Step 10 is the daily discipline that prevents Laodicea. The daily examination does not wait for crisis to resume. It runs in the good season — precisely because the good season is when Laodicea sets in.

The person who maintains a daily inventory is not performing accountability — they are living as someone for whom honesty has become the default. That is transformation at the level of character, not behavior. That is what the steps have been building.

The examined life and the prayerful life are the two disciplines that sustain everything the prior steps built. Step 11 is where the examined life finds its source.

The daily maintenance of Step 10 is only sustainable because of what Step 7 asked for and Step 11 will describe in full — the Spirit who entered the believer and sustains what no daily discipline alone can maintain. The examined life is the life of a person who knows they are not maintaining this on their own. The Spirit they received is the power behind the practice.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 10 Lesson 4 MEMBER LESSON. This is the completion lesson of Step 10 — but unlike previous completion lessons, the completion here is the establishment of a permanent practice, not the closure of a season. The tone is forward and practical. Step 10 continues into Step 11 and Step 12 without interruption. COVENANT CONTEXT FOR THE TEACHER 1 Corinthians 10:12 — the warning to the person who thinks they stand. The daily maintenance is most important in the seasons of apparent stability — when ...

ASSIGNMENT

Identify the one area of the four that most often shows up. What does the pattern show about the ongoing work of Steps 6 and 7? 3. Commit the practice to your mentor in writing. This is your Step 10 covenant. 4. Begin Step 11 immediately. ...

lessons.title: Draw nigh to God — sought through prayer and meditation and what the seeking is building toward
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
Draw nigh to God — sought through prayer and meditation and what the seeking is building toward ■ PUBLIC — Open Access

In Step 10 we saw that the examined life must be a daily practice. Step 11 is where that daily practice finds its source — the God who sustains what human discipline alone cannot maintain.

The God who draws near to those who draw near to Him is one Spirit, one LORD — James 4:8 KJV — and the nearness is not a metaphor. It is the lived reality of a Spirit who enters and sustains.

Step 11 is the deepening. The first ten steps have cleared the ground, addressed the past, and built the maintenance practice. Now there is only one thing left to name clearly — and it is the thing the entire program has been pointing toward from the first lesson. You are seeking God. Not a practice. Not a discipline. Not a principle or a method. The living God — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The God who made you, who sees you, who has been working in you across every difficult step of this program. That God. Sought. Through prayer and meditation. To improve the conscious contact that is not optional but essential to everything recovery requires. Step 11 says it plainly: sought through prayer and meditation to improve our conscious contact with God. The object of the seeking is not a feeling of peace. Not spiritual growth as an abstract goal. Not a healthier mindset. God Himself. Sought. Deliberately. Through two specific disciplines — prayer and meditation — that together constitute the seeking. "And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart." — Jeremiah 29:13 KJV With all your heart. That is the condition. Not the occasional prayer. Not the devotional when it is convenient. A seeking that is wholehearted — because a halfhearted seeking of God is no seeking at all. "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him." — Hebrews 11:6 KJV Diligently seek Him. He is a rewarder of the diligent seeker — not the casual one. And what God gives to the diligent seeker is not information about Himself. It is Himself — His presence, His power working in the person from within, the filling of the life that has been emptied of self-sufficiency and made available. The person who arrives at Step 11 having worked Steps 1 through 10 honestly has been seeking God across the whole year of this program — in the painful honesty of Step 4, in the courage of Step 5, in the surrender of Step 7, in the humility of Step 9. Step 11 names what has been happening and makes it explicit, intentional, and daily.

WHAT STEP 11 IS ACTUALLY SEEKING

The first ten steps have done specific work. Step 1 named the problem honestly. Steps 2 and 3 established a God worth believing in and made a decision toward Him. Steps 4 through 9 cleared the ground — the resentments, the fears, the harms, the character defects, the relational debts. Step 10 built the daily maintenance practice.

Step 11 is not a new discipline added on top of what came before. It is the living relationship that the first ten steps were building toward.

The person who has genuinely worked Steps 1 through 10 is not the same person who started. The old governance has been surrendered. The ground has been cleared. The amends have been made or are underway. The daily examination is in practice. What the cleared life now needs is not more program — it is contact. Ongoing, deliberate, daily contact with the God who was sought from Step 1 forward.

"Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you." — James 4:8 KJV

The promise is directional: the movement toward God produces a corresponding movement. It is not passive. It is not automatic. It is the daily choice of a person who has understood that what sustained the first ten steps was not willpower — it was the same God this step is now deliberately seeking.

Step 11 has two disciplines and one object.

The two disciplines are prayer and meditation. The object is God — not peace as a feeling, not spiritual development as a concept, not a better version of the self. God. Sought deliberately. Encountered personally. Engaged with every day.

The person who practices Step 11 without a clear object will drift — the prayer will become a ritual, the meditation will become reflection, the discipline will become performance. The object makes the discipline real. And the object of Step 11 is the God who has been present across the entire journey — who was there at the worst moment of Step 1, who initiated the belief of Step 2, who accepted the surrender of Step 3, and who has been directing the steps ever since.

PRAYER — SPEAKING TO THE GOD WHO HEARS

Prayer is the discipline of speaking to God — not about God, not toward a concept, but to the specific God who has made Himself known across the journey of these steps. The person who has worked Step 11 honestly discovers that prayer changes. What began in early recovery as crisis communication — help me, get me through this — becomes something more like conversation: what is Your will for this day? What are You doing in this situation? What do You want from me here?

"Pray without ceasing." — 1 Thessalonians 5:17 KJV

Paul wrote this to born-again believers — not as a command to be on their knees continuously, but as a description of the posture of a person whose life is in ongoing communication with God. The person who prays without ceasing is the person whose first instinct in any situation is toward God — not toward the phone, not toward the old patterns, not toward the self's usual management strategies.

"Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." — Philippians 4:6 KJV

Everything. Not only the significant moments. Not only the crises. Every thing. The ordinary decision, the difficult conversation, the daily uncertainty — all of it brought to the God who hears.

The prayer that Step 11 builds is not the prayer of a person asking God to approve what they have already decided. It is the prayer of a person who has genuinely surrendered the governance of the life — and who is asking, every day, for the direction to be made clear and the strength to walk in it.

MEDITATION — WHAT BIBLICAL MEDITATION ACTUALLY IS

Meditation has acquired connotations in the culture that are not what the Scripture describes. Biblical meditation is not the emptying of the mind. It is not passive receptivity or the absence of thought. It is the sustained, intentional dwelling on what God has said — holding it, turning it, asking what it means and what it requires.

"This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein." — Joshua 1:8 KJV

The purpose of the meditation is the doing. Meditation in Scripture is not contemplation for its own sake — it is the sustained engagement with the Word that produces the understanding that produces the obedience. The person who meditates on the Word is not simply thinking about it. They are letting it do what it does: correct, instruct, redirect, form.

"Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly... but his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night." — Psalm 1:1-2 KJV

The person whose delight is in the Word and who meditates on it day and night is described in the verses that follow: like a tree planted by rivers of water, bringing forth fruit in its season, whose leaf shall not wither. The meditation is what produces the rootedness. The rootedness is what produces the fruit. And the fruit is what Step 12 will carry into the world.

PRACTICAL MEDITATION IN DAILY RECOVERY: Take one verse from the daily reading. Read it slowly — three times. Ask three questions: What does this say? What does this mean? What does this require of me today? Do not move past it until the third question has an honest answer.

MEDITATION AS CRAVING INTERRUPTION

Biblical meditation is not only a spiritual practice — it is a physiological one. The mind that is genuinely occupied with the Word is doing something different than the mind that is following the craving. The obsessing mind — the mind that runs the same track toward the same substance — cannot run that track and meditate on the Word simultaneously.

"Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee." — Isaiah 26:3 KJV

Stayed on thee. The mind that is stayed — anchored, fixed, dwelling — is the mind that is not available to the craving in the same way. This is not magic. It is the practical result of giving the mind something more powerful to dwell on than what it has been trained to crave.

When the craving comes and the phone call is not possible and the physical removal is not possible — the Word is always possible. Open it. Read it slowly. Ask what it says. Ask what it means. Ask what it requires. By the time those three questions are answered, the craving has often passed — because cravings are time-limited, and the meditation provided the bridge across the time.

THREE SIGNS YOUR PRAYER HAS SHIFTED FROM SELF TO GOD

First: you begin to ask for what others need rather than only for what you need. The person whose prayer has shifted from self-seeking to God-seeking finds that intercession for others becomes natural — not obligatory. Second: you become less anxious about the outcome of what you asked for. The person praying according to God's will is not managing the answer. They have presented the matter to the One whose answer is better than their request, and left it there. Third: you begin to recognize when what you were praying for was not actually what you needed — and feel gratitude that God answered differently than you asked. That recognition is the evidence of a maturing prayer life. The prayer of Step 11 is not a performance of spiritual discipline. It is the daily conversation of a person who has discovered that God answers — and that His answer is worth aligning with. THE PROMISE OF THE FATHER "And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high." — Luke 24:49 KJV Jesus said this as His final instruction before ascending — not to strangers, not to people who had just heard Him for the first time, but to the disciples who had walked with Him for three years, who had seen the miracles, who believed He was the Christ. And He told them: wait. There is something you have not yet received. There is a promise of the Father that has not yet arrived. Do not go until it comes. What was the promise of the Father that the disciples — believing, following, committed — had not yet received? "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." — Acts 2:4 KJV This is what arrived. This is what they waited for. This is what Peter stood up and identified: "This is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." The promise of the Father was not a feeling of peace, not a renewed commitment, not a decision renewed in prayer. It was a specific, identifiable arrival — with a sound, with evidence, with a witness that could be seen and heard by everyone present. The curriculum has been walking toward this question since the preface. Now it is time to name it directly: The steps clear the vessel. The vessel is being cleared for something. The something is not the steps themselves. The steps point toward the God who fills what is genuinely surrendered to Him. And the filling He has promised — the promise of the Father that Jesus sent the disciples to wait for — is the Holy Ghost. "For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call." — Acts 2:39 KJV This promise was not exclusive to the day of Pentecost. Peter said it plainly: it is unto you. And to your children. And to all that are afar off. The same promise. The same arrival. The same evidence. For as many as the Lord our

God shall call. Draw nigh to God. This is what He is drawing nigh with.

The pattern across the whole of Scripture is that those who drew near to God found that He drew near to them. Not as a formula — as a relationship. The seeking produced the encounter. The encounter produced the sustaining. The sustaining produced everything that followed.

WHAT IS BEING BUILT — AND WHERE IT LEADS

The person who maintains Step 11 consistently — who prays daily, who meditates on the Word, who seeks God's will before their own — is building something that the first ten steps could not build by themselves.

The first ten steps did the clearing work. Step 11 builds the ongoing contact that sustains what was cleared and keeps it clear. The person who works Steps 1 through 10 and then stops — who does not maintain the contact of Step 11 — has cleared the house but left it empty. Jesus described what happens to the swept house that is left unoccupied. It becomes more vulnerable than it was before the clearing.

Step 11 is the discipline that keeps the cleared life filled with what belongs in it — contact with God, alignment with His will, the daily renewal of the surrender made in Step 3.

What this builds over time is not simply discipline. It is a relationship. The person who has sought God daily across weeks and months and years has encountered Him in ways that cannot be manufactured by effort. The seeking produces the encounter. The encounter produces the trust. The trust produces the obedience. The obedience produces the life that Step 12 will carry into the world.

"But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." — Isaiah 40:31 KJV

The waiting is active. It is the deliberate positioning of the life toward God — daily, consistently, over time. That waiting is what Step 11 is asking for. And what it produces is the renewed strength that the person who has walked twelve honest steps needs for what comes next.

HOW MUCH MORE WILL YOUR FATHER GIVE

"If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" — Luke 11:13 KJV Jesus said this in the context of teaching about persistent prayer — the friend at midnight, the ask-seek-knock sequence of verses 9-10. And then He named what the heavenly Father gives to those who ask with persistence and genuine seeking: the Holy Spirit. Not general blessing. Not vague divine favor. The Holy Spirit — specifically named as the gift the Father gives to those who ask Him. Step 11 is the step of drawing nigh to God — the deepening of the relationship through prayer and the daily Word. And Jesus identified what the Father gives to the person who draws nigh with genuine seeking: Himself, in the form of the Holy Spirit. The drawing nigh of Step 11 is building toward the specific gift that Luke 11:13 names. Ask for it. Not as a formula. As the honest request of a person who has read what the Father promises to give and wants what He is offering.

The person who genuinely seeks God finds that the seeking itself is answered. Not always immediately. Not always dramatically. But the pattern of Scripture is clear: draw nigh to God, and He will draw nigh to thee. The daily posture of drawing near is the posture of a person who has understood who they are and who God is.

The person sustained by prayer and contact in this step is ready to carry the message. Step 12 is the reason all eleven steps preceded it.

There is a provision at the end of this road that does not depend on human effort to sustain it. Every step from 1 through 10 has been preparation — not for a better version of the old life, but for the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus. The Spirit who enters does not come as one gift among many. He comes as the one who makes all that follows possible.

SCRIPTURE MEMORY

■ James 4:8 KJV — "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you."

■ Psalm 46:10 KJV — "Be still, and know that I am God."

ASSIGNMENT

Conscious contact practice This week establish or deepen your conscious contact practice. 1. Set a specific time for prayer each morning and each evening. Write the times. 2. Practice 10 minutes of stillness daily — no devices no noise. Write one thing you heard or noticed in each session. 3. Choose one passage from your daily reading to meditate on rather than just read. Write what emerges when ...

quiz.question: What does conscious contact mean in Step 11?
choices: A vague spiritual awareness throughout the day
Attending religious services regularly
Intentional deliberate sought-after relationship with God — not background noise but cultivated depth
Having strong feelings about God and prayer Conscious contact means intentional relationship — deliberate sought after cultivated. Not God as background noise.

quiz.question: According to James 4:8 KJV what happens when you draw nigh to God?
choices: He tests you to see if you are sincere
He will draw nigh to you
He gives you what you ask for
He removes all temptation James 4:8 — draw nigh to God and he will draw nigh to you. Move toward Him deliberately and He responds in kind. Step 11 is the drawing near.

quiz.question: According to Psalm 46:10 KJV what precedes knowing that He is God?
choices: Prayer and fasting
Church attendance
Being still

Completing the 12 steps Psalm 46:10 — be still and know that I am God. The stillness precedes the knowing. The addiction was partly a mechanism for not being still. Step 11 asks you to sit in the silence long enough to hear who is there.

quiz.question: What is the difference between prayer and meditation in Step 11?
choices: Prayer is formal and meditation is informal
Prayer is required and meditation is optional
Prayer is speaking to God and meditation is listening — stilling the internal noise long enough to hear what He speaks back

Prayer is done alone and meditation is done in community Prayer is speaking to God. Meditation is listening — being still long enough to hear what He speaks back. Most people are better at speaking than listening.

Week 43 Day 2 — Psalm 46:10 Be still and know that I am God. Spend 10 minutes in silence today. Write what you hear.

lessons.title: And He will draw nigh to thee — walking in the Spirit and what daily dependence actually looks like
lessons.author: RRN Staff
lessons.body:
And He will draw nigh to thee — walking in the Spirit and what daily dependence actually looks like ■ MEMBER — Login Required

In Step 10 we saw that the examined life must be a daily practice. Step 11 is where that daily practice finds its source — the God who sustains what human discipline alone cannot maintain.

MEMBER LESSON

Step 11 asks you to seek through prayer and meditation to improve your conscious contact with God. This lesson asks the next question: what does that actually look like on a Tuesday? Not in a prayer meeting. Not in a moment of crisis. On an ordinary Tuesday when nothing dramatic is happening and you just have to live.

Elijah, having just called down fire from heaven, sat under a juniper tree and asked God to take his life. That is where the angel met him — not at Carmel, but at the juniper tree. Not in the triumph, but in the exhaustion. God meets the person where they actually are.

Acts 2:38 contains three movements in one sentence. They are not independent options — they are a sequence. "Repent" — the genuine turning, the change of direction, the death of the old governance. "And be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ" — not a formula repeated, but the specific and only name given under heaven among men whereby we must be saved (Acts 4:12), applied in water as the covenant act that identifies the believer with the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ (Romans 6:4). "For the remission of sins" — the sending away, the legal acquittal, the clearing of the debt that self-governance accumulated. "And ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost" — the entrance of the Spirit, what Jesus called the promise of the Father, the power that makes everything that follows sustainable.

These are not four separate religious practices. They are one covenant response to one God — the complete answer to the question the crowd asked when the Word cut them to the heart: "Men and brethren, what shall we do?"

Peter did not say: do your best, join a community, manage your behavior. He said: repent. Be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Receive the Holy Ghost. The remission of sins — the debt cleared — is not the result of effort. It is the result of the covenant response. The person who repents and is baptized in Jesus name does not earn remission. They receive it. That is what makes it grace.

THE DAILY WALK

Paul wrote this instruction to born-again believers who had received the Spirit — the walking in the Spirit describes the daily life of someone already in that relationship, not the path to entering it: "This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh." — Galatians 5:16 KJV Walk in the Spirit. Not run. Not perform. Not achieve a spiritual high. Walk. Daily. Ordinary. Consistent. Walking implies movement and direction. It implies that every step is a choice. You do not stumble into walking in the Spirit. You choose it — moment by moment decision by decision — with the understanding that the alternative is always the flesh filling the vacuum.

DAILY BREAD — NOT WEEKLY SUPPLIES

"Give us this day our daily bread." — Matthew 6:11 KJV The disciples prayed for daily bread. Not weekly. Not monthly. Not a stockpile. Daily. There is a reason God provided manna in the wilderness one day at a time. When people tried to gather extra — to store it up and coast — it rotted. The provision was designed to require daily dependence. Your spiritual nourishment works the same way. The Word read deeply yesterday does not feed you today. The prayer offered last week does not carry you through this week. The connection to God is not a tank you fill up once. It is a daily walk — daily bread — daily renewal. "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby." — 1 Peter 2:2 KJV Newborn babes do not eat once a week. They eat daily. They eat urgently. They eat because life depends on it. That is the posture toward the Word that recovery requires.

THE MIND SET ON THE SPIRIT

"For they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh; but they that are after the Spirit the things of the Spirit." — Romans 8:5 KJV The word mind here means to set the mind on — to direct the attention toward. What you set your mind on shapes what you become. What you consume shapes what you crave. What you fill the hours with shapes the default direction of your life. A person walking in the Spirit has intentionally set their mind on the things of the Spirit. Not perfectly. Not without struggle. But intentionally. The Word is in the morning before the phone. Prayer happens before the decision not after the problem. The mind is brought back when it wanders. "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." — Romans 12:2 KJV Transformed by the renewing — not by trying harder but by what fills the mind. The transformation follows the renewal. The renewal follows the daily intake.

Scripture shows two distinct realities that must not be collapsed. The first is the moment the Spirit enters the believer — the New Birth, the point of indwelling, what Acts records consistently from the upper room to Ephesus. The second is the ongoing operations of the Spirit through the believer — what Paul the apostle describes in First Corinthians 12 as the diversities of gifts distributed as the Spirit wills.

These are not the same category. Entry precedes operation. The Spirit enters the believer first. The Spirit then operates through the believer in varied gifts for the building of the body. Confusing these two collapses the order that both Acts and Paul keep carefully distinct.

The question is not which gifts a person might receive. The question is whether the Spirit has entered — and Scripture shows consistently what that entrance sounds like when it comes.

THE CONFLICT IS REAL AND ONGOING

"For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would." — Galatians 5:17 KJV The conflict is described as ongoing. Present tense. Lusteth — active. The two are contrary — opposed. This is not a conflict that gets resolved before Step 12 and then disappears. It is the lifelong reality of a person who is genuinely walking with God. The difference between Step 1 you and Step 12 you is not that the conflict stops. It is that you now know what you are fighting and you have tools — the Word the prayer the accountability the Spirit-directed decision — that you did not have before.

WHAT WALKING IN THE SPIRIT LOOKS LIKE IN PRACTICE

Morning: Before anything else — before the phone before the news before the day's demands — bring your mind to God. Read. Pray. Surrender the day. Decision-making: Before a significant decision — not just after the crisis — bring it to God. What does the Word say? What does wisdom say? What does the Spirit say when the flesh is quieted? Temptation moment: Recognize it while it is forming not after it has solidified. The Spirit gives awareness before the fall — but only if you are practiced enough in the walk to hear it. Confession same-day: When you miss — when the flesh wins a moment — do not defer the acknowledgment. Promptly. Today. Not to morrow. Community: Walking in the Spirit is not a solo exercise. You need people who are walking in the same direction who will tell you the truth when you are deceiving yourself. "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death." — Philippians 3:10 KJV To know Him — not know about Him. Personal. Daily. Specific. That is the goal of Step 11.

THE SABBATH — REST THAT POINTS TO THE SOUL'S TRUE HOME

"Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." — Exodus 20:8 KJV "And the evening and the morning were the first day." — Genesis 1:5 KJV God built rest into creation before sin entered it. Evening first — then morning. Rest before labor. The day begins in the stillness before it moves into the work. This is exactly opposite to how the addiction operated: take now, pay later. Consume first, collapse eventually. The world moved the Sabbath from the seventh day to the first — and called the inversion truth. This is the pattern: the world receives the things of God and inverts them, institutionalizes the inversion, and calls the original the error. The person walking in God's order learns to recognize the inversion everywhere — and return to the original design. But the Sabbath always pointed beyond the day of rest to something deeper. "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For we which have believed do enter into rest." — Hebrews 4:9,3 KJV The rest that remains is not a day on the calendar. It is the soul that has entered into God — no longer striving, performing, managing from self-sufficiency. The daily walk in the Spirit is the daily entering of that rest. The Sabbath was always the shadow. God Himself is the substance.

THE SWEPT HOUSE — EMPTY IS THE MOST DANGEROUS CONDITION

"When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest, and findeth none. Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished. Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first." — Matthew 12:43-45 KJV Swept and garnished. Clean. Ordered. Empty. Empty is the danger. The unclean spirit returns to an empty house and finds room for seven worse than itself. The cleaning is real. The sweeping happened. But nothing moved in to fill the vacancy. This is why Step 11 follows Step 7 rather than ending the program. The removal of the defects in Step 7 creates vacancy. The character work of Steps 8, 9, and 10 begins filling it. Step 11 — the daily seeking of God through prayer and the Word — is what fills the house permanently. Not with religious activity. With the presence of God actively sought, actively received, actively cultivated until there is no room for what was swept out. The person who works Steps 1 through 7 and then stops — who has the swept house without the filling — is in the most dangerous position in recovery. Cleaner than they were. More vulnerable than they know. What has moved in to fill what was swept out? Name it specifically. If the answer is not God actively sought and disciplines actively maintained — the house has vacancy. And the unclean spirit knows it.

RENEWAL IS DAILY — THE INWARD MAN THAT MUST BE RESTORED EVERY MORNING

"For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." — 2 Corinthians 4:16 KJV

Day by day. Not once. Not at the completion of the program. Not at the dramatic moment of transformation. Day by day — the consistent, daily, ongoing renewal of the inward man that does not stop being necessary because it happened yesterday. The outward man is perishing. This is the honest acknowledgment that the physical dimensions of life — the body, the circumstances, the external things — are subject to decay and loss. Recovery does not stop that process. It does not guarantee that the circumstances improve at the rate the change deserves. But the inward man is renewed. Present tense. Active. Continuing. The renewal of the mind that Romans 12:2 describes. The transformation that 2 Corinthians 3:18 produces through beholding. The daily bread of Step 11 that Matthew 4:4 names as the necessity of life. All of it is the daily renewal of the inward man — the part that lasts, the part that grows, the part that the outward man's perishing cannot reach. Faint not. The renewal is happening even when the outward circumstances do not reflect it. Even when the body is tired and the consequences are still present and the restoration has not yet appeared. The inward man is being renewed day by day. That renewal is the foundation of everything Step 11 is building. Go back to it to morrow. And the day after. Day by day.

GOD IS THE AUTHOR — SALVATION TO THOSE WHO OBEY

"And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him." — Hebrews 5:9 KJV Walking in the Spirit is the daily expression of a life that has obeyed the Author. The salvation God authored — including the fullness of His Spirit — was promised to those who obey. The Step 11 daily disciplines are the ongoing obedience of a person who has received what God offered and continues in the direction of that receiving. THE SPIRIT THAT DWELLS AND THE SPIRIT THAT GOVERNS "But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." — Romans 8:9 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Rome — drawing the clearest possible line between the life governed by the flesh and the life in which the Spirit of God genuinely dwells. The condition is a dwelling — not a visit, not an influence, not an acknowledgment, but the Spirit of God making the person His habitation. The question Paul raises — not rhetorically but as the governing condition of the passage — is: does the Spirit of God dwell in you? Jesus told Nicodemus that the wind blows where it will and thou hearest the sound thereof — so is every one that is born of the Spirit. The birth of the Spirit produces evidence that can be heard. The dwelling of the Spirit of God produces a life that is not governed by the flesh — not managed by effort, not sustained by sincerity, but governed by a Presence that has genuinely taken up residence. The program has cleared the ground. The ground that was cleared was not cleared for emptiness. It was cleared for a Presence. "No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." — 1 Corinthians 12:3 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Corinth — showing them that the confession of Jesus as Lord is not a verbal declaration that any person can produce at will. It is the declaration that the Holy Ghost makes possible —

the Spirit bearing witness to what the Spirit knows to be true, through the mouth of the person in whom He dwells. This is not a test to be administered. It is a description of what genuine indwelling produces. The person in whom the Spirit of God genuinely dwells does not struggle to confess Jesus as Lord. The Spirit does not bear a reluctant witness. He bears the witness He was given to bear — clearly, completely, with the same evidence that He produced on the day of Pentecost when the promise of the Father arrived. The question the daily walk raises, in the light of Romans 8:9 and 1 Corinthians 12:3, is not an accusation. It is the honest examination that Step 10 established as the daily posture: What is governing the life today? And what evidence does the governing Presence produce?

THE WITNESS — THE SPIRIT BEARING WITNESS WITH YOUR SPIRIT

"The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God." — Romans 8:16 KJV Paul wrote this to born-again believers in Rome — describing the internal confirmation that accompanies genuine reception of the Spirit. Not a doctrinal position only. A witness. The Spirit itself bearing witness with the person's spirit — producing the internal confirmation that the relationship is real. This is different from believing that the relationship is real. The person who believes on intellectual grounds has something real. The person in whom the Spirit bears witness has something more — the Spirit's own confirmation of what the believing points toward. Romans 8:15 adds: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." The witness is voiced. Something comes out — a cry, a confession, a voiced expression of the relationship that is not composed by the person but produced by the Spirit within. Walking in the Spirit — the daily posture that Step 11 L2 describes — is the life of a person in whom the Spirit dwells and bears witness. The daily walk maintains and deepens what the initial reception established. What did your reception establish? What does the honest answer to that question show?

GOD SURNAMES HIS PEOPLE — WALKING IN THE NAME

There is a word in Isaiah that rarely gets the attention it deserves.

"I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me." — Isaiah 45:4 KJV

God does not merely call His people. He surnames them. A surname is a family name placed upon a person by another — carrying identity, ownership, authority, belonging. It is not something the person earns or chooses. It is conferred. It rests upon them by the action of the one doing the conferring.

The question this raises for Step 11 is not abstract. The person who walks in the Spirit — the person this lesson is describing — is not walking in their own name. They are walking under a name that has been placed on them. The daily life of prayer and meditation and renewed mind is the daily practice of a person who has understood whose name they carry.

Across the whole of the Old Testament, the phrase "called by His name" is covenant language. It does not mean God is aware of you. It means His name rests upon you. You belong to Him. You bear His identity before all people.

"If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray..." — 2 Chronicles 7:14 KJV

The humbling of Step 7. The prayer of Step 11. They belong to the same sequence — the sequence of a person who understands whose name is upon them and lives accordingly.

What does it mean practically to walk in the Spirit under His name? It means that the daily life — the decisions, the relationships, the ordinary moments — is lived as a person who belongs to God. Not as a performance. Not as an image. But because the name has been placed, and the name carries authority.

"And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus." — Colossians 3:17 KJV

This is Step 11 lived. Every ordinary thing done in the name of the Lord Jesus. Not the extraordinary moments alone. The ordinary work of an ordinary day — done as a person who knows whose name they carry.

What name has been placed on you? And are you living as someone who knows it?

THE NAME IN WATER — WHAT CALLING ON HIS NAME MEANS

There is a phrase that runs through the Old Testament and finds its New Testament fulfillment in a specific act. It is worth tracing carefully.

"Then began men to call upon the name of the Lord." — Genesis 4:26 KJV

From that first reference, calling on the name of the Lord is consistently tied to altar, to sacrifice, to covenant response — not mere speech, but the invocation of God's authority through His revealed name.

Joel promises: "Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered." — Joel 2:32 KJV

Peter quotes this promise on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:21 KJV) — and then immediately defines what calling on the name means in the New Testament:

"Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins." — Acts 2:38 KJV

He does not leave calling on the name undefined. He gives it concrete form: baptism in the name of Jesus Christ. The name is invoked over the believer in the water.

Acts 22:16 KJV makes this explicit: "Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord." This is one action described two ways. To be baptized in Jesus name is to call on the name of the Lord. They are not two separate acts — they are one covenant act described from two angles.

The name of the Lord — the specific name, Jesus Christ — is the name that is placed on the believer in baptism. This is not symbolic language. It is the fulfillment of what Numbers 6:27 pointed toward from the beginning of the covenant: "They shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them."

The Old Testament placed God's name upon His people through the priestly blessing. The New Testament places God's name — Jesus — upon His people through baptism. The pattern holds. The blessing follows the name.

The question that naturally arises here deserves an honest answer: is the name specific, or is "Father, Son, and Holy Ghost" the formula? Matthew 28:19 commands baptism "in the name" — singular. Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are titles describing one God in three manifestations. The name that belongs to that title is Jesus. The apostles understood this immediately. Every recorded baptism in the book of Acts is performed in the name of Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus. Acts 2:38. Acts 8:16. Acts 10:48. Acts 19:5. Acts 22:16.

If the apostles disobeyed Matthew 28:19, the book of Acts is a record of error. It is not. The apostolic practice clarifies the command. The name is Jesus.

What do you notice about the consistency of this pattern across every account in Acts?

THE HOUSE OF OBED-EDOM — THE INDWELLING IN THE YIELDED HOUSE

"And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and said, How shall the ark of the LORD come to me? So David would not remove the ark of the LORD unto him into the city of David: but David carried it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of the LORD continued in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months: and the LORD blessed Obed-edom, and all his household." — 2 Samuel 6:9-11 KJV The name Obed-edom means servant of Edom — but his life tells the story of what happens to a house that receives the presence of God. When David could not bring the ark to Jerusalem — when the attempt had already gone wrong, when the presence of God seemed too dangerous for the careless approach — it was this man whose house became the dwelling place. Nothing is recorded about Obed-edom's qualifications. No great achievement is cited. No notable history precedes the moment. He was simply the man whose house was available, and who received what was brought to him without resistance. And the LORD blessed Obed-edom, and all his household.

The ark of the covenant represented the presence of God — the place where God dwelt among His people, the seat of His glory, the visible evidence that He had taken up residence with them. When it rested in Obed-edom's house, everything in the house came under the blessing of what was dwelling there. "And it was told king David, saying, The LORD hath blessed the house of Obed-edom, and all that pertaineth unto him, because of the ark of God." — 2 Samuel 6:12 KJV Because of the ark. The blessing came not from what Obed-edom did but from what was dwelling in the house. This is the picture of the Spirit-indwelt life. Not the life that has achieved enough to merit the blessing. The life that has been cleared — through the inventory, the confession, the amends, the surrender of Steps 1 through 10 — and is now available to receive what God brings to those who have prepared space for Him. The steps have been the preparation of the house. The house is not the destination. The house is what receives the Presence that is the destination. David did not bring the ark to Jerusalem until he had seen what it did in Obed-edom's house. The three months of blessing were the testimony that drew him. When the report reached him — the LORD has blessed everything in that house because of the ark — David made ready to bring what was dwelling there to where it was always meant to go. The person who receives the Spirit in this program carries that same testimony into Step 12. Not the report of what they achieved. The report of what came to dwell in them — and what it did when it arrived.

The pattern across the whole of Scripture is that those who drew near to God found that He drew near to them. Not as a formula — as a relationship. The seeking produced the encounter. The encounter produced the sustaining. The sustaining produced everything that followed.

THE EMMAUS ROAD — GOD WALKS WITH YOU IN THE CONFUSION

"And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus... And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him." — Luke 24:13-16 KJV The two disciples walking to Emmaus were walking in the wrong direction — away from Jerusalem, away from the community, away from what God was doing. They were talking about everything that had happened and they had not yet understood any of it. And Jesus joined them and walked with them the whole distance. He did not appear in a flash of light. He did not announce Himself. He walked beside them in their confusion, asked them questions, let them tell Him what they had seen and what they had lost. And then He opened the Scriptures to them — beginning at Moses and all the prophets — and something happened in their hearts before their eyes were opened: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" The burning came before the recognition. The presence was real before it was understood. The person walking in Step 11 — learning to recognize the voice of God in the daily life, learning to distinguish the burning of genuine encounter from the noise of everything else — is on the Emmaus road. God walks beside the person who does not yet fully see Him. The recognition comes. It comes in the breaking of the bread — in the specific moment of genuine encounter — and they knew Him. And He vanished from their sight because they no longer needed the external evidence. The burning had already confirmed what the eyes now knew.

The person who genuinely seeks God finds that the seeking itself is answered. Not always immediately. Not always dramatically. But the pattern of Scripture is clear: draw nigh to God, and He will draw nigh to thee. The daily posture of drawing near is the posture of a person who has understood who they are and who God is.

The person sustained by prayer and contact in this step is ready to carry the message. Step 12 is the reason all eleven steps preceded it.

There is a provision at the end of this road that does not depend on human effort to sustain it. Every step from 1 through 10 has been preparation — not for a better version of the old life, but for the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus. The Spirit who enters does not come as one gift among many. He comes as the one who makes all that follows possible.

TEACHER NOTES

Step 11 Lesson 2 MEMBER LESSON. This lesson should feel like practical wisdom not spiritual performance. The goal is to help students build a sustainable daily rhythm — not to create pressure for peak spiritual experiences. GALATIANS 5:16: Walk in the Spirit. Emphasis on walk — not run not achieve. Ask students: what does walking in the Spirit look like differently than running a spiritual sprint? Walking implies consistency over intensity. Recovery is built on consistency. lessons.readingPlan:
Week 43 Day 1 — Acts 2:1-41 Read the Pentecost account carefully. Jesus had said the promise of the Father would come with power. What happened that could be heard? What did Peter say this was? What was the response of the crowd — and what three things did Peter tell them to do?
