APPENDIX A

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT WINE AND STRONG DRINK A Study for Teachers, Mentors, and Graduates

WHY THIS STUDY EXISTS

Every teacher and mentor who graduates from this program will encounter the same objection — from people in the field, from family members, from sincere believers who have been told that the Bible condones moderate drinking. The argument is common enough that it deserves a thorough answer. This study is that answer.
It is not offered as a debate tool. It is offered as a careful examination of what the Scripture actually says — with the same honesty the inventory required, and the same precision the hermeneutics of this curriculum demands.
The goal is not to win an argument. It is to give the person who asks the question an honest account of what the Word of God teaches.

THE FIRST PRINCIPLE: SCRIPTURE INTERPRETS SCRIPTURE

"All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." — 2 Timothy 3:16 KJV Every passage about wine in the Scripture must be understood in light of every other passage about wine. The person who reads Ecclesiastes 9:7 — "drink thy wine with a merry heart" — without reading Proverbs 23:29-32 — "at the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder" — has read half of what the Scripture says and drawn a conclusion from the half that suited them.
The honest approach reads all of it. And when all of it is read carefully, a consistent and important distinction emerges.

TWO KINDS OF WINE — THE DISTINCTION THE SCRIPTURE MAKES

The single most important fact for understanding the Bible's teaching on wine is this: in the original languages, one word is used for two very different things.
In Hebrew, the primary word for wine is yayin. It appears in passages that commend wine and in passages that condemn wine — because it encompasses both fermented and unfermented grape juice. Similarly, tirosh refers to the juice of grapes before or in the early process of production — sometimes translated as new wine or corn. The Greek word oinos in the New Testament carries the same range. A single word, two very different substances.
Fermented wine contains alcohol — the product of sugar decomposition through the process of fermentation.
Unfermented wine — the fresh-pressed juice of the grape, or juice preserved through boiling, filtration, or other ancient methods — contains none. The distinction is not one invented by modern temperance movements. It is documented thoroughly in ancient historical sources. Pliny, writing in the first century, describes methods of preserving grape juice from fermentation, and notes that wine preserved this way remained sweet and of superior quality. Jewish sources confirm that unfermented wine was considered the finer product and was specifically used

in sacred contexts.
This distinction is essential. When the Scripture commends wine, it is commending the wholesome fruit of the vine. When it condemns wine, it is condemning the fermented version that produces intoxication, dependency, and the damage that this entire curriculum exists to address.

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE COMMENDS — AND WHY

"He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man; that he may bring forth food out of the earth; and wine that maketh glad the heart of man." — Psalm 104:14-15 KJV The wine described here is presented alongside grass, herbs, and oil — the natural products of the earth.
Fermented wine is not a natural product of the earth. It is the product of decay — of sugar decomposing through a process that produces a substance that exists in no plant as God made it. Alcohol is not found in any growing thing. It is produced when the growing thing begins to break down. The wine that gladdens the heart in Psalm 104 is the fruit of the vine as God made it — wholesome, refreshing, and described by travelers throughout antiquity as having uniquely restorative properties when consumed fresh and cool.
"Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." — 1 Timothy 5:23 KJV This verse is the most commonly misused in the discussion of alcohol. Two observations are critical.
First: the fact that Paul had to tell Timothy to drink wine at all proves that Timothy was not in the habit of drinking it. A man who regularly consumed wine would need no such instruction. Timothy was, by all available evidence, a total abstainer who required specific guidance to depart from that practice for a medicinal purpose.
Second: what Paul recommended was what would be good for Timothy's stomach. Ancient medical writers — Athenaeus among them — specifically recommended sweet, unfermented wine for stomach complaints.
Fermented wine, by contrast, was recognized by physicians of the same era as damaging to the stomach, producing among its effects the very gastric complaints Timothy was suffering from. Paul's recommendation was for the medicine that would help — which was the unfermented juice of the grape, widely used as a digestive tonic in the ancient world.
Note also: Paul wrote in the same letter that leaders must not be given to wine (1 Timothy 3:3). He would not tell Timothy to consume the very substance he had just disqualified leaders from using. The consistency of the instruction confirms that what Paul recommended was not fermented.

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE CONDEMNS — WITHOUT QUALIFICATION

"Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise." — Proverbs 20:1 KJV The word translated mocker carries the sense of one who deceives — who promises what it does not ultimately deliver. The person in recovery who arrived here after years of the substance promising relief that always required more, and always eventually took more than it gave, has lived this verse. The mocker delivered — temporarily, partially, and at increasing cost — and the person following it ended in exactly the place Proverbs describes.

"Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder." — Proverbs 23:29-32 KJV This is the most complete clinical description of alcohol use disorder in any ancient text. Woe. Sorrow.
Contentions — the relational destruction. Babbling — the loss of coherent communication. Wounds without cause — the physical consequences the person cannot account for. Redness of eyes — the physical evidence visible to others. And then: the deceptive beauty of it in the cup, the pleasurable appearance that precedes the serpent's bite.
Every person who has worked the inventory of Step 4 has named what Proverbs 23 describes. The Scripture is not condemning a peripheral vice. It is describing, with extraordinary precision, the central experience of the person this curriculum serves.
"Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!" — Isaiah 5:11 KJV
"Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to him, and makest him drunken also." — Habakkuk 2:15 KJV The woe in Habakkuk belongs not only to the person who drinks but to the person who enables the drinking — who puts the bottle to another person's lips. The teacher or mentor who treats the "but the Bible allows wine" argument as acceptable cover for a person in recovery who wants permission to drink has given them the bottle.
This study exists in part so that no teacher or mentor who graduates from this program does that.

THE QUESTION OF JESUS AND WINE

The two passages most commonly cited to argue that Jesus approved of fermented wine are His first miracle at Cana (John 2) and His participation at the Passover supper. Both deserve careful attention.
At Cana, Jesus turned water into wine. The master of the feast declared it the best wine — better than what had been served earlier. The argument is that this proves Jesus created alcoholic wine, and therefore alcohol carries His endorsement.
Several things undermine this argument.
First: the wine that was produced was the direct work of creation — water becoming what the vine produces. The vine produces unfermented juice. Fermentation requires time and the presence of yeast and the decomposition of sugar. Jesus did not create a product of decomposition. He created what the vine would have produced — the pure juice of the grape, in the moment of its creation.
Second: the testimony of ancient Jewish sources is consistent that unfermented wine was considered the superior product. When the master of the feast declared the wine excellent, he was describing precisely the quality that the ancients attributed to unfermented wine. The best wine, by the standards of the Jewish world Jesus inhabited, was the wine that had not fermented.

Third: the quantity is decisive for anyone who reads carefully. The six water pots held between 27 and 30 gallons each — a total of more than 160 gallons. If Jesus created this quantity of fermented wine for guests who had already been drinking, He was providing enough alcohol to produce severe intoxication in a large gathering. No honest reading of the character of Jesus — the One who said the thief comes to steal, kill, and destroy — produces the conclusion that He manufactured mass quantities of an intoxicating substance for an already-drinking crowd.
At the Passover supper, Jesus took the cup and called it the fruit of the vine. The Passover requirements under the Law of Moses excluded all fermented substances from the feast — not only leavened bread but all fermented things. If leavened bread was forbidden because leaven represents corruption, the same principle applied to fermented wine. The blood of the sinless Lamb of God was not symbolized by a product of decomposition and corruption. Jesus called it the fruit of the vine — the precise phrase used for fresh, unfermented grape juice throughout the Jewish tradition.

THE 1 TIMOTHY 5:23 CLARIFICATION ON MODERATION ARGUMENTS

Some argue that passages like "not given to much wine" (1 Timothy 3:8, Titus 2:3) imply that some wine is acceptable, with only excess condemned. This argument fails on examination.
If the principle were that any amount of a harmful substance is acceptable as long as it does not reach excess, the same logic would apply to every substance the Scripture warns against. The principle the Scripture actually teaches is that any degree of indulgence in what produces sin is wrong — not because the amount is the problem, but because the nature of the substance is the problem. A little arsenic is not safe because it is a little. A little of what mocker's the soul, rages in the belly, and bites like a serpent is not made safe by quantity management.
Furthermore: the person who has recovered from addiction and the person who is vulnerable to addiction are not the right test cases for moderate use. Romans 14:21 addresses exactly this: "It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak." The stronger brother's liberty does not extend to placing what was bondage for the weaker brother back within their reach. The teacher or mentor who invokes personal liberty in this context has misread both the Scripture and their responsibility.

THE BODY AS THE TEMPLE

"What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." — 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 KJV The person who has received the Holy Ghost — whose body is now the temple of the Spirit of God — is not working with a body that belongs to them alone. The alcohol that damaged the liver, degraded the brain, and progressively weakened the body was being applied to the temple of God. The recovery from that damage is itself an act of stewardship — bringing the temple back toward the condition in which the Spirit who dwells there is honored by the vessel He inhabits.
No argument for moderate alcohol consumption survives the honest application of 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 to the life of a person who has come through this program. The body is the temple. What is brought into the temple matters. And what this program has walked the person away from does not belong in the temple under any quantity justification.

A SUMMARY FOR TEACHERS AND MENTORS

When the person you are serving raises the "but the Bible allows wine" argument, the answer is not a debate. It is a question: which wine? The Bible commends the wholesome fruit of the vine and condemns the fermented substance that produces what Proverbs 23 describes. The same Scripture that says "drink thy wine with a merry heart" also says "at the last it biteth like a serpent." Both are true. The question is which one is being discussed.
The person in recovery who is looking for biblical permission to drink has found what they were looking for before they opened the Scripture. The Scripture requires an honest reader who comes to the text willing to receive what it actually says — not what they need it to say to justify what they have already decided.
The honest reading, as this study has shown, produces one conclusion: the Scripture commends the wholesome fruit of the vine and condemns the fermented version that has already demonstrated its effects in the life of the person sitting across from you. There is no biblical permission for the person in recovery to drink. There is a clear biblical call to sobriety, vigilance, and the stewardship of the body in which the Spirit dwells.
"Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour." — 1 Peter 5:8 KJV The sober person is the person the adversary cannot reach through the avenue he has already used. Sobriety is not only a recovery discipline. It is a spiritual posture — the maintenance of the clear mind and the alert spirit that the enemy cannot exploit. This program calls people to that posture. This study gives them the scriptural grounding to maintain it when the argument is made that the Bible says otherwise.
It does not. Read honestly and completely, it says the opposite.

APPENDIX B

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE SAYS ABOUT THE BODY, DEFILEMENT, AND SUBSTANCES THAT HARM IT A Study on Smoking, Vaping, and the Stewardship of the Temple — For Teachers, Mentors, and Graduates

WHY THIS STUDY EXISTS

The question comes in several forms. Sometimes it is direct: does the Bible say anything about smoking?
Sometimes it arrives as an objection to accountability: I do not drink, so what does it matter if I smoke?
Sometimes it comes from a person who has addressed one bondage and has not yet recognized that another one remained — or was taken up in its place.
Tobacco and nicotine are not named in Scripture. Vaping did not exist in the ancient world. And because neither is specifically prohibited by name, some conclude that the Scripture has nothing to say about them.
That conclusion reflects a misunderstanding of how Scripture works. The Scripture does not function as a list of prohibited substances to be updated with each century's new products. It establishes principles — about the body, about stewardship, about bondage, about what belongs to God — that apply to every substance in every era. This study traces those principles and shows how they apply to tobacco, nicotine, and any substance used to alter the body's state in ways that damage it and produce dependency.

THE FOUNDATIONAL PRINCIPLE: THE BODY BELONGS TO GOD

"What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." — 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 KJV This is the governing passage for every question about what a born-again believer does with their body. The body is not the person's own. It was bought — at a price that the cross defines. It is the temple of the Holy Ghost — the dwelling place of the Spirit of God. And the instruction that follows from this reality is not a suggestion: glorify God in your body.
The temple of God in the Old Testament was maintained with extraordinary care. No defilement was permitted.
No corruption was introduced. The priests were held to a higher standard of bodily purity than the general population precisely because they served in the house of God. The new covenant does not lower that standard. It extends it — to every person in whose body the Spirit dwells.
What is introduced into the body of a born-again believer is introduced into the temple of the Holy Ghost. That is not a rhetorical point. It is a covenant reality. Tobacco smoke introduced into the lungs is introduced into the temple. Nicotine — which produces dependency, elevates heart rate, damages blood vessels, and has been identified by medical consensus as a primary contributor to lung cancer, heart disease, and stroke — is introduced into the temple.

The question is not whether the Scripture names the substance. The question is whether the substance defiles the temple. The answer, for tobacco and nicotine in any delivery form, is not in dispute.
"If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." — 1 Corinthians 3:17 KJV The severity of this language is not accidental. Paul uses the word destroy — the same word used for the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. The defilement of the temple of God is treated as a matter of the gravest consequence. The person who introduces what damages into the place where God dwells is not making a neutral personal choice. They are making a decision about the temple.

THE SECOND PRINCIPLE: BONDAGE AND THE PERSON BOUGHT WITH A PRICE

"All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any." — 1 Corinthians 6:12 KJV Paul writes this to born-again believers in Corinth — establishing the principle of spiritual liberty alongside the principle of spiritual bondage. Liberty in Christ is real. The new covenant believer is not under the Law with its specific prohibitions. But liberty does not extend to being brought under the power of anything. The person who cannot stop smoking is under the power of nicotine. The person who reaches for the vape before they reach for the Word is under a governing authority that is not God.
This is not a peripheral concern for people in recovery. It is the central concern. This entire program has been the process of identifying and addressing what has held governing power over the life. To address one form of bondage while accepting another because it is legal, or common, or not specifically named in a list of prohibited substances, is to misunderstand what recovery actually means.
The body that was bought with a price is not to be brought under the power of any substance. The word power in this passage is the same root used elsewhere for authority and governing control. Nicotine produces chemical dependency — the alteration of the brain's reward system in ways that make cessation physically painful and psychologically difficult. That is bondage. It may be a socially acceptable bondage. It is bondage.

THE PHARMACOLOGICAL REALITY — WHAT THE SUBSTANCE ACTUALLY DOES

The honest study of tobacco and nicotine produces findings that the Scripture's framework for the body addresses directly.
Nicotine is one of the most addictive substances known. It acts on the same neurological reward pathways as many controlled substances — producing dopamine release that the brain begins to require for normal function.
The physical dependency it creates is not meaningfully different in mechanism from the dependencies this program addresses. The difference is in legal status and social acceptance — not in what it does to the body or the will.
Tobacco smoke contains more than seven thousand chemical compounds. Hundreds are toxic. Dozens are identified carcinogens — substances that damage the DNA of cells in ways that produce cancer. The lungs, the throat, the mouth, the esophagus, the bladder, the kidneys, the pancreas, the cervix — all carry elevated cancer risk with sustained tobacco use. Heart disease and stroke — the leading causes of death in nations with high tobacco use rates — are directly linked to smoking and to the vascular damage nicotine produces even without

combustion.
Vaping — the delivery of nicotine through aerosolized liquid — was introduced to the market with the claim that it was a safer alternative to combustion. That claim has not survived careful examination. The aerosolized particles produced by vaping devices penetrate the deep lung in ways that produce inflammatory damage. Several compounds used in vaping liquids have been identified as pulmonary toxins. And the nicotine delivered is in many cases at higher concentrations than traditional cigarettes — producing faster and stronger dependency, particularly in younger users.
The person who has read this far through this curriculum and recognized that their body is the temple of the Holy Ghost has sufficient information to reach their own conclusion about whether these substances belong in the temple.

THE DEFILEMENT PRINCIPLE ACROSS SCRIPTURE

"Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God." — 2 Corinthians 7:1 KJV Paul writes this to born-again believers — calling them to active, ongoing cleansing from all filthiness of the flesh. Not some filthiness. All. The cleansing is not only spiritual — it includes the flesh. The body. The physical vessel in which the Spirit dwells.
The word filthiness here carries the sense of that which contaminates — that which, introduced into the clean vessel, diminishes its cleanness. Every person in this program has engaged in the process of removing what contaminated the inner life — through the inventory, the confession, the amends, the surrender. The same principle applied to the body produces the same question: what has been introduced into the physical vessel that the Spirit inhabits, and what does the commitment to holiness require about it?
"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." — 1 Corinthians 10:31 KJV The scope of this instruction is total. Whatever you do — not whatever you do in the formal categories of religious activity, but whatever: eating, drinking, every bodily act and habit. All of it is to be done to the glory of God. The honest application of this verse to the habit of smoking or vaping produces a question every person must answer for themselves: does this glorify God in my body?
The question is not rhetorical. It requires an honest answer.

THE STUMBLING BLOCK PRINCIPLE

"It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak." — Romans 14:21 KJV The teacher or mentor who smokes is not only making a decision about their own body. They are making a decision about the people who will observe them and draw conclusions about what recovery and covenant life produce. The person in early recovery who sees a leader smoke receives a message — not the intended one, but the received one: that one form of chemical dependency is acceptable while others are not. The distinctions the flesh will make from that observation are predictable.

The stumbling block principle of Romans 14 applies here as it applies to alcohol: the stronger person's liberty does not extend to placing what harms the weaker person within their reach. The person who used tobacco and nicotine as a coping mechanism — as a way of managing stress, anxiety, or boredom — is likely to find that those same triggers are present in early recovery. The leader who smokes in front of them has not helped them.

THE RECOVERY CONNECTION — TOBACCO AS TRANSFER ADDICTION

One of the most consistent patterns in the addiction recovery field is transfer addiction — the replacement of one substance or behavior with another when the first is removed. The person who stops using alcohol may increase tobacco use. The person who stops using opioids may dramatically increase nicotine consumption. The transfer feels like progress because one problem has been addressed. It is not progress. It is the same governing dynamic — the same use of a substance to manage what has not yet been surrendered — applied to a different substance.
This curriculum has addressed the root of the addicted life: the flesh seeking comfort, relief, and escape in things that are not God. Tobacco and nicotine serve exactly the same function for many people that alcohol, opioids, and other substances served — they manage the edge, reduce the anxiety, provide the ritual comfort of the regular dose. The root is the same root. The substance is different.
The person who has completed Step 6 — who has examined what the defects are and become entirely ready for God to remove them — has the theological and practical framework to recognize that the governing dynamic behind tobacco use is the same dynamic the program addresses. The question is whether the Step 6 examination included it.

THE COVENANT CALL TO STEWARDSHIP

"I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service." — Romans 12:1 KJV A living sacrifice. Not a damaged vessel offered because that is all that is left. A holy sacrifice — set apart, clean, maintained in the condition that honors the One it is offered to. The word reasonable here means logical, rational, fitting — the natural conclusion of understanding what the body actually is and to whom it belongs.
The person who has received the Holy Ghost and understands that their body is now the temple of God has a rational, logical, fitting obligation to present that body in the best condition they can maintain. That is not legalism. That is the reasonable service of a person who understands what they have received and in whom it dwells.
Every year of tobacco use produces measurable, documented damage to the vessels, the lungs, the heart, and the DNA of the cells in the temple. The cessation of that use allows documented recovery of lung function, cardiovascular health, and reduced cancer risk. The body that was bought with a price can, when the substance is removed, move toward the condition in which it was intended to be offered.

A SUMMARY FOR TEACHERS AND MENTORS

When the person you are serving raises the question of smoking or vaping — whether as a genuine inquiry or as a defense of a habit they do not want examined — the answer is not found in a list of prohibited substances. It is found in the principles the Scripture establishes about the body.

The body belongs to God. It was bought with a price. It is the temple of the Holy Ghost. What is introduced into it is introduced into the temple. The substance that produces dependency has brought the person under its power — which the Scripture directly addresses as incompatible with the liberty of the person bought with a price. And the habit that cannot be done to the glory of God falls under the scope of 1 Corinthians 10:31.
This is not the condemnation of the person who smokes. Many people in recovery carry this habit and are genuinely walking the road in every other area. But the honest application of the Scripture to the body — the same honesty the inventory required in every other area — reaches smoking and vaping as surely as it reaches alcohol. The temple principle does not have a smoking section.
The invitation is the same one this program has extended at every step: not condemnation, but honest examination. What is in the temple that was not placed there by God? And what does the commitment to holiness in the body require about it?
"Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost?" — 1 Corinthians 6:18-19 KJV Every sin against the body is a sin against the temple. That is the principle. The substance that is named changes with each generation. The principle does not.

APPENDIX C

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE SAYS ABOUT THE TONGUE, CURSING, AND THE WORDS WE SPEAK A Detailed Study for Teachers, Mentors, and Graduates

WHY THIS STUDY EXISTS

Profanity is the last habit most people in recovery examine. It is rarely included in the inventory. It does not appear on the amends list. It is seldom brought to the mentor relationship. And yet the Scripture devotes more sustained attention to the tongue than to almost any other aspect of human behavior — not because words are the most important thing, but because what comes out of the mouth is the most reliable indicator of what governs the inner life.
This study does not exist to produce guilt about specific words. It exists to give the teacher, mentor, and graduate a thorough account of what the Scripture says — and more importantly, why it says it. The goal is not compliance with a list of forbidden words. It is the honest examination of what the pattern of speech reveals about what actually governs the heart — which is precisely the kind of examination this curriculum has been requiring from the first lesson.

THE GOVERNING PASSAGE: THE TONGUE AND THE HEART

"For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh. A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things: and an evil man out of the evil treasure bringeth forth evil things." — Matthew 12:34-35 KJV Jesus said this to the Pharisees — who were scrupulous about their religious behavior and careless about their words. The principle is direct: what comes out of the mouth is reporting on what is in the heart. The mouth is not the problem. The heart is the problem. The mouth is only the evidence.
Every person who has worked through the inventory of Step 4 has engaged in an examination of what has been living in the inner life. The language that comes out consistently — in private, when no one is listening, when pressure comes, when things go wrong — is one of the most reliable pieces of evidence available about the state of the inner life that the inventory was examining.
The person who curses freely and habitually in private, in front of family, in moments of frustration, has a mouth that is reporting on a heart that has not yet fully come under the governance of the Spirit. This is not condemnation. It is the application of Jesus' own diagnostic principle to the honest examination this program requires.

THE TONGUE CANNOT BE TAMED BY HUMAN EFFORT

"For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison." — James 3:7-8 KJV

James writes this to born-again believers — people who have received the Spirit — and tells them that the tongue cannot be tamed by human effort. This is the most important thing to understand before the study proceeds: the solution to profanity and corrupt speech is not willpower, not word-substitution, not the cultivation of self-discipline in the area of language.
The same ceiling on human effort that Step 1 identified applies specifically and intensively to the tongue. James has just told us that every kind of creature that walks, flies, crawls, or swims has been tamed by human beings — and then says the tongue has not been. Cannot be. By the same effort that tamed everything else.
This points — as the entire curriculum has pointed — toward the necessity of a governing authority that comes from outside the person. The tongue that is genuinely governed is the tongue of a person whose heart has been changed at the source, whose inner life is being governed by the Spirit, whose words are flowing from a different abundance than the one the flesh filled the heart with across years of unexamined living.
The recovery application is direct: the person who is trying to stop cursing through willpower — monitoring words, substituting expressions, practicing self-correction — is working on the surface of a problem that lives much deeper. The tongue is the evidence. The heart is the location.

THE DEADLY POISON — WHAT THE TONGUE PRODUCES

"Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell." — James 3:5-6 KJV The imagery James uses is total and deliberate. The tongue is a fire. A world of iniquity. It defiles the whole body. It sets on fire the entire course of nature — the normal trajectory of a life, a relationship, a community. And it is set on fire of hell — the language is as strong as Scripture gets short of judgment passages.
The person in recovery who examines the damage their words have done across years of active addiction often finds that the damage their tongue produced outlasted the damage the substance produced. Relationships that might have survived the behavior were ended by what was said in the behavior. Children who might have been able to process the addiction carry specific words — spoken in anger, in contempt, in cruelty — that marked them in ways the substance alone would not have. The fire of the tongue, James says, defiles the whole body and sets on fire the entire course of what would otherwise have been.
The amends list of Step 9 for many people includes specific words spoken to specific people in specific moments.
Words that cannot be unspoken. The harm of the tongue belongs in the inventory.

WHAT THE SCRIPTURE SPECIFICALLY CALLS CORRUPT SPEECH

"Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers." — Ephesians 4:29 KJV Paul writes this to born-again believers at Ephesus — describing the standard for speech that flows from a life genuinely governed by the Spirit. The word corrupt here is sapros — the same word used for a rotten tree or spoiled fruit. Speech that is corrupt is speech that produces rot rather than life. It is speech that, when it lands on the person who hears it, leaves something worse than it found.

The positive standard Paul sets alongside the negative is equally important: not the absence of corrupt speech, but the presence of speech that ministers grace to the hearers. The goal is not words that avoid damage. It is words that carry grace — that leave the person who receives them better than they were before the words arrived.
This is a high standard. It is the standard of a person whose heart is full of the treasure that Jesus described — the good treasure out of which good things come. And it is a standard that is impossible to meet by effort at the level of the words. It requires the treasure to change first.
"But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth." — Colossians 3:8 KJV Paul lists filthy communication — aischrologia in Greek, literally shameful speaking — alongside anger, wrath, malice, and blasphemy. These are not peripheral habits the mature believer can keep while surrendering the more serious ones. They are listed together as things to be put off — removed as a garment that no longer fits the person wearing it. The person who has put on the new man (verse 10) no longer wears the speech patterns of the old one.
"But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks." — Ephesians 5:3-4 KJV The phrase not once named among you — applied to categories of sin including filthiness and foolish talking — sets an extraordinarily high standard. Not occasionally named. Not named with decreasing frequency. Not named except in moments of genuine stress. Not once. The standard is the absence of these things from the community of genuine covenant believers. Paul is describing what the Spirit-governed life looks like from the outside: a community whose speech is so consistently marked by grace and thanksgiving that the categories of corrupt speech are genuinely absent.

PROFANITY AND BLASPHEMY — THE SPECIFIC CATEGORIES

"Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain." — Exodus 20:7 KJV The third commandment. The word vain means empty, worthless, without substance — to carry the name of God in a way that empties it of its meaning, weight, and holiness. The casual use of God's name — as an expletive, as a filler word, as an expression of surprise or frustration — is the precise behavior the commandment addresses.
The name of God is treated as carrying no more weight than any other word. It is made vain.
For the person who has traced the Name thread through this curriculum — who understands that the name of God is identity, authority, covenant belonging — the use of that name as an expletive is not a minor linguistic habit. It is the treatment of the most excellent name as though it were nothing. The name above every name, used as a throwaway.
The same applies to the name of Jesus — spoken as a curse by people who have not considered what they are doing, or by people in recovery who have not yet examined this area. The name in which there is salvation, in which baptism is administered, in which the entire covenant culminates, spoken as the expression of frustration or contempt.

The New Testament does not change the standard of the third commandment. It deepens it. The name is now more fully revealed, more specifically identified, more loaded with covenant meaning than it was at Sinai. To take it in vain is not less serious in the new covenant. It is more.

COARSE LANGUAGE AND THE CHARACTER OF THE SPEAKER

Beyond the specific issue of blasphemy, the Scripture addresses the broader pattern of coarse, crude, and corrupt language as a character issue — not merely a social one.
"But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment. For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned." — Matthew 12:36-37 KJV Idle words — argos in Greek: ineffective, worthless, producing nothing of value. The scope of the accountability Jesus describes is not limited to lies or blasphemies. It extends to every word that is idle — every word spoken without purpose, without care, without regard for what it produces in the person who receives it.
The person in recovery has already discovered that words matter. Words spoken in the years of active addiction left marks that the inventory named and the amends addressed. The accountability Jesus describes does not wait until judgment — it is operating in every relationship, every family, every community where the words are landing. The idle word is not neutral. It is either building or decaying. There is no in-between.
"A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." — Proverbs 15:1 KJV Grievous words — harsh, cutting, coarse — produce a specific effect: they stir up anger. In families. In communities. In the person who speaks them as well as the person who receives them. The person in recovery who uses profanity freely in their household is regularly introducing a trigger into the environment — a tone, a texture, a kind of speech that produces a particular atmospheric condition. Children raised in an environment of profanity carry a different relationship to language and to the people around them than children raised in an environment of grace-filled speech. The fire of the tongue, James said, sets on fire the course of nature.

THE DOUBLE FOUNTAIN — WHY THE INCONSISTENCY MATTERS

"Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter? Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs? so can no fountain both yield salt water and fresh. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be." — James 3:11-10 KJV James uses two natural illustrations: a fountain that cannot produce both sweet and bitter water, and trees that cannot produce the fruit of a different species. Then he applies both to the mouth: out of the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
The person who prays earnestly in the morning and curses freely by noon has a double fountain. The inconsistency is not primarily a character flaw — it is a diagnostic. The fountain that produces both sweet and bitter water has a source that is not yet fully governed. The sweet water is real. The bitter is also real. Both are coming from the same inner place.

James does not condemn the person for the inconsistency. He does say it ought not so to be — and the ought implies both that it currently is and that it should not remain. The double fountain is the honest description of where many people in recovery find themselves: genuinely changed in significant areas, genuinely unchanged in others. The tongue is often one of the last areas surrendered because it is one of the last areas examined.

THE REPLACEMENT PRINCIPLE — WHAT TAKES THE PLACE OF CORRUPT SPEECH

"Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man." — Colossians 4:6 KJV The goal is not the absence of corrupt speech. The goal is the presence of its replacement — speech that is characterized by grace, seasoned with salt. Salt in the ancient world preserved. Speech that is seasoned with salt preserves what it touches — it does not accelerate the rot. It does not inflame what could be calm. It does not leave the person who receives it worse than it found them.
"Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." — Ephesians 5:19 KJV The overflow of a heart full of gratitude and praise is a mouth full of gratitude and praise. This is not a requirement to speak in religious language at all times. It is a description of what the heart that is genuinely full of the Spirit produces in speech — naturally, without effort, as the overflow of what is stored in the abundance of the heart.
The person who is struggling with profanity and corrupt speech is not primarily struggling with a language problem. They are struggling with a fullness problem. The heart is not yet full enough of what the Spirit puts there to overflow consistently in the kind of speech Colossians 4:6 describes. The solution is not word-monitoring. It is the deepening of what the heart is full of.
"Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer." — Psalm 19:14 KJV David's prayer connects the words of the mouth directly to the meditation of the heart — because they are connected. The heart mediates on what the mouth speaks from. The prayer that asks for acceptable words is also asking for a heart whose meditation produces them. Both — word and thought, mouth and heart — are placed before God for His governance.
This is the prayer of a person who has recognized that the tongue is not the problem. The heart is the problem.
And the God who sees the heart, who searches the thoughts and the intents, is the One who can do what no human effort can: produce the clean heart that the clean mouth will overflow from.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION FOR RECOVERY

The teacher or mentor who addresses profanity and coarse language in the people they serve should do so through the same diagnostic lens the entire curriculum uses. Not: here is the list of words you should not say. But: what is the mouth reporting about the heart? And what does the pattern of speech show about what is actually governing the inner life?
Four questions for honest examination:

First: what does your speech sound like when you are alone? Not in the meeting. Not in front of the mentor. In the car. In the house by yourself. In the moment when something goes wrong and no one else is present. The private speech is the most reliable report on the state of the inner life.
Second: what comes out under pressure? James 3:6 says the tongue sets on fire the course of nature — the normal trajectory of events. What does your tongue do when the trajectory goes wrong? What comes out when the frustration spills? That is the abundance of the heart that Jesus described.
Third: what does your speech do to the people who receive it? Does it minister grace to the hearers, as Ephesians 4:29 describes? Or does it leave the person worse than it found them? The test of speech is not whether it felt honest or expressive. The test is what it produced in the one who received it.
Fourth: is there a double fountain? Is the speech in one context — prayer, worship, ministry — genuinely different from the speech in another context in a way that reveals two different sources rather than one consistently governed one? The double fountain is not a failure. It is a location — the honest identification of where the remaining work is.
The person who can answer these four questions honestly has the information they need. The answer to what they find is not a program of linguistic self-improvement. It is the same answer the entire curriculum points toward: the heart surrendered more fully to the Spirit who governs it, the fullness of the inner life deepened until the overflow changes — not because the words were disciplined but because the source was transformed.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." — Psalm 51:10 KJV The clean heart produces the clean mouth. The right spirit produces the right words. Both are the work of God in the person who has brought the tongue — and the heart it reports on — to Him for the same examination this program has applied to every other area of the life.

"Walk it out faithfully."
